The factory's GitHub credential is likewise self-contained and
tenant-scoped (the github-app-auth design record, Pillars 1 and 2).
Every automated GitHub operation on the dispatch path — the
in-container fresh clones, the in-sandbox PR leg, the merge-poll, the
post-merge refresh — MUST authenticate with a GitHub App INSTALLATION
TOKEN minted from the App environment (`GITHUB_APP_ID` +
`GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY`, optional `GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_ID` /
`GITHUB_API_URL`) that the dispatch TARGET's own configured
`credential_wrapper` injects; no dispatch path reads a fleet PAT (the
retired `LIVESPEC_FAMILY_GITHUB_TOKEN`). Resolution is FAIL-CLOSED:
when the App environment is absent and the target repo has no
`credential_wrapper` to re-exec through, the dispatch MUST refuse with
an actionable diagnostic — it MUST NOT fall through to a fleet
credential or an ambient `gh` login. The fleet is adopter #0: an
adopter's dispatch target injects its own App through its own wrapper
the same way, so neither preflight nor dispatch carries a fleet-secret
prerequisite.

Token acquisition MUST be re-mintable at any time (first-class remint):
the Dispatcher holds a caching installation-token provider that
re-mints before the roughly one-hour token expiry, and it MUST resolve
a currently-valid token for every subprocess it spawns — never a
once-at-start export — so operations that outlive a single token's
validity (for example a seventy-plus-minute merge-poll) survive
transparently. The sandbox environment table receives an EPHEMERAL
freshly-minted installation token; the durable App private key and any
long-lived personal access token MUST NOT be projected into the
sandbox.

**The dispatch credential set.** A dispatch TARGET's configured
`credential_wrapper` MUST inject the FULL per-dispatch credential set:
the GitHub App environment (`GITHUB_APP_ID` + `GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY`,
optional `GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_ID`), the tenant work-items store
secret (`BEADS_DOLT_PASSWORD` on the beads substrate), AND the engine
LLM credential (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` today; the variable is
engine-specific by nature). Every credential-consuming seam on the
dispatch path MUST fail closed naming the specific missing variable,
and every such diagnostic MUST name the dispatch TARGET's own
configured `credential_wrapper` — never a fleet wrapper — as the
corrective injection path. The full required set is surfaced up front
(preflight and adopter docs), never discovered one failure at a time.
(Implementation tracked as `bd-ib-3m44nx` and `bd-ib-ls32yb`;
architecture record: the openbrain adopter dogfood, github-app-auth
`p3icf6`, 2026-07-03.)

**Per-tenant engine identity.** The Fabro server serving a dispatch MUST
publish, check out and renew credentials for that dispatch under the
dispatch TARGET tenant's own GitHub App identity. Two routes satisfy
this. (1) A per-tenant server instance whose global integration IS the
target's App (e.g. a dedicated `FABRO_HOME` carrying the adopter's
`app_id`, its PEM in the server process environment, and its own port
and authentication). (2) A SHARED server whose global integration is a
different App, serving the run under a PER-RUN APP SELECTION (below).
Without a per-run selection, a server serves every run under its one
global integration, so dispatching an adopter repo through a shared
server whose App is not installed for the target fails. A dispatch
preflight SHOULD verify that the App the run will use can reach the
target repo BEFORE launching. It refuses with an actionable diagnostic
rather than failing inside the engine run. Workflow-file-touching pushes
structurally require the App's `workflows` read-write permission grant,
which the factory sandbox's credential MUST NOT hold (§"Factory sandbox
credential constraints" in `constraints.md`). The preflight and the
adopter docs MUST therefore surface that grant as one DELIBERATELY
WITHHELD from the dispatch credential, and MUST name the
attended-host-session route for work requiring it — never as an
App-installation requirement to be granted. (Implementation tracked as
`bd-ib-z2ctra` and `bd-ib-w4iaaf`.)

**Per-run App selection on a shared server.** A dispatch target MAY
declare, per factory, the GitHub App a run on that factory uses. Under
`dispatcher.factories.<name>.github_app` it names an App-id secret and a
private-key secret. Both are secret NAMES the operator provisioned in
that factory's server-side vault, and neither is ever a value. The
Dispatcher MUST render the declaration into the run configuration as the
run's GitHub credential source, carrying the names only. It MUST refuse
before claim, naming the key, when the declaration is malformed: not an
object, missing either name, carrying an empty or non-string name, or
carrying any other key. The engine MUST resolve the selected source from
the server-held secrets in its worker. It MUST use that ONE selected
authority, as renewable repository-scoped installation tokens, for every
protected forge operation of the run: the native repository checkout,
every managed stage credential renewal (the projected `GITHUB_TOKEN`),
and the run's publication (branch push and pull-request creation). An
explicitly selected source whose secrets are absent or empty, whose key
does not parse, or whose App is not installed for or authorized on the
target repository MUST fail the run BEFORE any protected forge
operation, naming the selected secret names and the failing condition.
It MUST NOT fall back to the server's global integration or to anonymous
access. A run that selects no source keeps the server's global
integration unchanged. Selection is per run: concurrent runs on one
server under different Apps MUST each keep their own repository-scoped
authority through every credential refresh and vault snapshot. A
selection MUST NOT replace or mutate the server's global integration.
The selected private key and every token minted from it MUST NOT appear
in the run configuration, the immutable workflow version, `fabro
inspect` or `fabro dump` output, or the sandbox environment, consistent
with the ephemeral-token rule above. (Engine implementation tracked as
`bd-ib-voozdp`, in the Fabro owner fork; the Dispatcher binding is
tracked as its own child.)

**Target-local workflow.** An adopter MAY carry its own
`implement-work-item` workflow in the TARGET repo
(`<target>/.fabro/workflows/implement-work-item/`), and the Dispatcher
MUST resolve the committed workflow a dispatch runs in this order, most
specific first: (1) an explicit `--workflow <path>` argument, the
raw-path escape hatch; (2) the named variant selected per "Named
workflow variants" below, when that selection is not the reserved name;
(3) for the reserved name `implement-work-item`, the target's own
committed `<target>/.fabro/workflows/implement-work-item/` when it
exists, else the plugin payload's bundled workflow resolved via the
plugin root. Step (3) is the automatic target-local resolution this
paragraph previously reserved for a future amendment; it has been the
Dispatcher's behavior since 2026-07-20 and is ratified here as it runs.
Prepare steps remain TARGET-TOOLCHAIN facts, not fleet constants: the
typed integration inputs of §"Repository integration contract" express
them without a workflow copy, and an adopter that does carry its own
workflow keeps its own prepare chain in it, subject to the same
integration-input parity "Named workflow variants" below requires of a
registered variant. The resolved committed path MUST be journaled on
the dispatch record as `workflow_toml`.

**The materialized workflow directory.** When the Dispatcher materializes a
per-dispatch copy of the resolved workflow for the engine to run, the name of
the directory it materializes MUST be one the engine resolves as a local
workflow, under both `fabro validate` and `fabro run`, for every valid
work-item id. The name MUST contain no `.` character,
whatever characters the work-item id contains, and the mapping from work-item
id to directory name MUST be injective, so two distinct work-item ids,
including two that differ only where one has a `.` and the other another
character, never share a materialized directory. This paragraph fixes those
properties, not an encoding scheme. The `workflow_toml` journal field keeps
naming the resolved committed path, never the materialized copy. Measured
2026-10-26 with the petri Fabro client: two byte-identical copies of a working
materialized workflow directory, named `wf-plain` and `wf-dotted.6`, returned
`Validation: OK` and `workflow not found` respectively under `fabro validate`,
and every work item whose id contains a dot, which includes every dotted plan
child, failed at `fabro-run` before any run existed. Scenario 250 in
`scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**The materialized workflow.toml stays inside the engine's size limit.** The engine refuses a workflow file larger than 524,288 bytes, and it refuses it at `fabro-run`, after the Dispatcher has claimed the item. This repository MUST therefore bound the size of the `workflow.toml` the Dispatcher materializes for the reserved `implement-work-item` workflow in two places. First, the `just check` aggregate MUST run the repository check `check-materialized-workflow-toml-size`. That check MUST materialize the bundled `implement-work-item` workflow for a representative dispatch through the same materialization code a real dispatch runs, with the launch overlay and prepare steps included and a goal of exactly 20,480 bytes (above the 16,684-byte goal of the largest measured dispatch, bd-ib-qbtf7s on v0.262.3). It MUST fail when the materialized `workflow.toml` exceeds 471,859 bytes, 90 percent of the engine's limit, printing the measured size, the 471,859-byte threshold and the 524,288-byte limit. It MUST pass otherwise, printing the measured size, so growth is visible before it fails. Second, before the Dispatcher claims the item, every dispatch MUST measure the `workflow.toml` it materialized. When that measurement exceeds 524,288 bytes, the Dispatcher MUST refuse the dispatch before any claim is written and before any Fabro run exists, as a journaled pre-run refusal whose stage names the measured size and the limit. The refusal MUST leave the item in the status it held before the dispatch, with no dispatch claim. The two bounds are independent: the build-time check MUST NOT be read as making the dispatch-time refusal unnecessary, because a dispatch's goal and overlay can exceed what the representative materialization measured. This paragraph governs the reserved workflow and every registered variant, per "A registered variant is the reserved workflow's peer, not its exception" below. Measured 2026-10-30 by petri-factory-on-gmktec: on v0.261.1 the materialized workflow.toml reached 524,287 bytes for livespec-dev-tooling-2zii7l, and bd-ib-dsprir, at 526,975 bytes, was refused at fabro-run after its claim. Scenario 279 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**Named workflow variants.** A dispatch target MAY declare
`dispatcher.workflows`, a table mapping a variant name to a directory path
relative to the target repository root, and `dispatcher.default_workflow`, a
variant name. Both are OPTIONAL target-declared capabilities in the same class
as `dispatcher.acp_nodes` and `dispatcher.node_timeouts` — configuration the
target chooses to carry — and NOT integration points the orchestrator requires
of a governed repository, so the "One schema" and "One resolver" rules of
§"Repository integration contract" do not govern them, and the
members-and-adopters disposition of this addition under the closed-set clause
is: a repository that declares no registry, member or adopter, incurs no new
dispatch-time obligation, and the obligations below bind only a repository
that declares one. Each registered directory MUST hold a COMPLETE workflow —
`workflow.toml`, `workflow.fabro` and its prompt files — and the Dispatcher
MUST NOT merge a variant with the bundle or with another variant; a variant is
a whole directory, never a partial overlay. The name `implement-work-item` is
reserved: it is always defined, it resolves by step (3) above, and a registry
entry MUST NOT redefine it. The variant a dispatch uses MUST resolve, most
specific first: (a) an explicit `--workflow-name <name>` argument on
`dispatcher.py dispatch`, `dispatcher.py loop` and the `drive` operation's
`impl:<id>` action; (b) the name a prior dispatch of the same work-item
recorded in its `dispatch_workflow` metadata, so a retry re-runs the variant
the first attempt ran, provided that name is still registered or reserved; (c)
`dispatcher.default_workflow` when it names a registered entry; (d)
`implement-work-item`. The selector MUST NOT be read from an environment
variable: the per-dispatch value is a recorded argument, for the reason §"ACP
node adapter configuration" gives — an ad-hoc shell MUST NOT be able to change
which graph the factory runs with nothing in the committed record or the
journal to show for it. Every dispatch MUST write the resolved name to the
work-item's `dispatch_workflow` metadata, a top-level metadata key, and MUST
journal it as `workflow_name` on the dispatch record beside `workflow_toml`.
The Dispatcher MUST refuse the dispatch before any Fabro run exists, in the
same shape as the layer-names-an-absent-node refusal of §"ACP node adapter
configuration" — a journaled pre-run refusal whose stage names every cause
that applies — when: the selected name matches no registry entry and is not
the reserved name; the selected registry directory lacks `workflow.toml` or
`workflow.fabro`; or a registry entry is named `implement-work-item`; or the
work-item carries an approved groom draft awaiting its apply dispatch and the
selected name is not a registered groom variant (§"Grooming and slice-size
calibration" → "Consensus-gated automated groom cut"). These are not
`Defective` schema points and do not take the schema-validation exit-3 path,
because the keys are not schema fields.

**A registered variant is the reserved workflow's peer, not its
exception.** Every clause of this specification scoped to the
`implement-work-item` workflow by name — §"ACP node adapter
configuration", §"ACP node timeouts", and the typed-workflow-inputs
clause of §"Repository integration contract" — applies to every
registered variant exactly as it applies to the reserved workflow, and
each such clause's refusals fire for a variant on the same conditions. A
registered variant MUST declare the same eight ACP nodes — `dod_gate`,
`implement`, `fix`, `review_fix`, `proof_capture`, `review`,
`disposition`, `proof_verify` — so that the per-repository adapter
layer and the per-node timeout table resolve against it without naming an
absent node; a variant differs from the reserved workflow in its graph
edges, retry and review discipline, prompts, run configuration and sandbox
image, never in the node names those layers address. Every registered implementation variant MUST also declare the command stages
`pr_refresh` and `pr`. A groom-kind variant retains its ACP `pr` node because
it publishes a filing plan for the host, not a Git branch or pull request;
that node and its `pr_adapter` input are the sole exception to publication
adapter retirement. A groom-kind variant MUST declare an unreachable command
`pr_refresh` so the common timeout table resolves and MUST declare the eight
common ACP nodes but MAY leave `dod_gate`, `publish_draft`, `proof_capture`
and `proof_verify` unreached by its edges
(§"Definition-of-Done and Proof-of-Done stages"). A registered
variant MUST reference exactly the reserved workflow's `inputs.*` token set,
with this single explicit groom-kind adjustment: subtract `pr_adapter` from
the groom variant's referenced and rendered sets before comparison. No other
token is excluded. Its unreachable `pr_refresh` MUST carry the same command
and input references as the reserved `pr_refresh`; the remaining integration
tokens MUST retain real references in the groom workflow's existing stages
or prompts. The Dispatcher renders the reserved set for implementation and
that set plus `pr_adapter` for groom-kind. Title and body are transported as
run-scoped environment data (`LIVESPEC_PR_TITLE` and a sandbox-readable
`LIVESPEC_PR_BODY_FILE`), not new `inputs.*` tokens; the publish branch remains
`LIVESPEC_PUBLISH_BRANCH`. Thus every declared integration point reaches every
variant and no variant opts out of an integration input. The CI
seam-equivalence check, and the `check-no-fleet-toolchain-literals`
gate of the fleet-toolchain literal ban (`constraints.md`
§"Governed-repository integration constraints"),
MUST read the bundle AND every directory this repository registers under
its own `dispatcher.workflows`, and MUST fail rather than report clean
for a registered directory whose scan yields nothing to check, so a
registered variant is held to the same integration-input and
dispatch-path-seam parity as the bundle. (Implementation: plan epic
`bd-ib-yqpdrt`, children `bd-ib-27puvv`, `bd-ib-u7arwz` and
`bd-ib-asrazi`.)

**Default-branch resolution.** Every dispatch-path stage that
references the target's primary branch — the post-merge janitor's
pull-primary refresh above all — MUST resolve the TARGET repo's
default branch (`git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, or
`gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef`) and MUST NOT hardcode
`master`; adopter repos commonly default to `main`. This is the same
resolution the `canonical_branch` key documents (§"`compat` block");
the dispatch path reuses that single resolution rather than carrying
its own ref constant. (Implementation tracked as `bd-ib-hkzcfb`.)

**A sandbox runs its tools from pinned clones and works in the latest clones.**
A factory sandbox MUST hold two kinds of clone of other repositories, and it MUST
NOT use one kind for the other's purpose.

- *Run-from clones.* Every tool the sandbox EXECUTES that comes from a repository
  other than the target (for example livespec core's checker, resolved through
  `LIVESPEC_CORE_PLUGIN_ROOT`) MUST run from a run-from clone of that repository.
  A run-from clone MUST be separate from every work clone. It MUST be checked out
  at the release the governed tree under test declares for that repository (for
  livespec core, `.livespec.jsonc` `compat.pinned`), which is the same release the
  repository's CI runs for that tree. It MUST be shallow, and it MUST be read-only
  to the run's agent and gate processes. Where the governed tree declares no
  release for that repository, the run-from clone MUST be taken at that
  repository's newest release tag, never at its default-branch tip. When the
  janitor refreshes the run's tree, the Dispatcher MUST re-resolve each run-from
  clone's release from the refreshed tree's declaration and MUST re-clone any
  whose declared release changed, before the refreshed tree is checked. A tool
  from a repository other than the target MUST NOT execute from a work clone; the
  target repository's own tooling runs from the target's clone, which is the tree
  under test.
- *Work clones.* The target repository's clone and the sibling clones under
  `/livespec-siblings`, which the run reads for cross-repository state and the
  agent reads and edits, MUST be taken at the default branch's latest commit at
  the moment they are cloned. They MUST be writable, and MUST carry enough history
  for archaeology and debugging: non-shallow, or a depth the repository declares
  sufficient. A cross-repository conformance read, such as livespec's
  `wiring-completeness-cross-repo`, MUST read the work clones.

Scenario 336 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**Helper programs are fetched in the sandbox from the dispatching build's own commit.**
A *helper program* is a program the Dispatcher materializes into a dispatch's
sandbox from this plugin's own source, such as the commit runner and the gate
preview. The Dispatcher MUST NOT carry any helper program's source in a
dispatch's rendered run configuration. It MUST write a *helper manifest* there
instead, naming the orchestrator repository, the commit of the installed plugin
build, and one sha256 digest per helper program, each digest taken over that
helper's composed bytes as the Dispatcher composes them. A setup step of the
dispatched workflow MUST fetch the plugin source at the manifest's commit,
sparse and shallow, MUST compose every helper program from it with the same
composition the Dispatcher uses, MUST write each to its sandbox path with its
file mode, and MUST verify every digest. Because it is a setup step, it re-runs
when a run resumes onto a re-acquired sandbox. A composed helper whose digest
differs from the manifest, a manifest commit that cannot be fetched, or a source
path missing at that commit MUST fail the run before `dod_gate`, with the failure
cause `LIVESPEC_PREPARE_PAYLOAD_DIGEST_MISMATCH` followed by `<helper>: <reason>`.
A dispatch whose installed plugin build commit is not reachable on the forge
MUST be refused before any dispatch claim is written, and the journaled refusal
MUST name the commit. The rendered run configuration MUST carry no
gzip+base64-packed helper payload; per-dispatch data that is not in the
repository, namely the `dod_gate` subject and the pull-request body, MAY stay
inline, packed. The setup step's own script MUST stay short and MUST NOT inline
any helper program's source, because the engine renders a completed command
stage's script into the prompt of every later agent stage. The dispatching host
still needs no orchestrator clone, as this section's opening paragraphs state;
the sandbox takes a pinned fetch of the orchestrator for its helper programs the
way it takes run-from clones for its tools.

Scenario 336 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.


### Definition-of-Done and Proof-of-Done stages

Vocabulary for this section and §"Proof of Done record": the *rendered
goal* is the per-item brief the Dispatcher renders into the run goal (the
artifact §"Dispatch-brief lessons injection" calls the goal brief); the
*dispatch-time snapshot* is the item record as read when that goal was
rendered. A *structured needs-human ending* is the existing failed outcome
of an ACP node that the reserved workflow routes to its `needs_human`
terminal (§"A factory run never awaits a human"), carrying a failure reason
the Dispatcher records as the needs-human question; a failed outcome the
Dispatcher classifies as provider-limit is not a structured needs-human ending.
A *Definition-of-Done
finding* is one line naming the item, the offending element of its
Definition of Done section, and the remedy; it is surfaced on whichever
of three surfaces first detects it — the host-side wall's refusal text,
the `dod_gate` node's needs-human question, or the capture and groom
displays — and is never a doctor finding. The *host-side wall* is the
pre-dispatch and approve refusal machinery of §"Effective acceptance
criteria"; the *gate* is the `dod_gate` node.

**Sandbox capabilities.** A *sandbox capability* is a named surface the
sandbox can exercise for proof: the baseline `terminal` (a shell and the
governed repository's own toolchain) plus each additional surface the
image carries, such as `headless_browser`, `tmux` or `herdr`. The
sandbox image the Dispatcher selects MUST publish its capabilities as
the file `/etc/livespec/sandbox-capabilities`, one lowercase snake_case
name per line. A governed repository MAY mirror the list as the
committed `dispatcher.sandbox_capabilities` array, so that the filing
and approve displays can show it without a sandbox. The committed `dispatcher.sandbox_capabilities` array is the GRADING SET. Every taking of the Definition-of-Done judgement (§"Effective acceptance criteria" → "One rubric, one subject"), the `dod_gate` node included, MUST grade proof-mode feasibility against that array and against nothing else, because it is the one source every taking can read. The published file is the authority for what the image provides. Where the file exists, the `dod_gate` node MUST compare it with the grading set and MUST report in its own output, as a configuration mismatch, each name the array lists that the image does not publish and each name the image publishes that the array omits. The Dispatcher MUST journal every mismatch. A configuration mismatch is not a finding against the item and MUST NOT fail the gate. An assertion graded feasible on a listed name the image does not publish meets the missing-capability ending of `proof_capture`, which names that capability. Where the repository commits no array, the capability set is UNKNOWN for every taking, whether or not the image publishes a file: no taking may raise a missing-capability finding, and each MUST report `sandbox-capabilities: unpublished` in its output. Every taking MUST take the grading set from the committed array alone and MUST NOT infer capability from the item's own prose. The fleet sandbox image MUST publish the file, because it is the authority the node compares the grading set against. A repository MUST NOT list a name in its array that the image it dispatches to does not publish, and the journaled mismatch is how a violation is found. The committed array MUST be accompanied by the committed key `dispatcher.sandbox_capabilities_measured_image`, a string naming the sandbox image whose published capability file the array was measured from, in the form the image source resolves it (an image reference, or its digest). The key is read only beside an array, and it is not API-configurable, for the reason the array is not. The mirror tracks the image the committed configuration resolves for a dispatch that names no catalog environment, by the resolution §"Sandbox image source" and §"Sandbox image enumeration" define: `dispatcher.fabro_sandbox_image` when set, else the repository's own committed `implement-work-item` workflow pin, else the pin of the executing build's bundled workflow. It never tracks a catalog environment. When the image a dispatch resolves differs from the recorded measured image, the filing, groom and approve displays and every host taking of the Definition-of-Done judgement MUST report a STALE-MIRROR configuration mismatch that names both images. When the repository records no measured image, or the recorded or resolved image cannot be established, they MUST report an UNVERIFIABLE-MIRROR configuration mismatch that names its cause, and MUST NOT treat the array as verified. A dispatch whose resolved factory declares a catalog environment launches an image no committed file can name, so its comparison is not made: it is reported as UNVERIFIABLE-MIRROR with the cause `catalog_environment` and the environment id, and is never reported as stale. A stale-mirror or unverifiable-mirror report is a configuration mismatch in the sense above: it is not a finding against the item, it MUST NOT fail the `dod_gate` node or refuse an admission or a dispatch, the Dispatcher MUST journal it, and the grading set remains the committed array alone. The repository check `check-sandbox-capabilities-measured-image` MUST fail, naming both images, when a committed array's recorded measured image differs from the image the committed configuration resolves by that same resolution; a repository that records no measured image, and a resolution that is a catalog environment, pass the check with the unverifiable cause reported. Scenario 276 in `scenarios.md` exercises these sentences. Scenario 139 in `scenarios.md`
exercises this paragraph and the gate's capability duties below.

**The stages.** The reserved `implement-work-item` workflow MUST carry three
additional ACP nodes with these names and positions: `dod_gate`, the first node
after `start` and before `implement`; `proof_capture`, entered from
`publish_draft` or from a changed-head `pr_refresh` whose decision is
`reproof_required` ("Proof carry-forward across a refresh" below) and exiting
only to `review`; and `proof_verify`, entered from `review` or from `proof_grade_route` and, on
success, exiting to the command node `proof_grade`. It MUST also carry the command node `publish_draft`,
entered only from a green janitor outcome and exiting to `proof_capture`, which
MUST push the item's publish branch and, when no pull request for that branch
exists, open one as a DRAFT; it MUST be idempotent across janitor re-entries
and MUST fail closed to `needs_human` when origin cannot be reached. It MUST
NOT refresh the run onto the default branch; the pre-aggregate refresh of the
`janitor` visit that precedes it does ("The run refreshes before the janitor,
and publish_draft pushes the janitor-passed head" below), and a refresh there
that conflicts, a commit of the refresh that the repository's commit hook
refuses, or a refreshed head that the repository's gate rejects, MUST
instead take the refresh-repair route of "Refresh repair" below while that
route's budget lasts. When the `publish_draft` push is refused, its failure
output MUST name which cause refused it. A pre-push hook refusal MUST name
the hook's failed targets, by the structured-summary rule of
§"Failed post-merge janitor target attribution". A non-fast-forward rejection MUST
direct the operator to reconcile the stale publish branch. An origin that
cannot be reached MUST be named as such. A GH001 rejection, origin refusing the
push with GitHub's GH001 large-file error, MUST name each path the rejection
names together with the size it reports. A pre-push hook refusal and a GH001
rejection MUST instead take the publish-repair route of "Publish repair" below
while the refresh-repair budget lasts. Every other refusal, including a
protected-branch refusal, a non-fast-forward rejection, an origin that cannot
be reached and an authentication failure, still fails closed before
`proof_capture`, and so does a pre-push hook refusal or a GH001 rejection once
that budget is spent. Scenario 224 in `scenarios.md` exercises
these sentences. It MUST also carry the command node `proof_grade`, entered
only from a `verified` outcome of `proof_verify`. `proof_grade` MUST read the
newest `verified` record on the pull request whose run identifier the Dispatcher
attributes to this dispatch, using the same record reader the acceptance pass
grades with, and MUST exit zero, routing to `pr_refresh`, exactly when every
`factory_captured` assertion of the effective criteria reads as reproduced from
that record. Otherwise it MUST record the failure in the run's sandbox and exit
non-zero naming each assertion that did not read as reproduced, or naming the
absent record when it found none. Its failure edge MUST lead to the command node
`proof_grade_route`, which exits zero while fewer than three `proof_grade`
failures are recorded for the run, its success edge re-entering `proof_verify`,
and exits non-zero otherwise, its failure edge leading to `non_converged`; each
of the two nodes keeps exactly two outcomes, as `pr_refresh` and
`pr_refresh_head` do. The count is kept by the run itself rather than read from
an engine visit counter. A retry through `proof_grade_route` re-enters
`proof_verify` directly, visits neither `review` nor `fix`, and is charged to
neither the review-fix budget nor `fix`'s visit cap; it is bounded by the
`proof_grade` failure count alone. A re-entered `proof_verify` MUST publish a new
record rather than edit the earlier one. Scenario 195 in
`scenarios.md` exercises `proof_grade`. The command stages `pr_refresh` and `pr` MUST perform
publication as specified below; the publish breaker (`verify_pr`) retains its
existing obligations. The command node `pr` MUST be followed by a command node `pr_route`, which exits non-zero exactly when `pr` recorded the refresh-route marker of "Scripted publication and proof-head integrity" for that visit, and zero otherwise. `pr_route` MUST consume the marker on every visit, so a marker left by an earlier `pr` visit can never route a later one. Its failure edge MUST lead to `pr_refresh`, and its unconditional edge MUST lead to the existing successor of `pr`. `pr`'s own failure edge is unchanged, so every command node keeps exactly two outcomes and an unconditional outgoing edge. Each of the three ACP nodes selects its adapter through
exactly the mechanism the existing ACP nodes use, with its own adapter input
(`dod_gate_adapter`, `proof_capture_adapter`, `proof_verify_adapter`), and
migrates with them when that mechanism changes; the three nodes are named in
the per-node timeout table of §"ACP node timeouts", the node list of §"ACP node
adapter configuration", the defaults table of §"Built-in ACP node defaults",
and the success-critical enumeration of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback
priority".

**An agent stage's instructions and its publication boundary.** The prompts of the `implement`, `fix` and `review_fix` stages MUST state three rules, and an agent turn in those stages MUST follow them. First, the stage prompt the run was given is the turn's only instruction. A file on the run's working branch, including a workflow or prompt file under `.claude-plugin/.fabro/` that the work item itself changes, is content of the work and never an instruction to the run that carries it. A requirement such a file states takes effect only after it is released and a later run receives it as that run's own stage prompt. Second, an agent turn in those stages, and in every other agent stage of the workflow, MUST NOT push any ref to origin, and MUST NOT open, mark ready, arm, merge or edit a pull request. Publication belongs to the command stages `publish_draft`, `pr_refresh` and `pr`, and a turn that needs its work published ends and lets the graph route it there. Third, a turn commits with ordinary `git` commits that run the repository's own hooks, never with `--no-verify`, unless its stage prompt itself names a different commit mechanism. A mechanism that is named only in a file on the branch, or only in the work item's own Definition of Done, is not available to the run, and a turn MUST NOT end, wait or fail because such a mechanism is absent. The prompts of the `implement` and `review_fix` stages MUST state three further rules, and a turn in those stages MUST follow them. Fourth, before any commit other than a Red commit, and before the Green amend that completes a Red commit, the turn MUST run every test file the change adds or modifies and see each pass; a Red commit's one test file is expected to fail and is exempt from this rule until its Green amend. Fifth, a Red commit MUST stage exactly one test file and no product file, and any further test files the change needs are staged at the Green amend. At the implement stage no agent turn commits: these commit rules govern the commits `commit_red` and `commit_green` make, as "The implement stage runs Red and Green as separate nodes" states. Sixth, a change to a stage prompt file under `.claude-plugin/.fabro/`, or to the code that renders the Dispatcher's launch overlay, MUST update, in the same commit, the tests that pin that prompt or that overlay, so the commit does not leave a pinning test failing. These three rules exist because a commit hook run is slow and reports a failing test only as a gate refusal: measured 2026-10-26, three `review_fix` turns (runs 01M5VYNE2N8S, 01M5VK9D2241 and 01M5VT8SBEHX) were refused by the commit hook's coverage gates because tests they committed genuinely failed. One had edited stage prompts and the overlay without updating the tests pinning them, one added a test that failed at setup, and one staged two test files on its Red commit. Each spent one or two hook runs of 24 to 45 minutes learning what a targeted test run would have shown in seconds. The prompts of the `implement`, `fix` and `review_fix` stages MUST also state a seventh rule, and a turn in those stages MUST follow it. Seventh, an agent turn in those stages MUST NOT create, change, rename or delete any path under the governed repository's `<spec_root>`, where `<spec_root>` is the `spec_root` value of its `.livespec.jsonc`, including `<spec_root>/history/` and `<spec_root>/proposed_changes/`. A change to the specification reaches the repository only through that repository's own propose-change and revise operations and the independent review they require, never as a by-product of an implementation run, and an implementation whose Definition of Done appears to need a spec change MUST end the turn through the needs-human protocol naming that need rather than editing the spec. The rule is enforced at publication: before it pushes, `publish_draft` MUST compute the paths the run's own commits change, relative to the merge base of the janitor-refreshed head it pushes with the default branch, so that a spec change that arrived through the default branch is never counted, and, when any of them is under `<spec_root>`, MUST refuse to publish, write a needs-human reason that names every such path and the remedy (drop those changes and file the spec change through propose-change), and fail closed before any push or pull request, exactly as it refuses run-owned files under `.github/workflows/`. The two refusals are independent, and a run that changed paths of both kinds MUST have both named. The rule governs the runs of an implement-kind workflow variant only. The spec-side operations that write `<spec_root>` on the host (propose-change, revise, critique, prune-history, the drift run of each Dispatcher reconcile pass, which files spec-side proposed changes, and the in-session `implement` skill's `capture-spec-drift` handoff) are not factory runs and are unaffected. The repository's heading-coverage map is not under `<spec_root>` and is unaffected. Scenario 202 in `scenarios.md` exercises the first three rules and the seventh rule of this paragraph, and Scenario 249 exercises the fourth, fifth and sixth.

**Publication is mechanically confined to the scripted publication stages.** The second rule above MUST NOT rest on prompt prose alone; an agent stage MUST be unable to publish. The publication actions are: a push of any ref to origin; and opening a pull request, marking one ready, arming or disarming its auto-merge, merging it, or editing it, by any route, `gh`, the forge's REST or GraphQL API, or `git` included. In every agent stage of the implement-work-item workflow, which is every node whose turn an agent takes, the agent's environment, files and processes MUST hold no credential that can perform a publication action, and no credential or key from which one can be minted: neither the run's forge token nor the GitHub App credentials that mint it. Publication-capable credentials MUST be available only to the command stages `publish_draft`, `pr_refresh` and `pr`, which keep every publication action they are specified to take, and to the preserving steps this paragraph names below, and within each of them only to its own publication or preservation step. Repository-controlled code that those stages run, their hooks and gates included, MUST run without the credential: it MUST reach a push only through a credential helper that the hooks and gates cannot read, never through an environment variable or a file they can read. The publication tooling that holds the credential MUST be the Dispatcher-materialized sandbox tooling outside the run's working tree, which no agent stage can modify, so that nothing an agent writes can act with the credential when a publication stage next runs. The forge writes an agent stage's own contract requires MUST go through a trusted broker that runs outside the agent's process tree and holds the credential itself. Those writes are a new comment on the run's own pull request that the stage's contract requires (a Proof of Done record posted through the posting primitive of "Proof of Done record", and the `review` stage's findings record, included) and an upload of proof assets through the proof asset store. The broker MUST perform only those writes, only for the run's own pull request and proof asset store, and MUST take the stage it serves from the workflow that launched the node, never from anything the agent can set. Reading the forge stays allowed. A command node is not an agent stage. A command step that preserves a run's work, namely each preserving step of §"Dispatcher admission, WIP cap, and post-merge acceptance" → "Each committing step of a run preserves the run branch's tip to an ordered work-in-progress ref", the needs-human preservation step included, therefore keeps the credential its own contract requires, and its preservation MUST push only the run's own `refs/heads/needs-human/<run-id>` ref or the run's own work-in-progress refs. Such a step MUST run no repository-controlled code while it holds the credential. In addition, the sandbox `gh` wrapper and `push_origin` helper MUST refuse a publication action from an agent stage before it reaches the forge, exiting non-zero and printing `LIVESPEC_AGENT_PUBLICATION_DENIED` with the stage and the refused action, so that the attempt is named rather than surfacing as an authentication failure. Measured 2026-10-26: on run 01M5X2C5FJKSQW84SFG81E6885 (bd-ib-svm3fe) the `implement` agent ran `gh pr create` and then `gh pr merge --rebase` itself with the run-wide token, merging pull request 3731 partway through the run; on bd-ib-q156 a late agent stage ran `gh pr ready` and a merge of pull request 2633. Scenario 202 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A tree a factory run resumes or seeds can pass under the harness judging it.** A tree that a factory run resumes or seeds from MUST be judged on what it contains, not on the difference between its age and the dispatching build's harness. Whatever the tree's age or its dev-tooling pin, in every fleet repository, the tree's own test suite run by a commit hook inside an agent stage MUST NOT fail because a harness mechanism the dispatching build projected into the sandbox acted on that suite. This requirement sets no staleness bound. An agent stage's own call of the projected `gh` wrapper or `push_origin` helper MUST still be refused as the preceding paragraph states. The harness MUST meet this by keeping the guard's activation out of test processes: a process running the tree's test suite inside an agent stage, whether a commit hook or the agent started it, MUST NOT inherit `LIVESPEC_AGENT_STAGE`, and the means MUST be harness-owned, requiring no change to the tree or to the repository. A test case that exercises the guard MAY set the variable in its own child environment, and that case MUST still observe the refusal. Measured 2026-11-07 on a host, not in a factory sandbox: on the seed tree 4e2cdbbf0 of run 01M6VBWZNCDH5WGJM7VQH9M77Z (bd-ib-72hvx5), six test files that pass on a developer host failed 13 cases with `LIVESPEC_AGENT_PUBLICATION_DENIED` under that run's projected `push_origin` with `LIVESPEC_AGENT_STAGE=review_fix` set, and passed in full with the variable cleared. Scenario 326 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**The implement stage runs Red and Green as separate nodes.** The implement-work-item workflow MUST realize the implement stage as four nodes in this order: a `red` ACP node, a `commit_red` command node, a `green` ACP node and a `commit_green` command node. The `red` prompt MUST direct the agent to write the failing test the work item's Definition of Done needs, to run only that test, and to make no commit. The `red` prompt MUST also direct the agent to create, change or delete no product file, because the implementation belongs to the `green` turn. A product file is a path that the repository's product-path classification counts as product, the same classification that "a Red commit MUST stage exactly one test file and no product file" relies on. Before it stages anything, `commit_red` MUST compare the working tree and the index against the dispatch base, with engine checkpoint commits already folded. When any product file differs, `commit_red` MUST refuse without committing and append a handoff section that names each such path. That refusal re-enters `red` exactly as any other `commit_red` refusal does, and the re-entered turn starts from the dispatch base. The `green` prompt MUST direct the agent to make that test pass by changing implementation files, to run only the tests its change touches, to make no commit, and never to change the Red test file. Before it commits, `commit_red` MUST fold every commit above the dispatch base that the engine made at a node boundary back into the index; it MUST then stage the one Red test file that the `red` section of the handoff file names, and no product file, and run `git commit` with the repository's commit hooks running exactly as for a foreground commit, so that its Red commit sits directly on the dispatch base. Before it commits, `commit_green` MUST fold every commit above the Red commit that the engine made at a node boundary back into the index, so that its amend lands on the Red commit; it MUST then stage the implementation and run `git commit --amend` with the repository's commit hooks running exactly as for a foreground commit. Neither command node may pass `--no-verify`, set any variable that skips or relaxes a check, or change the severity of any hook. When `commit_red` refuses, the run MUST re-enter `red`; when `commit_green` refuses, the run MUST re-enter `green`; each re-entry is bounded by its ACP node's `max_visits`. A `green` turn that finds the Red test wrong MUST be able to end with a declared test-wrong outcome that routes the run back to `red`, bounded by the `red` node's `max_visits`. Before the re-entered `red` turn starts, the run MUST return the branch and the working tree to the dispatch base, leaving only the handoff file to carry what the earlier laps learned, so that the branch never carries more than one Red commit above the dispatch base and the Red commit `commit_green` amends is always the one the latest `commit_red` made. When a re-entry or a test-wrong route finds its bound exhausted, the stage MUST end with a failed outcome and the run takes the implement stage's failure edge; after an exhausted test-wrong route the cause MUST carry the latest `red` and `green` sections of the handoff file. A `red` turn that finds the Definition of Done already satisfied on the dispatch base, so that no failing test can be written, MUST be able to end with a declared already-satisfied outcome instead of a Red test, and that outcome is governed by "An implement turn that reports completion with no diff ends as already satisfied"; a `red` turn that ends with neither a Red test nor that declaration leaves `commit_red` nothing to commit, which is a refusal. No agent turn of the implement stage makes a commit, so no agent turn of the implement stage waits on a commit hook. The stage name `implement` continues to name the implement stage as a whole: wherever this specification addresses the `implement` node or stage by name — the ACP nodes a registered variant declares, the adapter resolution of §"ACP node adapter configuration" and its built-in defaults, the `dispatcher.node_timeouts.implement` key, the `loads` declaration, the success-critical node set, the stage prompt rules of "An agent stage's instructions and its publication boundary", the stages a resumed run never visits, and a rider's stage names — it addresses the `red` and `green` nodes alike, each resolving the value separately for its own turn. The rules of that paragraph on how a turn commits govern no `red` or `green` turn, because neither makes a commit, and `commit_red` staging exactly the one Red test file meets its rule on what a Red commit stages. `commit_red` and `commit_green` are command nodes and resolve no adapter; their timeouts are keyed by their own names under §"ACP node timeouts". Scenario 285 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph and the next.

**The implement nodes hand off through one append-only file.** The `red`, `commit_red`, `green` and `commit_green` nodes MUST pass context through a single handoff file at the git path `livespec-implement-handoff.md` (the path `git rev-parse --git-path livespec-implement-handoff.md` names), which no checkpoint commit can carry into the branch. Each node MUST append a section and MUST NOT rewrite an earlier one. The `red` section MUST name the Red test file, the Definition of Done assertion it proves, the command that ran it and that run's failure output, what the test verifies and does not verify, and the code locations the Red turn identified for the change. A command node's section MUST carry its exit status and, when it refused, the hook's failed target names and the last 80 lines of the hook's own output, taken from the recorded output and never from an agent's reply. A `green` section MUST state what changed and which tests ran, or the test-wrong declaration and its reason. Each ACP node of the implement stage MUST start a fresh agent session whose carried context is the work item, its Definition of Done and the handoff file, never the transcript of another node.

**An implement turn that ends incomplete does not succeed.** The `green` node's outcome MUST be decided from a structured completion field in the turn's final output, not from the turn merely ending. The `green` prompt MUST direct the turn to end its final reply with that field, stating whether the work item's Definition of Done is complete in the tree the turn leaves for `commit_green` to commit. A `green` turn whose completion field reports the work incomplete re-enters `green` while its `max_visits` remains, with the handoff file carrying the previous turn's section. When that budget is exhausted, the stage MUST end with a failed outcome, so the run takes the same failure edge as any other `green` failure, and the dispatch outcome detail MUST carry its cause, naming partial progress. A turn whose final output carries no completion field MUST be treated as incomplete. A turn whose field reports the work complete keeps the succeeded outcome and routes to `commit_green`. The `fix` and `review_fix` stages keep the commit-run wait and refused-attempt rules of "A commit leg completes past one tool call" unchanged, as follows. A `fix` or `review_fix` turn's latest commit attempt that did not go through the detached commit runner counts as refused when the turn left changes staged and the repository's commit hook, run by the run itself over those staged changes, exits non-zero naming at least one failed target; otherwise that attempt is not refused. Except when the turn is ended by its node's resolved timeout, before a `fix` or `review_fix` stage's outcome is decided, the run MUST wait until every commit run the turn started through the detached commit runner of "A commit leg completes past one tool call" has reached its own terminal state. That wait MUST NOT consume the node's retry budget or count as a turn, and its mechanism is left to the implementation; it is the wait that "A commit leg completes past one tool call" names for a commit run the agent left `running` after its one wait. A node-timeout cut remains governed by "A commit run outlives a node-timeout cut". A latest commit attempt made through the runner counts as refused when its commit run reached `failed` and that run's recorded output shows the repository's commit hook ran and named at least one failed target; that run's failed target names and hook error lines MUST then be taken from the commit run's full recorded output, never only from the final lines its terminal report carries. Scenario 204 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**An implement turn sees its commit gate's verdict before it ends.** The `red` and `green` prompts MUST direct the agent, before it ends its turn, to run the gate preview over the changes its turn leaves, to fix every failed target the preview names that the turn can fix within its own scope, and to run the preview again after each fix. The gate preview is a program the Dispatcher materializes into the sandbox beside the commit runner. It MUST run the same checks the repository's commit hooks would run when the turn's commit node commits, over exactly the paths that commit node would stage, and MUST NOT create a commit, move `HEAD` or change the index the commit node will read. It MUST report its exit status and the failed target names, read from the checks' own output. It MUST NOT pass `--no-verify`, set any variable that skips or relaxes a check, or change the severity of any check. When the environment it inherits already carries a variable that skips or relaxes a check, such as `LIVESPEC_CHECK_SKIP`, the preview MUST unset that variable for its own run, MUST run every check the commit node's hooks would run as if the variable were absent, and MUST name each variable it unset in its report beside the exit status and the failed target names. A preview run MUST NOT count as a commit attempt and MUST NOT consume any re-entry budget. Each `red` and `green` handoff section MUST record the exit status and failed target names of the turn's last preview run, or state that the turn ran no preview and why. When the preview program is absent from the sandbox, the turn MUST state that in its handoff section and end its turn as it otherwise would; the commit node's own hook run stays the only verdict that decides a commit. Scenario 285 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A purely mechanical commit refusal has its own re-entry budget.** A repository MAY declare `dispatcher.implement.mechanical_targets`, a list of commit-hook target names whose failures an implement turn can repair mechanically, such as lint, formatting, keyword-only-argument, file-size and per-file-coverage targets, and `dispatcher.implement.mechanical_reentries`, a non-negative integer that defaults to 2 when the list is declared and to 0 when it is not. When `commit_red` or `commit_green` refuses and every failed target name its recorded hook output reports belongs to the declared list, the run MUST re-enter that node's ACP node without spending the re-entry that its `max_visits` bounds, while mechanical re-entries remain for that node in the run. A refusal that names any target outside the list, or whose recorded output names no failed target, MUST spend the ordinary re-entry exactly as before. The handoff section of a commit node whose refusal took a mechanical re-entry MUST say so and MUST name the failed targets and the mechanical re-entries remaining. When the mechanical re-entries are spent, a further purely mechanical refusal MUST spend the ordinary re-entry, and when that is also spent the stage MUST end with a failed outcome whose cause names both budgets as exhausted. The engine visit bound the workflow declares for each re-entered node MUST admit both budgets, so that neither budget is cut short by that bound. Scenario 285 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**An implement turn that reports completion with no diff ends as already satisfied.** When the `red` turn declares the already-satisfied outcome and the run's tree is unchanged against the dispatch base, the run MUST NOT end at the generic dead-implementer truncation. It MUST end with an already-satisfied outcome that names the item and the dispatch base, and it MUST journal that outcome distinctly from a dead-implementer truncation. After that outcome the Dispatcher MUST release the run's factory claim and MUST rest the item in `acceptance`, where `needs-attention` surfaces it with the route by which its Proof of Done can still be obtained: `reconcile-merged` when a merged pull request for the item exists, and otherwise a proof-only run against the dispatch base. A `red` turn that leaves the tree unchanged against the dispatch base without that declaration still ends at `dead_implementer` with today's truncation record once the `red` node's `max_visits` is exhausted.

**Scripted publication and proof-head integrity.** `pr_refresh` and `pr`
MUST be command stages with their own resolved timeouts, not agent turns.
`pr_refresh` MUST fetch the authoritative default branch and query the publish
branch on origin. It MUST establish the run's previously published head from
its recorded publication or validated resume provenance, never from a stale
local tracking ref. Except as the next paragraph provides for a pull request
that has already merged, a missing or unobservable remote, or a foreign or
unexpectedly changed publish head, MUST fail closed with a named cause and
recovery artifact pointer. A conflicted rebase or merge, a commit of the
refresh that the repository's commit hook refuses, and a refreshed head
that the repository-declared gate rejects, MUST take the refresh-repair route of
"Refresh repair" below while its budget lasts, and MUST fail closed with a named
cause and recovery artifact pointer once that budget is spent. A previously completed refresh may be
recognized idempotently from durable run provenance and matching remote state.
A publish head on origin that differs from the run's previously published head
is neither foreign nor unexpectedly changed when it descends from that head and
every commit it adds is an engine checkpoint commit of this run that changes no
tree, its message naming this run's id. `pr_refresh` MUST then take that
observed head as the recorded remote head of the run's publish branch for every
lease this section requires, and MUST treat the added commits as the run's own
empty commits under the unchanged-head rule below. A head that adds any other
commit, or that does not descend from the run's previously published head,
remains foreign. Measured 2026-10-27 on run 01M5XFBSKGY0 (bd-ib-qksrl6): after
`pr_refresh` republished at 7e89feeb and routed back for reproof, the engine
pushed two empty checkpoint commits of the same run onto origin's publish
branch, and the next `pr_refresh` failed closed on that head as foreign.
Scenario 226 in `scenarios.md` exercises this sentence.

**A pull request merged before its refresh.** When `pr_refresh`'s first query
of the run's own publish branch on origin, made before it rebases, pushes or
disarms anything, finds that branch absent, it MUST read the run's pull request
before it decides the remote is missing. A branch found absent after this visit
pushed, including the re-read after a rejected push, is outside this paragraph
and keeps the cause the rest of this section names for it. When the forge reports that pull request
MERGED with a non-null merge commit, the publication is finished, and
`pr_refresh` MUST take the merged-reconcile ending instead of failing closed.
On that ending `pr_refresh` MUST NOT fetch-and-rebase, push, disarm, re-prove or
re-arm, and the run MUST end successfully without entering `pr`, so the
Dispatcher observes the merge, runs the post-merge janitor and enters acceptance
exactly as it does for a merge its merge wait observed. The ending MUST record,
in the run's publication state and in the dispatch outcome detail, the pull
request number, the merge commit, the pull request's merged head, the head named
by the latest `verified` or `carried_forward` record of this run or that no such
record exists, and whether those two heads are equal. The ending MUST NOT write
a `verified` or `carried_forward` record for the merged head. When the merged
head is not the head the latest `verified` or `carried_forward` record of this
run names, or no such record exists, the acceptance pass's proof evidence leg
MUST judge every `factory_captured` assertion UNOBSERVED, yielding
NEEDS_ATTENTION, unless a `verified` record taken on the merged head, or a
`carried_forward` record naming the merged head, lists the assertion as
reproduced; a `verified` record taken on any other head MUST NOT pass a
`factory_captured` assertion for the merged head. The human-attested and
host-captured legs keep their existing rules. When the publish branch
is absent and the pull request is not MERGED, the forge reports a null merge
commit, or the pull request's state cannot be read, `pr_refresh` MUST fail closed
as an unobservable remote with a named cause and recovery artifact pointer. A
foreign or unexpectedly changed publish head MUST fail closed whatever the pull
request's state. Measured on run 01M51D4RYHCB, and again on run 01M5W2YHVAMB on
2026-10-26 after pull request 2633 auto-merged at 15:51:25Z and the forge
deleted its branch, `pr_refresh` failed closed on the deleted branch, and both
runs ended at `needs_human` for work that had landed. Scenario 248 in
`scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A publication that already landed is finished at publish_draft.** `publish_draft`, before it pushes or opens a pull request, MUST check whether the item's publication has already landed, and MUST make the same check before it fails when the forge refuses pull-request creation because the branch has no commits beyond the default branch. It has landed when all of these hold. First, the forge reports a pull request as MERGED with a non-null merge commit. Second, the Dispatcher attributes that pull request to a dispatch of this item, an earlier dispatch included, because the item's dispatch records name it; a matching branch name alone does not establish that. Third, its base is the default branch, and its merge commit is contained in the default branch's tip as read from origin at the check. Fourth, the run's head adds no change to that tip, that is, its diff against the tip is empty. When it has landed, the publication is finished: `publish_draft` MUST NOT push, open a pull request or route to repair, and the run MUST take the merged-reconcile ending of the preceding paragraph, with that paragraph's recording and its rule that the ending writes no `verified` or `carried_forward` record. The acceptance pass then judges the merged head by the proof evidence leg, so a record of an earlier dispatch of the item that is bound or matched to the item and applies to the merged head counts. In every other case `publish_draft` keeps its existing behaviour. These include a run whose head adds a change to that tip, a run with no attributed merged pull request, a merged pull request into another base, and a state the check cannot read. This paragraph changes no other stage. Measured 2026-10-26 on bd-ib-svm3fe run 01M5X2C5FJKSQW84SFG81E6885: the item's change had merged at 22:30:05Z as pull request 3731 from an earlier run's preserved work, and the forge had deleted its branch. The run's `publish_draft` passed the full pre-push gate in 835 seconds, pushed the branch anew, and then failed on pull-request creation with "No commits between master and feat/bd-ib-svm3fe". `refresh_repair` then found no repair brief, and the run ended at `needs_human` with no question asked, for work already on the default branch. Scenario 256 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

When the default branch has advanced beyond the current base, `pr_refresh` MUST
rebase, run the existing repository-declared `sandbox_check_suite` and then,
when the repository declares one, `sandbox_merge_gate_suite` (with
`LIVESPEC_MERGE_GATE_BASE` naming the default-branch commit it just
refreshed onto), each as a foreground command with its own timeout, and
push only after both pass; a failure of either is a refreshed head the
repository-declared gate rejects. Before it rebases, `pr_refresh` MUST read whether the run's pull request carries an auto-merge request and, when it does, MUST disarm it. When the request cannot be read or cannot be disarmed, `pr_refresh` MUST fail closed naming that measurement or action, before any rebase or push. Within a run, only `pr` arms auto-merge, and only for a head named by the latest `verified` or `carried_forward` record of this run, so a disarmed pull request stays unarmed until `pr` re-arms it. The one arming outside a run is the host-side hold release of §"The per-item merge hold". That release MUST NOT arm while a run of the item is live, and it MUST arm only a pull request whose current head is either named by the latest `verified` or `carried_forward` record of the item's latest run (the proved head), or differs from the proved head only in its commit message. A head differs from the proved head only in its commit message when the two commits are distinct, each has exactly one parent, that parent is the same commit, and their trees are the same tree object. When the release arms such a message-only move it MUST report the proved head, the current head and their shared tree in its result. In every other case it MUST refuse, MUST name the measurement that failed (the tree comparison when the trees differ, the parent comparison when the trees match but the parents differ or either commit does not have exactly one parent), MUST report both heads, and MUST leave the pull request unarmed. When the release cannot read the tree or the parent of either head it MUST refuse, naming the read that failed, and leave the pull request unarmed. The release MUST NOT write a `verified` or `carried_forward` record for a message-only move, and this exception MUST NOT change what `pr` arms within a run.
A rewrite MUST use an explicit lease against the recorded remote head of this
run's own publish branch. Hooks MUST run normally. It MUST NOT use bare force,
`--no-verify`, or rewrite another ref.
When the forge rejects that leased push, `pr_refresh` MUST read origin's
publish branch once more before it names a cause, because a rejection is the
forge's report about the write and not a measurement of where the ref now
points. Here the leased head is the recorded remote head the lease was taken
against, and the pushed head is the refreshed head the push carried. When
origin's publish branch then points at the exact pushed head, the write
landed although the forge reported an error, and `pr_refresh` MUST fail
closed with the named cause `LIVESPEC_PR_REFRESH_PUSH_LANDED_ERRORED`, whose
detail MUST name the forge's error text, the pushed head, and the head of the
run's pull request ref (`refs/pull/<number>/head`) as origin reports it, and
MUST state that the publish branch and the pull request may disagree. In that
case `pr_refresh` MUST NOT report `LIVESPEC_PR_REFRESH_LEASE_FAILED` and MUST
NOT state that the remote moved or that another writer pushed. When origin's
publish branch then points at neither the leased head nor the pushed head,
`pr_refresh` MUST report `LIVESPEC_PR_REFRESH_LEASE_FAILED` and route to
`needs_human` exactly as it does for a lease failure today. When origin's
publish branch points at the leased head, the write did not land, and
`pr_refresh` MUST keep its existing lease-failure cause and routing; this
paragraph does not change that case. When origin's publish branch cannot be
read after the rejection, `pr_refresh` MUST fail closed with the named cause
`LIVESPEC_PR_REFRESH_PUSH_OUTCOME_UNOBSERVABLE`, stating that whether the
write landed cannot be established, and MUST NOT report
`LIVESPEC_PR_REFRESH_LEASE_FAILED`. A head of the pull request ref that
cannot be read MUST be named as unobservable in the landed-but-errored detail
and MUST NOT change which of these causes is reported. Each of these causes
MUST carry the recovery artifact pointer this paragraph already requires.
Scenario 184 in `scenarios.md` exercises these sentences. A changed head MUST take the decision of
"Proof carry-forward across a refresh" below: on `reproof_required` the run
MUST return to `proof_capture`, then `review` and `proof_verify`, and on
`carried_forward` it MUST proceed to `pr`; in either case only a proof record
naming the new head — a `verified` record taken on it, or a `carried_forward`
record carrying an earlier `verified` record to it — can reach final
publication. Repeated default-branch movement is bounded to three counted refreshes per
run, after which the run terminates with an explicit non-convergence cause and
preserved work. A counted refresh is a `pr_refresh` refresh onto an advanced
default branch that conflicts or whose refreshed head fails the
repository-declared gate, or any refresh entered through `pr_route` on a
forge-reported conflict after the run's first clean refresh, which counts once
at that visit even when it applies cleanly. Any other clean refresh, one whose
rebase applied without conflict or with only conflicts that "Declared record
files merge without a repair round" resolved, whose refreshed head passed that
gate and whose leased push succeeded, does not count toward that bound. A run refreshes cleanly onto an
advanced default branch at most once: after its first clean `pr_refresh`
refresh onto an advanced default branch, a later `pr_refresh` visit of the run
MUST NOT refresh onto the default branch again, except a visit entered through
`pr_route` on a refresh-route marker that `pr` recorded because the forge
reported the pull request in conflict with the default branch, and MUST
proceed to `pr` with the run's published head, which only a `verified` or
`carried_forward` record naming it lets reach the arming. Default-branch
movement after that clean refresh is left to the merge path, including
"Armed pull request overtaken by the default branch". An unchanged head proceeds to `pr`, except that when the
default branch is already contained in the published head and that head
carries any of the run's own empty commits (commits the run itself created
that change no tree, such as engine checkpoint commits), `pr_refresh` MUST
republish the head without them, under the explicit lease against the
recorded remote head of the run's publish branch that this paragraph
requires. A rewrite whose only change is dropping empty commits, over a
tree identical to the proof-verified tree, MUST take the `carried_forward`
decision of "Proof carry-forward across a refresh" and MUST NOT re-prove. A
head carrying none of the run's empty commits MUST NOT be republished.
Scenario 226 in `scenarios.md` exercises this sentence. All touched nodes MUST
retain an unconditional outgoing edge accepted by the supported engine, and
command nonzero exits MUST take their failure edge.

**The run refreshes before the janitor, and publish_draft pushes the janitor-passed head.** The `janitor` visit that is followed by a `publish_draft` visit MUST first refresh the run's working branch onto the default branch's current tip, using the same refresh mechanism `publish_draft` used before this paragraph, and only then run the repository's full check aggregate on the refreshed head. A green aggregate there records its green verdict for that exact tree under §"Pre-push gate refinements" ("A green aggregate on the exact tree carries to its push"). `publish_draft` MUST NOT refresh again. It MUST push exactly the head that `janitor` passed, so that the pre-push gate honours that verdict instead of re-running the aggregate. When the default branch advances after the janitor's refresh, `publish_draft` still publishes the janitor-passed head; integrating that later advance remains `pr_refresh`'s job. No check, target or gate is removed or weakened: the aggregate runs once, in full, on the tree that is pushed. A refresh that applies cleanly onto an unchanged tip is a no-op, and the janitor then runs exactly as before. When the refresh integrates the default branch's tip by a merge commit, the janitor MUST create the merge without committing it and MUST then commit it through the repository's commit hooks; it MUST NOT bypass a hook. When that commit's pre-commit hook ran the repository's full check aggregate, the same aggregate `sandbox_check_suite` names, to a passing result on exactly the merged tree the commit records, that hook run IS the janitor visit's full check aggregate for that tree: the janitor MUST record its green verdict for that tree as it records its own, and MUST NOT run the aggregate on that tree a second time in the same visit. A merge-gate command that `dispatcher.janitor.merge_gate_suite` declares MUST still run after that verdict, on the same tree, exactly as it runs after a passing `sandbox_check_suite`. When the hook ran only part of the aggregate, or the janitor cannot establish that the hook's run judged exactly the committed tree, the janitor MUST run its own full aggregate on the merged head exactly as before. When the hook's aggregate fails, the merge is not committed, and the janitor MUST take the route an aggregate failure on a changed refreshed head takes: it restores the pre-refresh head and records a refresh-repair brief naming each failed target. The commit-msg replay gate's suite-green leg on that merge commit is governed by livespec-dev-tooling's contract, whose Same-tree reuse bullet reuses the pre-commit aggregate run instead of starting a second suite; this paragraph does not change that leg. Measured 2026-11-07 on bd-ib-hap62u run 01M6VBZF4371: a refresh merge made by a plain merge ran no pre-commit hook, its commit-msg suite-green leg ran the full suite in 1611.80 s, and the janitor's own aggregate then outran the 4340 s janitor ceiling. A janitor aggregate failure on a head whose refresh was a no-op keeps its existing route. Scenario 305 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**Refresh repair.** When the pre-aggregate refresh of a `janitor` visit, or `pr_refresh`, cannot refresh the run
onto the advanced default branch — because the rebase or merge conflicts,
because the repository's commit hook refuses a commit the refresh itself makes
(the merge commit of a merge refresh, or a commit a rebase replays) while no
path is conflicted, or because the refreshed head fails the
repository-declared gate: for `janitor`, its own full aggregate on a head whose refresh changed the tree; for `pr_refresh`, the gate that runs before or during its publishing push — the stage MUST restore its pre-refresh head,
MUST record a refresh-repair brief, and MUST route to the existing `fix` agent
node. The pre-refresh head is the head the stage held when it began that
refresh: for `janitor`, the head the preceding `implement`, `fix` or `review_fix` stage left; for
`pr_refresh`, the run's previously published head as established above from its
recorded publication or validated resume provenance, which also covers a
resumed run that has no `janitor` visit of its own. Restoration MUST abort any
in-progress rebase or merge AND reset the run's working branch to the
pre-refresh head, so it applies equally when the refresh itself completed and
only the gate rejected the result. The brief MUST name the stage, the
pre-refresh head, the default-branch commit the refresh targeted, and either
each conflicted path together with the run commit that was being applied, or
each failed gate target, or, for a commit-hook refusal, each target the hook
names as failed together with the last 80 lines of the hook's own output.
When the conflicted paths include a generated record file, the brief MUST carry
one line `regenerate: <path> via <generator argv>` per such file. The `fix` turn
MUST resolve every other conflicted path first and MUST then resolve each named
file by running its generator, never by editing its text. When a failed gate
target's failure names a generated record file, the brief MUST carry the same
`regenerate:` line for that file beside the failed target. The stage MUST distinguish a refreshed head that the
gate rejected from a push that origin refused or could not reach, and from an
authentication failure; only a conflict, a commit-hook refusal of the refresh's own
commit, or a gate rejection takes this route, a `publish_draft` push refusal
takes it only as "Publish repair" below states, and every other cause keeps its
existing fail-closed behaviour. A commit-hook refusal of the refresh's own
commit MUST NOT end the run at `needs_human` with
`LIVESPEC_REFRESH_REPAIR_ABSENT`. The `fix` turn
integrates the default branch into the run's work, resolving the conflict or
the gate failure inside its own turn. Hooks MUST run normally there, and the
turn MUST NOT use `--no-verify`, bare force, or a rewrite of any ref. After a
refresh-repair round the run re-enters `janitor`, then `publish_draft`, then
`proof_capture`, exactly as an accepted fix round does, so only proof for the
repaired head can reach publication.

**Publish repair.** When origin refuses a `publish_draft` push with GitHub's GH001
large-file error, or the repository's pre-push hook refuses it, `publish_draft`
MUST record a repair brief and MUST route to the existing `fix` agent node, as a
refresh-repair round does. The brief MUST name the stage, the head whose push
was refused, and the cause. For a GH001 rejection, the cause is each path the
rejection names together with the size it reports. For a hook refusal, it is
each target the hook names as failed together with the last 80 lines of the
hook's own output. The `fix` turn MUST remove each named path from every commit
of the run that origin does not already hold, or repair each named target. It
MUST NOT rewrite a commit origin already holds, MUST let hooks run normally, and
MUST NOT use `--no-verify` or bare force. A publish-repair round is a
refresh-repair round for every other rule of this section: it is counted by
"Refresh-repair accounting", the run then re-enters `janitor`, then
`publish_draft`, then `proof_capture`, and the `publish_draft` visit after it
follows a refresh-repair round. When the refused push would need a third
round, the recovery artifact pointer that "Refresh-repair accounting" requires
names the head whose push was refused. A protected-branch refusal, a
non-fast-forward rejection, an origin that cannot be reached and an
authentication failure MUST NOT take this route. Whichever route a
`publish_draft` push refusal takes, it MUST NOT end the run at `needs_human`
with `LIVESPEC_REFRESH_REPAIR_ABSENT`; a refusal that fails closed names its own
cause. Scenario 329 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A fix turn grades each tree once, through its commit hook.** This paragraph governs a `fix` turn or a `review_fix` turn that completes successfully and routes to `janitor`, whether the `fix` turn was a fix round or a refresh-repair round. A `fix` or `review_fix` turn that ends through the needs-human protocol, by its node's resolved timeout, or by any other failure keeps its existing handling, which this paragraph does not change. A successful `fix` or `review_fix` turn MUST leave the run's working branch at a head whose last commit in that turn passed the gate its commit hook ran under the next paragraph: the affected-tests gate's scoped tests and their coverage, or the full check aggregate when that gate cannot scope the change. The `fix` and `review_fix` prompts MUST NOT direct a run of the full check suite beyond what its commit hook runs, because the `janitor` visit that follows a successful `fix` or `review_fix` turn runs the full check aggregate on the run's tree. A hook run that did not grade the committed tree, such as a Red commit on the hook's fast path, does not satisfy the obligation. A change to the tree after the last passing hook run MUST be committed through the commit hook again before a successful turn ends. A turn whose last commit is an OPEN RED, a commit carrying the Red-Green commit protocol's `TDD-Red-*` trailers and no `TDD-Green-*` trailers, has not met this obligation, even when its commit-settle node settles that commit `passed`, because the commit hook accepts a correctly failing Red. When `fix_commit_settle` or `review_fix_commit_settle` settles an open Red as the turn's last commit, the run MUST re-enter that same stage, `fix` or `review_fix`, instead of routing to `janitor_admission`. The re-entered turn's brief MUST name the open Red commit and MUST direct the turn to complete that commit's Green amend rather than author a new Red commit. A last commit that carries both trailer sets, or no TDD trailers, routes to `janitor_admission` as before.
