edit; or set the item's `acceptance_policy` to `human-only` where
machine grading is genuinely inapplicable). The `human-only` remedy does
not waive the Definition of Done section (§"Effective acceptance
criteria" → "Who must carry the section"). The item RESTS where it is;
it is not moved to `backlog` or `blocked` on these grounds. Being in `ready` MEANS approved-to-start
(approval ≡ `ready` membership). The admission valve (`ready →
active`) is mechanical — dependencies clear, a free WIP slot,
an assignee resolvable, and `factory_safety` null (a non-null value is
refused at admission and host-routed); permission was settled upstream at
`approve`.
`admission_policy` is the delegation dial on the `approve` routing
ONLY: the human always holds the ultimate decision but MAY delegate
the GO per item or blanket for low-risk work — that delegation IS
`admission_policy` (`auto` = the GO is delegated; `manual` = the human
gives it explicitly).

**`approve` on an auto-admission item held by intake.** For an item in
`pending-approval` whose EFFECTIVE `admission_policy` is `auto`, `approve` MUST
re-run the intake Definition-of-Done check against the item's current text
before deciding. When that check reports no mechanical finding, `approve` MUST
move the item to `ready`, journaled with its actor like any other approval.
When it still reports a mechanical finding, `approve` MUST leave the item in
`pending-approval`, MUST refuse with a result naming each mechanical finding,
and MUST record those findings on the item as a ledger comment. Advisory
findings MUST NOT block the release. On BOTH effective admission policies,
`approve` MUST refuse an item whose title, description, acceptance criteria or
notes carry a goal-template opening delimiter: it MUST leave the item in
`pending-approval` and MUST return a result naming each such field. A ledger
comment MUST NOT be a cause of this refusal, because the goal render
neutralizes comments (§"Dispatcher policy settings" → "A goal-template opener is neutralized in a comment and refused in a field"). For an
effective-manual item that is the only check added; `approve` on such an item
is otherwise unchanged. This keeps `approve` the single journaled door from
`pending-approval` toward `ready`; no second verb is added. Scenario 334 in
`scenarios.md` exercises the refusal.

The maintainer's rationale, verbatim (source: repo
`thewoolleyman/livespec`,
`plan/archive/work-item-state-machine/conversation/transcript.md`):
"If we don't respect the groomed attribute and add autonomous
execution, then the factory can just go wild and go completely off
track and never stop, Piling up a bunch of incorrect work that should
have never been performed at the review gates, or even worse if the
review gate is automated, pushing it all to production." (The quote is
byte-exact to the transcript, including the mid-sentence capital
"Piling".)

### Per-state operator verb vocabulary

Which operator verbs are valid in which lifecycle state, which transition
each door owns, and when a policy dial still governs anything. This
vocabulary is OWNED here and consumed by console adopters:
`livespec-console-beads-fabro`'s own contract defers per-item verb
suppression to it explicitly ("depends on the per-state valid-verb
vocabulary, which is owned by `livespec-orchestrator-beads-fabro`"), so
until it existed no consumer could suppress a verb without inventing a
vocabulary it does not own. Design record: repo
`thewoolleyman/livespec-console-beads-fabro`,
`plan/console-happy-path-mvp/research/verb-vocabulary-brainstorm.md`
(seven maintainer-decided points, 2026-07-21..26, each recorded with its
source verification), with the filing draft at
`plan/operator-surface-redesign/research/verb-vocabulary-propose-change-draft.md`.

Rationale: an operator surface that offers a verb which is meaningless or
inert for the selected item's state cannot be told apart from a broken
one. The narrowings below exist so that every offered verb is actionable
and every transition is attributable in the journal.

#### Per-lane valid operator verb sets

| Lane | Valid operator verbs |
|---|---|
| `backlog` | groom (every backlog item, uniformly); release-spec-tier (human-only; spec-change-tier-held items only); move→ready (admission); move→blocked; set-admission; set-acceptance; merge-on-review-cap; review-fix-cap; acceptance-rework-cap |
| `pending-approval` | approve (the single door toward `ready`; for an effective-auto item it re-runs the intake Definition-of-Done check first); release-spec-tier (human-only; spec-change-tier-held items only); reject (rework \| regroom); set-admission; move→backlog (withdraw); move→blocked (park); set-acceptance; review caps per the dial-window rule |
| `ready` | release-spec-tier (human-only; spec-change-tier-held items only); move→backlog (withdraw); move→blocked (park); driver-dispatch (host-only-refused items only); set-acceptance; set-workflow-scope-override (declared-workflow-edit refusals only); acceptance-rework-cap; merge-on-review-cap; review-fix-cap |
| `active` | observe only — no operator verbs beyond set-acceptance / acceptance-rework-cap per the dial-window rule and release-spec-tier (human-only; spec-change-tier-held items carrying `rework:pending` only); for an item carrying `rework:pending`, `dispatch --item` (the `drive` `impl:<work-item-id>` action) drives the pending rework; and the terminal-claim recovery `move→ready`, valid only for an `active` item whose run is terminal, that carries neither `rework:pending` nor a `merge-hold:` label, whose dispatch-scoped ownership lock no live process holds, which §"Stranded claim release" does not reconcile, and for which the forge was read and reports no merged pull request |
| `acceptance` | accept (the single door into `done`); reject (rework \| regroom); move→backlog (de-scope); move→blocked (park) |
| `blocked` | release-spec-tier (human-only; spec-change-tier-held items only); move→ready (unblock); move→backlog (an item needing decomposition routes here first — groom is `backlog`-only) |
| `done` | nothing (but see "Status-independent verbs" below) |

`release-spec-tier` (§"The four maintainer touchpoints", touchpoint 1) is valid in `backlog`, `pending-approval`, `ready` and `blocked`, and in `active` for an item carrying `rework:pending`, only while the item carries a spec-change-tier hold. It MUST refuse while a run of the item is live or a live process holds the item's dispatch-scoped ownership lock.

**Status-independent verbs.**
`set-factory-safety:<id>:<needs-host-secrets|mutates-host-machinery|needs-privileged-host|needs-host-only-input>`
is NOT lifecycle-gated and is therefore intentionally not enumerated per-row
above (including the `done` row): it
sets the intrinsic `factory_safety` runnability axis (orthogonal to both status
and `admission_policy`), so it is valid on a work-item in ANY lane. It is a
field-setter, not a transition or policy-window verb, so the per-lane narrowing
that keeps every enumerated verb actionable does not apply to it. Its clause is
below. `clear-factory-safety:<id>:<rationale>` is its inverse and is likewise
status-independent and not enumerated per row.

`close-duplicate:<work-item-id>:<successor-id>` is valid in every lane except `done`, and is likewise not enumerated per row. Driven only by a human, it closes an item that duplicates the work item `<successor-id>`, in any non-closed lifecycle status and whatever spec-change-tier hold the item carries, with no factory run and no change to any other item. It MUST record `<successor-id>` as the item's `superseded_by`, MUST write a durable ledger comment on the item naming the successor and the invoker, and MUST append one dispatch-journal record naming the item, the successor and the invoker, as the other human valves journal theirs. It MUST refuse, naming the reason and writing nothing, when `<successor-id>` does not resolve to a work item in a tenant the Dispatcher can read, when `<successor-id>` equals `<work-item-id>`, when the item is already closed, and while a run of the item is live or the item carries an unreleased dispatch claim. The close is a disposition, not a ratification: it states no behaviour, and a linked proposed-change topic the item carries keeps its own revise decision.

`relink-spec-tier:<work-item-id>:<topic>` is valid in every lane except `done`, and is likewise not enumerated per row. It is a field-setter on the spec-change-tier hold, not a transition: it replaces the held item's linked proposed-change topic with `<topic>` and MUST NOT write a status, release the hold, or change any other item. Because the hold is still released only by the ratification of the replacement topic together with a `stated` re-run judgement, the route MAY be driven by a human or by an agent session. It MUST refuse, naming the reason and writing nothing, when the item carries no spec-change-tier hold; when `<topic>` is not a canonical topic stem, that is, when `/livespec:propose-change`'s topic canonicalization would change it; when `<topic>` names no proposed change, either a pending `<spec-root>/proposed_changes/<topic>.md` or a revision record under `<spec-root>/history/vNNN/proposed_changes/`; and when `<topic>` has no pending proposal and its latest revision record carries decision `reject`, because a hold waiting on a rejected topic could never release. On success it MUST record a durable ledger comment on the item carrying the actor, the previous linked topic and the replacement topic, and it MUST append the replacement as a spec-change tier record whose linked topic is `<topic>` and whose verdict, generalization target and clause provenance are the standing record's, so the hold read, the pre-dispatch wall's exit-`5` refusal and the next intake or drain pass all name the replacement topic. Relinking an item whose replacement topic is already ratified MUST NOT itself release the hold; the next intake or drain pass re-runs the judgement against the ratified specification and releases it exactly as the autonomy-tier bullet states.

#### Door rules — every transition has exactly one journaled owner

- `ready` is entered by `approve` (from `pending-approval`), by an
  operator move from `backlog`/`blocked`, or by the terminal-claim recovery
  move from `active` that the `active` row above admits; each is journaled
  with its actor. The move from
  `pending-approval` to `ready` is REMOVED: it is an unjournaled
  duplicate of the `approve` valve, so the ledger cannot attribute the
  transition.
- `active` is entered ONLY by a journaled dispatch — factory dispatch,
  `driver-dispatch`, or the groom front-end's groom dispatch of a `backlog`
  item (§"Grooming and slice-size calibration" → "Consensus-gated automated
  groom cut") — OR by a rework return from `acceptance`, which is either the
  `reject:rework` valve or the Dispatcher's own `acceptance-auto-rework`
  disposition. Bare operator moves into `active` are removed from every lane.
  Both rework returns are journaled — the Dispatcher's
  `acceptance-auto-rework` disposition, and the valve's durable
  `human-valve-reject-rework` record (shipped as `bd-ib-ktxb`, PR #1048) — so
  every rework return into `active` is journaled and the one-journaled-owner
  rule holds for both. Both are named here because a door rule that omits a
  shipped writer is false, not merely incomplete.
- `done` is entered ONLY by `accept`, or by the `close-duplicate` valve for an item another work item supersedes. The move `acceptance → done` is
  REMOVED — it is an unjournaled duplicate of the accept valve.
- `pending-approval` is never a move target; it is entered only by
  intake Definition-of-Ready routing.
- `reject` is valid at the two human valves ONLY — `pending-approval`
  and `acceptance`. Its two kinds land in different lanes:
  `reject:rework` returns the item to `active`, and `reject:regroom`
  returns it to `backlog`. Mid-flight abort of an `active` run is NOT
  in this vocabulary: cancelling a running dispatch needs
  run-cancellation semantics, and journaling a rejection while the run
  continues would record an outcome that did not happen.
- The `reject:rework` valve MUST write a durable journal record for the
  `acceptance → active` transition it performs, carrying at minimum the
  acting party, the stage identifier, and the work-item id, symmetric
  with the Dispatcher's `acceptance-auto-rework` record. Emitting that
  object solely in the drive CLI's response payload MUST NOT be treated
  as satisfying this requirement: a response is transient and
  unattributable once the invocation returns, whereas the
  one-journaled-owner guarantee requires a durable record. This
  requirement is MET by the shipped valve (`bd-ib-ktxb`, PR #1048,
  integration-tested), and the `active`-entry rule above states without
  qualification that every rework return into `active` is journaled. The door is required to gain
  attribution rather than be removed because the Dispatcher already
  performs this same transition automatically under
  `acceptance-auto-rework`, and because `reject:rework` is the only
  operator route from `acceptance` back into work — `reject:regroom`
  routes to `backlog`, which would restore admission eligibility for
  work that has already merged.

#### Policy dial window

A policy dial is valid only while the decision it governs is still
ahead of the item:

- `set-admission` — through `pending-approval`.
- `merge-on-review-cap` and `review-fix-cap` — through `ready`. Both are
  snapshotted into the run at dispatch, so a change made while the item
  is `active` can never reach the in-flight run; offering them there
  would be inert.
- `set-acceptance` and `acceptance-rework-cap` — through `active`.
- Nothing on `done`.

#### `set-workflow-scope-override:<id>:citation-only`

This ready-lane-only operator assertion records that an item's mention of a
path under `.github/workflows/` is a citation rather than a declaration of
intent to edit that path. `citation-only` is the single allowlisted value.
Applying it writes the durable beads label
`workflow-scope-override:citation-only` without changing item status. The
assertion is valid only for an item whose published
`awaits_scope_override` signal is true; the alternative is to revise the
item's own scope with an inline negation declaration that makes the absence
of workflow edits explicit.

The admission predicate evaluates non-null `factory_safety` FIRST, before
consulting this override. Consequently the assertion can admit only an item
refused by the declared-workflow-edit heuristic and can never admit an
intrinsically host-only item. It is an explicit operator override of a
factory-boundary heuristic, not a general relaxation of factory safety. A
work-item introducing a first-class operator verb MUST include specification
coverage for that verb in its acceptance criteria, because the action-id
grammar is a consumer contract rather than an implementation-private parser.

#### `driver-dispatch:<id>`

A journaled dispatch door for work that the factory will not sandbox.
It is valid ONLY on `ready` items whose `factory_safety` is non-null —
exactly the set the admission valve already refuses and host-routes,
whose refusal already directs the operator to "host-route it to a host
sub-agent instead". It journals the actor and a driver-session
reference and moves `ready → active`; the driver session parks its
result at `acceptance`, where the normal accept valve applies.

Because the eligible set is precisely the set the Dispatcher refuses,
no dispatcher/driver race is possible and no claim mechanism is
required. That scope is load-bearing, not incidental: widening
`driver-dispatch` to any `ready` item WOULD require a claim mechanism,
and MUST NOT be done without one.

#### `set-factory-safety:<id>:<needs-host-secrets|mutates-host-machinery|needs-privileged-host|needs-host-only-input>`

A status-independent operator verb that SETS the target work-item's
`factory_safety` field to the supplied host-only reason. The reason MUST be one
of the four canonical `factory_safety` values —
`needs-host-secrets`, `mutates-host-machinery`, `needs-privileged-host`, or
`needs-host-only-input` (§"Work-item beads-issue mapping") — exactly as the field's own closed enum
defines them; an out-of-enum or empty reason is refused. A null `factory_safety`
— the default — remains factory-eligible;
opting an item out of factory eligibility MUST go through this verb, so the
reason is recorded on the item in the journal, rather than through a raw
`bd label add` that leaves no attributable record. Because `factory_safety` is an
INTRINSIC runnability axis orthogonal to lifecycle status, the verb is valid on a
work-item in ANY lane — it is not gated to a single lifecycle state. It does NOT
change item status and MUST NOT alter `admission_policy`, the orthogonal
human-approval axis. Once set, the admission predicate — which evaluates non-null
`factory_safety` FIRST — host-routes the item, and `driver-dispatch:<id>` becomes
the applicable door. A work-item introducing a first-class operator verb MUST
include specification coverage for that verb in its acceptance criteria.

#### `clear-factory-safety:<id>:<rationale>`

A status-independent operator verb that CLEARS the target work-item's
`factory_safety` field, returning it to null and therefore to factory
eligibility. It is the inverse of `set-factory-safety`, and it MUST be the
only sanctioned route back into factory eligibility: lifting a host-only
hold through a raw `bd label remove` leaves no attributable record, which is
exactly what `set-factory-safety` exists to prevent on the way out.

The `<rationale>` is the remainder of the action id after the second colon
and MAY itself contain colons. A rationale that is empty or only whitespace
MUST be refused, with a message naming the missing rationale, and the item
MUST keep its `factory_safety` value. A `clear-factory-safety` on an item
whose `factory_safety` is already null MUST be refused, with a message saying
no hold is set, and MUST write nothing to the ledger or the journal.

On an accepted clear, the verb MUST append the rationale, the invoker and the
removed reason to the item's ledger comments and to the dispatch journal
BEFORE it removes the value, so that a failed mutation leaves an explained
intent rather than a silent change. Like `set-factory-safety`, it is valid on
a work-item in ANY lane, it does NOT change item status, and it MUST NOT
alter `admission_policy`.

`groom` needs no door — a groomed item remains `backlog` throughout the
drafting conversation, and the groom exit is a close-regroomed-out into
replacement slices.

### Journal invoker attribution

Every record the Dispatcher's journal append path writes MUST carry two
fields stamped ONCE by the append layer and inherited by every writer
above it: **`invoker`** (a non-empty opaque identity string) and
**`invoker_source`** (exactly one of `flag`, `env`, `fallback`). Writers
MUST NOT stamp these fields themselves; a record supplied with either
field is refused by the append layer as a programming error, so the
attribution cannot be forged one caller at a time. EVERY journal write
MUST route through the append layer: writing the journal path directly
is forbidden, the two shipped direct writers (the acceptance-rework
disposition writer and the ledger-close status-normalization writer,
which today bypass the layer and carry no timestamp) are migration
obligations of this contract's implementation, and a mechanical control
MUST prove no code appends to the journal path outside the layer —
without this, the stamped-once guarantee governs only part of the
journal, and the bypassed acceptance-rework record is the very
provenance carrier §"Rework-pending re-dispatch" designates.

The identity enters on the published CLI surface and resolves in this
order:

1. `--invoker <id>` on the invocation (`invoker_source: flag`) —
   accepted by every published state-changing entry point
   (`dispatcher.py` `loop` / `dispatch` / `reconcile-merged` / `resume`, the
   `drive` operation's valve actions, and the `probe` subcommand once
   ratified — every later-ratified state-changing entry point inherits
   this input as a filing obligation of its own proposal).
2. Otherwise the `LIVESPEC_INVOKER` environment variable, when set and
   non-empty (`invoker_source: env`).
3. Otherwise the derived fallback `unattributed:<os-user>@<hostname>`
   (`invoker_source: fallback`). The fallback is a MARK, not an
   identity: it records that no caller asserted who acted.

Identity strings are opaque to this contract; the RECOMMENDED convention
is `<role>:<name>` (for example `human:<name>`, `session:<session-name>`,
`foreman:<seat>`, `console:<principal>`), and callers acting on a
human's explicit order SHOULD carry that human in the identity they
assert. Where a ratified door already journals a door-specific actor
field (the v051 valve records), that field remains; `invoker`/
`invoker_source` is the uniform envelope-level attribution. The `release-spec-tier` valve's attestation actor (§"Grooming and slice-size calibration" → "An autonomy tier is assigned") is such a door-specific actor. When an invoker is asserted, by `--invoker` or by `LIVESPEC_INVOKER`, the attestation's ledger comment and its dispatch-journal entry MUST record that asserted invoker as the actor. When no invoker is asserted, both MUST record as the actor the identity computed from the invoking session. That is the invoking agent session's id when the session sets one, otherwise the forge login of the human at the terminal, computed exactly as the plan-record and proof-record posting primitives compute their publishing identity. The recorded actor MUST name which of the two kinds it is, as `session:<agent-session-id>` or `human:<forge-login>`, so an actor computed from an agent session is distinguishable from one computed from a forge login. Only when no invoker is asserted and no session identity can be computed does the attestation record the `unattributed:<os-user>@<hostname>` mark as its actor. This computation never changes the journal entry's envelope `invoker` and `invoker_source`, which the append layer stamps by the three-step order above.

**Delegated valve authority.** A maintainer MAY delegate the pressing of
human valves to a named delegate (for this fleet, the coordinator seat under
ruling R493). The delegation is first-class: the press asserts the reserved
role `delegate`, as `--invoker delegate:<delegate-name>`, and MUST also name
the delegation it acts under with `--delegation <ref>`. `drive` MUST verify
the press against **`dispatcher.valve_delegations`** (committed
`.livespec.jsonc`, a list; default empty), each entry an object with the
non-empty strings `ref` (the delegation's identifier, e.g. `R493`),
`delegate` (the `<delegate-name>` it authorizes), `grantor` (the delegating
human, a `human:<name>` identity) and `record` (where the grant is recorded,
e.g. the plan-scope-event's epic and timestamp). A press is a **verified
delegated press** exactly when its invoker role is `delegate`, its
`--delegation` ref equals one entry's `ref`, that entry's `delegate` equals
the invoker's `<delegate-name>`, and the action's verb is on the **delegable
valve allowlist**: `resolve-blocked`, `approve`, `accept`, `reject` and
`release-spec-tier`. Like `dispatcher.require_invoker`,
`dispatcher.valve_delegations` is deliberately NOT API-configurable: a
delegation is granted only by a committed, reviewable change, so no press
can invent the reference it cites. A list that does not parse, or an entry
missing any of the four fields or whose `grantor` is not a named `human:`
identity, makes the whole setting unreadable, and an unreadable setting
verifies no press.

The delegation NEVER covers a credential, irreversible or outward-facing
act, and the allowlist is the mechanical form of that exclusion: the
factory-safety opt-out and its clearance (host secrets and host machinery),
the merge hold (a forge write), the policy, cap, queue and workflow-scope
edits, `impl:` and `driver-dispatch:` dispatches, and every entry point
outside `drive` (the provider-exhaustion and ACP-hold clearances among them)
are not delegable. `drive` MUST refuse, before any store read that could
lead to a write, any journal write or any ledger write: a `delegate:`
invoker without `--delegation`; `--delegation` without a `delegate:`
invoker; a delegated press of a verb off the allowlist; and a ref that
matches no entry, or matches an entry for a different delegate, or cannot be
verified because the setting is unreadable. Each refusal names the action,
the asserted invoker and ref, and why. No environment variable or flag
bypasses this verification.

A verified delegated press satisfies every gate on the allowlisted valves
that admits a human operator's press, the `human` answer disposition of
§"Dispatcher policy settings" included. Its records MUST say plainly that
the delegate acted under maintainer delegation and MUST NOT carry a
`human:<name>` identity: `invoker` stays the asserted
`delegate:<delegate-name>`, every journal record the press writes
additionally carries a stamped `delegation` object (`ref`, `grantor`,
`record`) applied by the same append layer that stamps `invoker`, an answer
comment's header names the delegation ref and grantor after the invoker, and
a green press appends one ledger comment to the item opening with the marker
`livespec-delegated-valve-press` that names the action id, the delegate, the
ref, the grantor and the record. A refused press writes none of these.
Scenario 301 binds this behavior.

**`dispatcher.require_invoker`** (boolean, committed `.livespec.jsonc`,
default **`false`**) governs the fallback: when `true`, a published
state-changing invocation whose identity would resolve by `fallback`
MUST be refused at startup as a precondition error (exit `3`), naming
the two accepted inputs — BEFORE any store mutation, journal write, or
run creation, so no act is half-performed and no attribution gap is
created by the refusal itself. When `false`, the fallback applies and
the record is written marked `invoker_source: fallback`. This setting
has NO per-item override (attribution is a property of the invocation,
not the item) and is deliberately NOT API-configurable: it MUST NOT be
editable through the console Settings surface or any remote API,
because a dial that relaxes attribution MUST NOT be reachable over the
surface whose acts it attributes (§"Control surface and audit").
Read-only invocations (`--dry-run`, status reads) resolve and stamp
identity identically when they journal, but are never refused on
attribution grounds.

### Intent preservation

- Every load-bearing semantic definition in this specification MUST
  carry its rationale and MUST cite its design record (repo-qualified
  location plus decision identifiers when they exist).
- When ratified statements of this specification are found to
  conflict (by critique, doctor, or any revise pass), the cited
  design record — the recorded maintainer intent — is the tiebreaker.
  Consistency with the shipped implementation is NEVER the tiebreaker.
- If no design record is cited or reachable for the conflicting
  statements, that absence is itself a finding that MUST be surfaced
  to the maintainer; it MUST NOT be self-resolved.


## Dispatcher classify-tier invocation surface

The Dispatcher's `classify-tier` subcommand is a classification-only path. It
gives a work-item that never passes filing or dispatch again, such as a parked
plan child that plan-child disposition refuses because its tier cannot be
determined, a sanctioned way to acquire the spec-change tier record the
refusal needs. The disposition refusal itself is unchanged. Its governed CLI
surface is:

`classify-tier --repo <path> --item <work-item-id> [--json]`

- `classify-tier` MUST classify the named work-item's spec-change tier through the same spec-stated judgement the pre-dispatch wall uses.
- When the item carries no `livespec-spec-change-tier` record, it MUST append exactly one such record, with `stage: classify`.
- It MUST NOT dispatch: it creates no Fabro run, claims nothing, and leaves the item's assignee unchanged.
- When the recorded tier is not a held spec-change tier, it MUST leave the item's status and labels unchanged.
- When the recorded tier IS a held spec-change tier, the hold applies exactly as it does when filing or dispatch records that tier, and it is released only as those holds are.
- When the item's latest `livespec-spec-change-tier` record carries a behaviour digest (the digest of the item's asked-for behaviour statement that the record was judged on) equal to the digest of the item's current asked-for behaviour statement, and was taken against the current spec identity of the spec-change tier decision (§"Effective acceptance criteria"), it MUST append nothing and MUST report the existing classification.
- When the item's latest record's behaviour digest or spec identity differs from the item's current one, or the record carries no behaviour digest, it MUST take the judgement afresh and append exactly one new record with `stage: classify`, and the hold MUST apply when that record is a held spec-change tier. Scenario 344 in `scenarios.md` exercises this.
- It MUST exit non-zero, writing nothing, when the judgement cannot be obtained.

## Dispatcher loop invocation surface

Host-session dispatch and delegation MUST bind the launch obligation and
independent recovery coverage in §"Bounded session waits and observable inventory"
before reporting a protected launch. The execution inside a factory turn MUST
NOT use blocking host-session waits.

The Dispatcher's `loop` subcommand is the factory's drain entry point. Its
governed CLI surface is:

`loop --repo <path> --budget <count> [--parallel <count>] [--item <work-item-id>]... [--dry-run] [--json]`

- **This grammar is NOT exhaustive of the flags `loop` accepts.** It names
  the flags this contract GOVERNS — those that determine WHAT the run
  selects, how far it goes, and how it reports. `loop` additionally carries
  OPERATIONAL flags that tune HOW a dispatch executes rather than what it
  selects (the workflow file, the Fabro binary, the janitor ref, the journal
  path, the PR-merge poll bounds, close-on-merge, and the ledger pre-check).
  Those are IMPLEMENTATION SURFACE: this section neither enumerates nor
  freezes them, and their presence is NOT a spec→impl gap.
- **No run-mode flag.** The surface carries NO run-mode argument: there is no
  arming flag and no scope-selecting mode. The Dispatcher's dispositions are
  governed by the `dispatcher.*` policy settings (§"Dispatcher policy
  settings"), which it reads from `.livespec.jsonc` itself — never by a
  per-run mode argument. This is the same rule §"Dispatcher policy settings"
  already imposes on the console's factory-drain launcher (which "invokes the
  Dispatcher `loop` with NO per-run policy flag").
- **Default selection (no `--item`): drain the ranked queue.** With no
  `--item`, `loop` MUST select dispatch-eligible items from the ranked queue
  — the same single ranking authority the `next` surface advertises, so the
  drain order never diverges from what `next` reports (§"Work-item
  beads-issue mapping") — and dispatch them, subject to `--dry-run` below
  (which plans the identical selection but dispatches nothing). This
  unattended drain is the factory's steady-state path; it is what the
  console's factory-drain launcher invokes.
- **Clock-fired work supply.** The repository MUST ship a host-installable work-supply service and timer whose every firing starts ONE unattended drain pass for one named tenant repository: `loop --repo <tenant> --budget <count>` with NO `--item`. A firing is not a host-session launch: it reports no protected launch and arms no session wait. The pass's own Dispatcher engine owns every dispatch it admits through terminal disposition, and a pass that dies leaves its claims to §"Stranded claim release". Each pass is one bounded process; the work supply is not a daemon (constraints.md §"Process boundaries"). Each pass is therefore an ordinary unattended drain, governed by the ranked queue, `wip_cap`, every admission condition and the fail-closed unattended cost gate below exactly as any other unattended drain, and the work supply MUST NOT add, relax or bypass any of them. The installer MUST install one timer instance per named tenant repository, MUST take each instance's firing interval from the operator, and MUST refuse an instance whose credential environment wrapper is not an executable file on the host, naming the instance and the wrapper path. At each firing the service MUST resolve the plugin build it executes from the plugin install registered for that tenant repository by its governing runtime at that moment, so the next firing after a release executes the released build without reinstalling anything. When no registered install exists for the tenant, the firing MUST refuse, naming the tenant, and MUST NOT fall back to a build pinned at install time or to a guessed path. A pass whose dispatched runs are still in progress MUST NOT prevent the next firing from starting a new pass, so capacity that frees during a long pass is offered to ready work within one interval; each new pass is governed by `wip_cap` as any unattended drain is. Concurrent passes are concurrent Dispatcher engines against one tenant: this clause adds no exclusion between them, licenses no host-scoped admission lock, and does not bar a ledger-level exclusive admission under §"Per-repo WIP cap". The installer MUST state the default interval and MUST refuse an interval shorter than a documented minimum, naming the instance, the interval given and the minimum. With the work supply installed for a tenant and no interactive session running a drain, the pass started by the first firing after an item becomes admission-eligible MUST consider that item: it MUST either admit it or journal it with the exclusion reason the admission conditions every unattended drain honours (including `wip_cap` and the pass's `--budget`) assign it. A tenant whose first-ranked admission-eligible item has a free counted-claim slot and budget MUST see it dispatched by that pass.
- **`--budget <count>` (REQUIRED) bounds one invocation.** The Dispatcher
  MUST dispatch at most `budget` items in a single `loop` run. It is a
  per-run ceiling on how many items the run takes on, NOT a concurrency
  limit.
- **`--parallel <count>` (default `1`) bounds concurrency within the
  invocation.** It MUST NOT raise the per-repo WIP cap: the drain stays
  bounded by `wip_cap` (§"Per-repo WIP cap"), which remains the authority on
  the counted-claim bound — NOT a count of items at status `active`.
- **`--item <work-item-id>` (repeatable) scopes the run to hand-picked
  items.** One or more `--item` flags RESTRICT the selection to exactly the
  named work-items. `--item` NARROWS the ranked selection; it never bypasses
  it — a named item that is not dispatch-eligible (dependencies unclear, no
  resolvable assignee, no free WIP slot, resting at `pending-approval`
  under an effective `admission_policy` of `manual`, or carrying a non-null
  `factory_safety` — or, for an item carrying `rework:pending`, the rework
  re-dispatch eligibility of §"Rework-pending re-dispatch", through which a
  marked item is eligible rather than as an exception to this rule) MUST
  NOT be dispatched,
  exactly as if it were not named (§"Dispatcher admission, WIP cap, and
  post-merge acceptance"). The presence of `--item` is ALSO the contract's
  marker that a human hand-picked the dispatch and is present — the
  fail-closed cost gate below keys on it. This is the path the `drive`
  `impl:<work-item-id>` action invokes (§"The skill surface").
- **`--dry-run`: plan the selection, dispatch nothing.** `--dry-run` MUST
  compute and report exactly the selection the same invocation would dispatch
  — honoring `--budget`, the WIP cap, and any `--item` scoping — and MUST NOT
  launch a Fabro run, MUST NOT mutate the ledger, and MUST NOT write the
  work-item store. It is READ-ONLY with respect to the work-item store: the
  "what would this drain do?" surface. (Journaling the planned selection is
  permitted — the journal is an append-only audit record, not the work-item
  store.) Because a `--dry-run` invocation launches no run, it produces no
  per-run cost signal and therefore no cost-gate verdict (below). The
  Dispatcher MUST additionally report, for every work-item that was `ready`
  and considered but NOT selected, that item's identifier together with a
  single machine-stable exclusion reason. The reason MUST be drawn from a
  closed set naming at least: the WIP cap or budget being reached, an
  unsatisfied blocking dependency, and exclusion by an explicit `--item`
  filter. A ready item that was considered and not selected MUST NOT be
  omitted silently from the report. The exclusion report MUST accompany the
  selection in the same invocation's output under `--json` and on stdout,
  and MUST be distinguishable from the selection rather than merged into it,
  so a caller can tell "would be dispatched" from "was ruled out, and why".
  The exclusion report MUST NOT change what `--dry-run` selects, and this
  reporting obligation does NOT relax the read-only requirement above.
  Journaling the exclusion report alongside the planned selection is
  permitted, on the same footing the selection is granted: the journal is an
  append-only audit record and MUST NOT be the only surface carrying the
  exclusions. Where an item is excluded for more than one reason, the
  Dispatcher MUST report the reason that actually governed the exclusion
  decision rather than an arbitrary member of the set, so that acting on the
  reported reason is sufficient to change the outcome.

The Dispatcher's guarded recovery surface for an already-merged item is
`reconcile-merged --repo <path> --item <work-item-id> [--pr <number>] [--json]`
and, only after an operator has confirmed the original dispatcher process is
dead, `reconcile-merged --repo <path> --item <work-item-id> [--pr <number>]
--force [--json]`. It MUST
refuse unless the named item is currently `active`, rests in `acceptance`, or
rests at `ready` with recovery routing holding its next dispatch because the
pull request of its latest dispatch is merged (§"Factory-configurable ACP
fallback priority" → "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work"), or rests
at `pending-approval` or at `ready` without such routing because it was built
outside the factory and a merged pull request carries it. For such a locally
built item, the merged pull request MUST resolve from the head-ref or title tier
of the resolution below; a pull request that only mentions the item in its body
MUST NOT resolve it, and the valve MUST refuse naming the missing merged pull
request. The valve then applies every guard and the post-merge disposition below
exactly as for an `active` item, with the item's resting status in place of
`active` in each state effect: a green janitor writes `pending-approval ->
acceptance` or `ready -> acceptance`, and every failed guarded precondition
leaves the item at its resting status. Scenario 245 in `scenarios.md`
exercises this entry.
For an `active` item, and for such a `ready` item, this valve exists for a
dispatch whose merged PR did not complete post-run disposition. For the `ready`
item it applies every guard and the post-merge disposition below exactly as for
an `active` one, with `ready` in place of `active` in each state effect: a green
janitor writes `ready -> acceptance` where an `active` item's writes `active ->
acceptance`, and every failed guarded precondition leaves the item `ready`. For an item resting in `acceptance` it MUST NOT re-merge anything. Whether it
runs the post-merge janitor depends on what that item's latest dispatch
journaled about the janitor:

- When the item's latest dispatch journaled that its post-merge janitor did NOT
  run, the item is still OWED that janitor. That is the case when the janitor
  checkout's bootstrap failed after the merge and the dispatch parked the merged
  item in `acceptance` with a needs-attention verdict saying the janitor did not
  run. The valve MUST then run that owed post-merge janitor against the merged
  default-branch tip, under every guard, the dispatch-scoped ownership lock and
  the janitor rules that apply to an `active` item, and journal the janitor's
  result against that dispatch. Only on a green janitor MUST it then re-run the
  acceptance pass described in the next item. A red or unrunnable owed janitor
  MUST leave the item in `acceptance` with a needs-attention verdict naming the
  janitor stage and its failing target or bootstrap error. It MUST NOT close the
  item, MUST NOT re-run acceptance on that attempt, and MUST exit non-zero.
- Otherwise, the janitor already ran, and the valve MUST NOT re-run it. It MUST
  re-run only the acceptance pass of
  §"Post-merge acceptance (`acceptance → done`)" against the records now on the
  pull request, apply that pass's ordinary disposition, and write a missing
  Proof of Done pointer (§"Proof of Done record" → "The pointer"). This is the
  route by which a host-leg record posted after the original pass reaches a
  verdict.

The valve MUST decide which case applies from journaled janitor evidence, never
from the item's status alone. For an item that a factory run merged, that
evidence is the latest dispatch's janitor record. For an item that no factory
run merged, it is the janitor record of the reconciliation that established the
item's current reconciled pull request and merge SHA, which that reconciliation
MUST journal with the pull request and merge SHA it ran against. For an item
resting in `acceptance`, that evidence MUST concern the pull request and merge
SHA this invocation resolves or selects. When the journal cannot be read,
carries no such janitor record, or carries one for a different pull request or
merge SHA, the valve MUST refuse before running acceptance, name the missing or
mismatched evidence, and leave the item's status unchanged.
It MUST additionally refuse ANY item carrying the `rework:pending` label,
whatever its status, except a handed-off rework (§"Rework-pending re-dispatch"
→ "Marker lifecycle") whose own pull request merged, which §"Stranded claim
release" hold 8 completes: such an item's dispatch COMPLETED its post-run
disposition — the disposition's outcome was rework — and the remedy is the
rework route of §"Rework-pending re-dispatch" (the next drain pass, or
`dispatch --item`), which the refusal message MUST name. `--force` MUST NOT
bypass this refusal: reconciling a rework-pending item would re-run a
disposition that already ran.

A live dispatch MUST hold a dispatch-scoped ownership lock for the whole
dispatch, including the post-merge janitor and disposition window. The lock
content MUST include at least the dispatcher process id, a start timestamp, the
work-item id, and the dispatch id when one is available. Before resolving the PR
or provisioning any janitor checkout, `reconcile-merged` MUST read that lock and
refuse by default when the lock exists and its process id is alive. The refusal
message MUST report the lock age and tell the operator to confirm liveness with
`fabro ps`, wait for the janitor window to close, or use `--force` only after
confirming the original dispatcher process is dead. A stale lock whose process
id is no longer alive MUST NOT block reconciliation, because that is the
stranded-dispatch case this valve exists to recover. `--force` bypasses only the
live-lock refusal; it MUST NOT bypass source lane checks, merged-PR resolution,
post-merge janitor execution, or acceptance journaling.

The reconcile valve MUST use a janitor checkout path that is distinct from the
normal dispatch loop's `janitor-<work-item-id>` path, such as
`janitor-reconcile-<work-item-id>`. This path ownership rule is independent of
the liveness lock: even if a guard is stale, absent, or bypassed with `--force`,
a reconcile run MUST NOT preclean or remove the live dispatch's janitor
checkout. The post-merge janitor MAY still hold a per-checkout lock before
precleaning or provisioning, and that lock MUST continue to block concurrent
callers that target the same checkout path.

The valve MUST resolve the PR number and merge SHA from GitHub, among pull
requests merged onto the default branch (the search MUST include a
default-branch base filter), by ranking the candidates in three tiers: first a
pull request whose head ref is the expected `feat/<work-item-id>` branch, then
one whose title carries the work-item id, then one whose body mentions the
work-item id. The valve MUST resolve from the highest tier that holds any
candidate and MUST NOT let a candidate of a lower tier make a higher tier's
resolution ambiguous. If that highest tier holds more than one candidate, the
valve MUST refuse with a clear ambiguous-PR error listing that tier's candidates
rather than silently choosing the first result. Scenario 244 in `scenarios.md`
exercises this ranking.
The valve MUST also accept an optional `--pr <number>` selector naming one
merged pull request of the item, for an item that landed through more than one
merged pull request. With the selector, the valve MUST resolve that pull request
and its merge SHA from GitHub instead of ranking candidates, and MUST NOT refuse
because other merged pull requests identify the item. It MUST refuse, naming the
pull request, when that pull request is not merged onto the default branch or
does not identify the item by head ref or title. A selected pull request then
stands in every later step of the valve exactly as a resolved one does, and the
valve MUST journal the selected pull request's number and merge SHA in the
reconciliation's journal record. Without the selector the ranking above is
unchanged. The
valve MUST NOT require or trust ledger audit metadata for that resolution. After
a merged PR resolves, the valve MUST NOT launch Fabro and MUST NOT rebuild the
change; it reruns the same post-merge janitor used by the dispatch engine
against a fresh checkout of the merged ref. A green janitor MUST enter the
existing post-merge acceptance path unchanged, including the `active ->
acceptance` ledger-complete write, acceptance journal records, and
policy-governed `acceptance -> done` auto-accept when applicable. A red janitor,
missing merged PR, wrong source lane, ambiguous merged PR, or held janitor
checkout lock MUST leave the item `active` (or at its resting status, for an
item that entered at `pending-approval` or `ready`) and report the failed
guarded precondition or janitor stage. This is a distinct guarded entry path and does
not widen the `drive move` target set; `acceptance`, `done`, `pending-approval`,
and `active` remain forbidden `move` targets.

### Stale publish-branch reclaim before a re-dispatch

A run that terminates AFTER `publish_draft` pushed its branch leaves that
branch on origin. The next dispatch of the same item is a NEW run whose
head is not a descendant of the dead run's tip, so `publish_draft`'s plain
fast-forward push is refused non-fast-forward, and the only remedy that
refusal can name — clear the branch by hand — discards the dead run's
published head and every record attached to it. The Dispatcher therefore
reclaims the branch on the host, before the run exists, as a pre-dispatch act
of both `dispatch` and `loop` for every selected item. It runs after the
admission valve, for the items admission selected to launch, and only for those
whose recovery route is `fresh` or `seeded` (§"Factory-configurable ACP
fallback priority" → "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work"). A
deferred item keeps its branch and any pull request on it. It runs AFTER
the dispatch preamble's orphan reconciliation (§"A factory run never
awaits a human"), so a run that reconciliation terminated is already
terminal when the reclaim asks; the live-run hold below covers the run
reconciliation could not or did not terminate.

- **Only a re-dispatch asks.** An *earlier dispatch* of an item is a
  record that names a run id or a declared dispatch id for the item in the
  dispatch journal of ANY worktree of this repository, meaning every
  checkout that shares its git common directory; a dry-run plan and a
  pre-run refusal are not earlier dispatches. A dispatch journaled only on
  another host is invisible here, in which case the reclaim does not run
  and `publish_draft` refuses exactly as it did before the reclaim existed.
  A worktree journal that cannot be read MUST be journaled as
  `publish-branch-reclaim-held` with the reason `journal-unobservable`,
  naming the path, rather than read as no earlier dispatch. Scenario 225 in
  `scenarios.md` exercises this bullet. For an item with no earlier dispatch the Dispatcher MUST NOT
  query origin for a surviving publish branch: a first dispatch has no
  possible yes, and a remote probe on that path would put a forge outage
  on the critical path of every dispatch. For any other item it MUST ask
  origin (`ls-remote`, never a local remote-tracking ref) whether the
  item's publish branch survives and at which head.
- **Liveness is asked of every factory the journal names.** The
  Dispatcher MUST ask each factory that any earlier dispatch of the item
  names (resolved through `dispatcher.factories`) whether a run whose id
  the journal records for the item is non-terminal; a factory that does
  not answer makes the measurement `factory-unobservable`, and a factory
  that answers that it holds no such run has answered that the run is not
  live.
- **A dead run's branch is preserved, then cleared.** When the branch
  survives and no asked factory reports a live run for the item, the
  Dispatcher MUST first create the preservation ref
  `refs/livespec/preserved-publish/<work-item-id>/<head>` on origin at
  that head, and only then delete the publish branch. Because the head is
  part of the ref name, preserving the same head twice is a no-op and two
  different dead heads of one item preserve to two refs; a preservation
  ref MUST NOT be updated to a different object. The journal MUST carry
  one `publish-branch-reclaim` record naming the branch, the head and the
  preservation ref; that record is the forward pointer from any earlier
  preserve-by-reference comment that named the branch. Deleting the branch
  closes the draft pull request the dead run opened on it; that pull
  request and every record on it remain readable. `publish_draft` is
  unchanged here: it pushes a plain fast-forward and MUST rewrite no ref
  except, on the visit that follows a refresh-repair round, the run's own
  publish branch over the run's previously published head, established from
  its publication record when the run has recorded one and otherwise from its
  validated resume provenance, with an explicit lease against the recorded
  remote head of this run's own publish branch ("Refresh repair" above). The
  reclaim is a HOST-side act because the host is the one party that can answer
  whether the run that pushed the branch is still alive, and every other
  lease-guarded rewrite of a publish branch belongs to the `pr_refresh` node.
- **Every arm that cannot measure holds, and says so.** When origin
  cannot be asked, when a factory cannot be asked, when a factory reports
  a live run for the item, or when the preserve or the delete fails, the
  Dispatcher MUST leave the branch exactly as it stands and MUST journal
  one `publish-branch-reclaim-held` record naming the reason (one of
  `journal-unobservable`, `origin-unobservable`, `factory-unobservable`,
  `live-run`, or the failed ref operation), the branch and head where
  established, and the live run
  ids on the live-run arm. A hold MUST NOT refuse the dispatch: the
  dispatch proceeds and `publish_draft` refuses the non-fast-forward push
  exactly as it did before the reclaim existed, so the worst outcome of
  the reclaim is the refusal it was added to remove. A reclaim MUST NOT
  proceed on an unobservable answer, because a gauge that proceeds when
  blinded turns an honest refusal into a silent ref deletion whose record
  reads like a healthy reclaim.
- **Acceptance attribution survives the reclaim.** A verified record the
  dead run published on the pull request the reclaim closes remains
  attributable to that dead dispatch under §"Post-merge acceptance
  (`acceptance → done`)" → "The proof evidence leg". The reclaim changes
  which branch the NEXT run publishes, never which dispatch a record
  belongs to. An operator who wants to KEEP that work drives the resume
  below instead of a plain dispatch; the two routes are exclusive per
  dispatch and the journal shows which one ran. For an item released under
  §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" → "Provider-limit release and
  re-dispatch", released by that section's adapter launch release, or released
  after a first stall cancel under §"Dispatcher progress watchdog", the
  Dispatcher makes that choice itself as that
  section's "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work" specifies.

Scenario 144 in `scenarios.md` exercises this section. The resume surface
below is the route that KEEPS the dead run's work; this reclaim is the
route that makes a fresh start possible without a hand edit, and a resume
MUST NOT run it.

### Resume from a published pull request (`resume --item`)

The Dispatcher's recovery surface for an item whose earlier run published
a pull request and then terminated before merging it is
`resume --repo <path> --item <work-item-id> [--factory <name>] [--invoker <id>] [--json]`.
A plain re-dispatch of such an item starts at `implement` and spends a
full sandbox rebuilding, re-capturing and re-verifying work that already
exists on the pull request; the resume FINISHES the earlier run instead.
It is a published state-changing entry point and inherits `--invoker`
(§"Journal invoker attribution"). `drive` gains no new action for it;
the `impl:<id>` action remains a plain dispatch. The exceptions to both
statements are an item released under §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback
priority" → "Provider-limit release and re-dispatch", an item released by that
section's adapter launch release, an item released after a first stall
cancel under §"Dispatcher progress watchdog", and an item released for recovery
under §"Stranded claim release" → "Stale assignee clearance": for each the Dispatcher
itself invokes this resume, under its own invoker identity, when every
precondition below passes, and otherwise follows the recovery routing of that
section's "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work", which dispatches a
plain run seeded from the failed run's preserved work, a fresh run, or holds the
dispatch, as that routing specifies.

**What it resumes.** The *earlier run* is the dispatch whose identifier
the latest proof record on the item's open pull request carries, resolved
through the dispatch journal by the run identifier on its first line, accepting
for each journaled dispatch the identifiers the legacy match accepts (§"Post-merge acceptance (`acceptance → done`)" → "The proof
evidence leg"); a record published before this clause was ratified names
no head and cannot anchor a resume. The *published head* is the full
commit sha that record names (§"Proof of Done record" → "The record").
When no proof record on the pull request carries the identifier of the
item's latest journaled dispatch, and that dispatch's journal carries a
`watchdog-stall-cancel` record or a `run-wall-budget-exceeded` record
(§"Dispatcher progress watchdog"), or a `credential-use-deadline-reached` record
(§"Worker credential projection"), naming a published head, that cancel
record anchors the resume instead, under every restriction below. A proof
record that carries the dispatch's identifier always takes precedence over
a cancel record. The cancel record anchors only when its stage is
`proof_capture`, or when the run was between its last completed
`publish_draft` and `proof_capture`. A cancel in any other stage, including
a later `janitor`, `fix` or `publish_draft` of a rework loop, does not
anchor, because its head would not carry the rework. Under this anchor the
earlier run is that dispatch, the published head is the head the record
names, and the resumed-at stage is `proof_capture`. The factory's own record
of the run, when the factory still holds it, takes precedence for the stage.
The resume record MUST name the factory record as the source that decided
the stage when that record is available; when the factory authoritatively
reports that it no longer holds the run, the cancel record decides the
stage and the resume record MUST name it as the source.
When the pull request's current head differs from the head the latest proof record names, the earlier run's own republication anchors the resume instead, and only from the factory's own record of that run. That anchor applies when the factory that the earlier dispatch names still holds the earlier run and its record shows ALL of the following: (a) the run completed a `publish_draft` visit after the visit that published the latest proof record; (b) the published head the run's terminal checkpoint carries equals the pull request's current head; (c) the head the latest proof record names is an ancestor of that head; and (d) the run terminated while executing `proof_capture`, or between that completed `publish_draft` visit and `proof_capture`. Under this anchor the earlier run is that run, the published head is the pull request's current head, the resumed-at stage is `proof_capture`, and the resume record MUST name the factory record as the source that decided both. When the factory answers that it no longer holds the run, or cannot be read, this anchor does not apply and the moved-head refusal below stands. Because the resumed run enters at `proof_capture`, fresh capture, review and replay run on the published head, and the earlier record is never read as proof of it.
The *resumed-at stage* is the node the earlier run was executing when it
terminated (an earlier `pr` entry MUST normalize to `pr_refresh`), or, when it terminated between nodes, the target of the edge
its last succeeded node's outcome selected. The Dispatcher MUST read it
from the earlier run's record on the factory the earlier dispatch names;
when that factory answers that it no longer holds the run, the Dispatcher
MUST derive the stage from the verdict of the latest record carrying the
earlier run's identifier — `verified`: `pr_refresh`; `captured`: `review`;
`not_captured` or a behaviour `not_reproduced`: `fix`; a fidelity
`not_reproduced`: `proof_capture`, read from the record's own
classification of each difference; no such record:
`proof_capture` — and the resume record MUST name which source decided
it. When the earlier run terminated through `exit` after `pr` armed auto-merge, the resumed-at stage is `pr_refresh`, and the resume record MUST name the factory record as the source that decided it. An authoritative not-found answer from the factory observes the run
as not live; only an unanswered or errored query is unobservable.

**What a resume does.** A resume is a hand-picked dispatch: it MUST
admit the item through the ordinary admission valve (`ready → active`),
subject to every dispatch-eligibility rule of §"Dispatcher admission, WIP
cap, and post-merge acceptance" and §"Dispatcher loop invocation surface"
(dependencies, the WIP cap, `admission_policy`, `factory_safety`,
`rework:pending`), hold the dispatch-scoped ownership lock, run the
host-side mechanical wall of §"Effective acceptance criteria", resolve its factory through the selection order of §"Factory
addresses resolved from a host registry", taking that order's resume-only
recorded-factory step, and including `LIVESPEC_FABRO_FACTORY` and factory
overflow selection, declare a dispatch
id to the sandbox, and journal exactly as a dispatch does — including the
§"Fail-closed cost gate (keyed on `--item` presence)" record, under
the hand-picked posture. It MUST
additionally journal one `resume` record before the run exists naming the
earlier run's identifiers, the pull request number, the published head,
the resumed-at stage and the source that decided it. It MUST NOT run the
stale publish-branch reclaim above: the surviving publish branch is the
branch the run resumes on, and no preservation ref is created.

The resumed run MUST run the workflow the earlier run's dispatch record names
(`workflow_name`), with a sandbox that checks out the publish branch at the
published head, entered at the resumed-at stage; it MUST NOT visit `dod_gate`
or `implement`, or replay a completed node on an unchanged head. Its run record
MUST distinguish entry from subsequent rework: a changed-head `pr_refresh` MUST
take the decision of §"Definition-of-Done and Proof-of-Done stages" → "Proof
carry-forward across a refresh", and on `reproof_required` MUST run fresh
capture, review and replay even if those nodes completed on the earlier head.
The three-refresh bound starts at zero for each resumed run; the existing
two-resume host bound still applies. A resume MUST NOT write or clear the
item's `dispatch_workflow` metadata, so the next plain dispatch of the item
re-runs the recorded workflow from `start` as §"Self-contained plugin dispatch"
→ "Named workflow variants" provides. Whether the engine is entered at the
resumed-at node directly or through a graph the Dispatcher derives from that
workflow for the one run is implementation surface, bounded by `constraints.md`
§"Fabro runtime constraints"; a derived graph is not a registered variant, is
never selectable by the variant precedence, and is never recorded as the item's
workflow. Entering at the resumed-at stage means no node precedes it in the
resumed run, so the latest record on the pull request when that stage starts is
the one the earlier run left there. From the resumed-at stage onward the run
behaves as the same stage does in a first run: a `review` that requests changes
still re-enters `janitor`, `publish_draft` and `proof_capture` before `review`
(§"Definition-of-Done and Proof-of-Done stages"), the `pr_refresh` node still
rebases and force-pushes only its own branch, and the resumed run's outcome
maps to §"Dispatcher exit codes" as a `dispatch --item` outcome does. Because
the proof-loop caps of that section are per run, the chain is bounded on the
host instead: the Dispatcher MUST refuse a THIRD resume of the same item from
the same pull request (remedy: a plain dispatch).

**Attribution.** The earlier run's `captured` and `verified` records are
the resumed dispatch's own: the `resume` record links the earlier run's
identifiers to the resumed dispatch, transitively through a chain of
resumes, and the acceptance pass MUST attribute a record carrying any
identifier so linked to the resumed dispatch, so a `verified` record the
earlier run published grades the resumed run's merge. The Proof of Done
pointer written for a resumed item MUST name the resumed run's identifier
beside the record's own run id (§"Proof of Done record" → "The
pointer"). A record the resumed run publishes carries the resumed run's
identifier as any record does. Nothing else about acceptance changes: a
resumed item closes through §"Post-merge acceptance (`acceptance →
done`)" and Scenario 138 as any other.

**Refusals.** The resume MUST refuse — before the admission valve, before
any run exists and before touching any ref — as a precondition error
(exit `3`, §"Dispatcher exit codes"), naming the mismatch and the
remedy, when:

- the item is not `ready`, naming its status (remedy:
  `resolve-blocked:<id>:ready` for an item resting at `blocked /
  needs-human`; `reconcile-runs` for a stranded claim that §"Stranded claim
  release" reconciles; and, for an `active` item whose run is terminal,
  which that release does not reconcile, and which carries neither
  `rework:pending` nor a `merge-hold:` label (those keep their own routes,
  §"Rework-pending re-dispatch" and §"Dispatcher policy settings" → "The
  per-item merge hold"): no status move, naming the condition, when a live
  process holds the item's dispatch-scoped ownership lock or that lock
  cannot be read; otherwise, when the forge reports the item's pull request
  merged, `reconcile-merged` if that command's own preconditions hold for
  the item and, if one does not, no status move, naming the failing
  precondition; `move:<id>:ready` when the forge was read and reports no
  merged pull request; and no status move, naming the failed read, when the
  forge cannot be read) — a resume never steps
  around the ledger's human decision. The named remedy MUST be one that
  changes that item's state; a refusal MUST NOT name a remedy that would
  leave the item unchanged. Scenario 221 in `scenarios.md` exercises the
  remedy rule. For a resume the Dispatcher routes
  itself, this bullet is graded at recovery routing, before admission, and not
  again after the claim;
- the item's publish branch carries no open pull request, or no proof
  record on it names a head and no `watchdog-stall-cancel` record anchors
  one as above (remedy: a plain dispatch);
- the pull request's current head does not equal the published head,
  naming both shas, and no republication anchor applies as above (remedy: a plain dispatch, which reclaims the
  branch). A `pr_refresh` node that rebased and pushed before terminating leaves
  exactly this state, and the refusal is deliberate: proof verified on
  one tree is not proof of another;
- the item's current Definition of Done section differs from the earlier
  run's dispatch-time snapshot, naming the difference (remedy: a plain
  dispatch), so the inherited records prove exactly the assertions the
  resumed dispatch is graded on and the resumed dispatch's snapshot is
  the earlier run's;
- the earlier run is live on its factory, naming the run id and its
  status (remedy: wait for the run to end, or reconcile it per §"A
  factory run never awaits a human"); this check runs after the
  preamble's orphan reconciliation, so it names a run that
  reconciliation could not or did not terminate, and an item `active`
  under that live claim is refused on this bullet AND the not-ready
  bullet together;
- the item's dispatch-scoped ownership lock exists and its process is
  alive, naming the lock age, as `reconcile-merged` refuses;
- the pull request is closed, or it is merged and the item is not in the
  case of "A proof-only resume of a merged pull request" below, naming the
  state. For a merged
  pull request the remedy is `reconcile-merged --item`, which requires a
  real merge and stays the only valve for one, and the refusal names it
  only when that command's own preconditions hold for the item; while one
  does not hold (a live or unreadable ownership lock among them), the
  refusal names that condition in place of the remedy;
- the pull request has already anchored two resumes, naming them (remedy:
  a plain dispatch);
- the item holds a needs-human ref or a failed-checkpoint preservation ref, as §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" → "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work" defines them, or a run's latest preserved capture, that belongs to the run that published the pull request's current head or to a later run of the item, whose tip commit descends from that head and whose tip tree differs from that head's tree, naming the ref, its tip and the head (remedy: a plain dispatch, which recovery routing seeds from that ref). The run a ref belongs to is established exactly as that section establishes it. A ref whose run cannot be established is graded by that section's `publishing-run-unobservable` hold, not by this bullet. An ancestry or tree comparison this bullet needs that cannot be taken is the unreadable-measurement refusal below, and MUST NOT be read as the absence of such a ref.

When more than one refusal applies, the refusal MUST name every
applicable mismatch, in the order listed, each with its remedy; a
refusal that names only the first does not satisfy this clause. When the forge cannot report the pull request's head or state, or a
factory cannot report the earlier run's liveness, the resume MUST refuse
with the same exit code naming the measurement it could not take; it
MUST NOT proceed on an unobservable answer. A refusal leaves the item,
the branch and the pull request exactly as they stood.

**A proof-only resume of a merged pull request.** When the item's pull request is merged and the item rests in `acceptance` parked NEEDS_ATTENTION by the proof evidence leg of the acceptance pass because no applicable counted `proof_verify` record grades each of its `factory_captured` assertions on the merged head, whether no such record exists or the record it was graded on carries no per-assertion verdict, `resume --item` MUST take the proof-only arm instead of refusing on the merged pull request. The arm is not limited to an item that an earlier run published. For an item that no factory run merged, the merged pull request is the one "The host leg" of "Proof of Done record" defines as the pull request of its latest merged run, so a hand-finished merge qualifies, and the same holds for an item whose run ended in `publish_draft` or `refresh_repair` after the merge and never reached the proof stages. For any merged pull request in this case, `resume --item` MUST take the arm whatever ended the item's earlier run, if there was one, and MUST NOT re-enter the implement path. An item parked for an `unbindable` record is not in this case; its clearing action is a superseding record. The arm is exempt from the refusals that assume an unmerged item resting in `ready`: the item rests in `acceptance` and stays there throughout, it needs no open pull request, no anchoring proof record and no published-head match, and it makes no claim through admission. Its anchor is the confirmed merged pull request, that pull request's head commit at merge, and the parking record that names the proof leg, and the dispatch journal MUST record those three as the resume's provenance. The refusals for a live earlier run, a live ownership lock, a measurement the resume cannot take, and the two-resume limit still apply. The refusal for a live earlier run tests an earlier run only where one exists, so an item with no earlier run is not refused for the want of one. The arm MUST check out the pull request's head commit at merge, never the default-branch merge commit, read-only, and MUST run only `proof_capture`, `proof_verify` and `proof_grade` against it: a successful capture routes to `proof_verify`, a `verified` outcome routes to `proof_grade`, and every outcome of `proof_grade` and every other outcome of capture or verification ends the run. The arm's graph MUST carry no edge to any stage outside those three, apart from ending the run. It MUST run no implement, review, janitor, publication or merge stage, MUST push nothing and MUST open no branch or pull request. The run is associated with the existing pull request, so that the proof broker of "Publication is mechanically confined to the scripted publication stages" posts its records there. Every record the arm publishes MUST be posted as a new comment on the existing merged pull request through the posting primitive, bound by "Proof of Done record" → "The binding" to the item, that pull request and its head commit at merge, and carrying the resumed run's identifier. A `proof_verify` record the arm publishes MUST carry each `factory_captured` assertion's own `Reproduced:` line, graded by the same `proof_grade` node the implement workflow uses. When the arm ends, the Dispatcher MUST re-run the acceptance pass for the item, as `reconcile-merged` does, and that pass reads the new records by their binding through the same Proof of Done record reader that grades them. The acceptance pass that follows the arm is a re-run of a parked item. When it fails an assertion the arm did not reproduce, the item MUST stay in `acceptance` with a parking record naming each such assertion and the arm's record. That pass MUST NOT stamp rework, move the item to `blocked`, or count toward the rework cap, whatever the item's acceptance policy, and the arm never routes to `fix`. The arm counts toward the pull request's two-resume limit. Measured 2026-10-26: bd-ib-svm3fe's pull request 3731 merged with no Proof of Done record, reconcile-merged parked it NEEDS_ATTENTION on its proof leg, and it had to be accepted by hand; the merged-reconcile ending of "A pull request merged before its refresh" writes no proof record by design, so every item it ends leaves its merged head unproven unless this arm exists. Scenarios 257 and 277 in `scenarios.md` exercise this paragraph.

**Unchanged.** `publish_draft` still pushes a plain fast-forward and MUST
rewrite no ref except, on the visit that follows a refresh-repair round, the
run's own publish branch over the run's previously published head, established
from its publication record when the run has recorded one and otherwise from
its validated resume provenance, with an explicit lease against the recorded
remote head of this run's own publish branch; apart from that one
republication, the `pr_refresh` node's lease-guarded force push stays the only
rewrite of a publish branch; `reconcile-merged` still refuses an
unmerged pull request; and a plain `dispatch` or `loop` of the same item
still reclaims the stale publish branch under the section above.
Scenario 142 and Scenario 143 in `scenarios.md` exercise this section.

### Fail-closed cost gate (keyed on `--item` presence)

- **Gate coverage — which runs are gated at all.** The cost gate applies
  only to a dispatched run that reached a successful terminal outcome and
  carries a confirmed run record (a run id resolvable against the cost
  source). Observation of failed-run and availability-probe cost is
  independent of gate applicability. Two classes of run are therefore NOT
  gated:
  - A run that did NOT reach a successful terminal outcome yields no gate
    verdict — even though such a run MAY have consumed spend. A run
    released for a provider-limit failure additionally yields the
    attempt-cost record of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" →
    "Cost follows every attempt", which is an observation and never a gate
    verdict.
  - A run whose id CANNOT be resolved against the cost source MUST be
    journaled as a **skipped** gate record naming the work-item and the
    unresolvable-run-id reason, and MUST NOT refuse. This disposition is
    **FAIL-OPEN** — deliberately, and it stays fail-open even under the
    `enforce` posture with no `--item`.
- **Verdict keying.** For a GATED run whose cost signal is **UNOBSERVABLE**
  (no cost is readable for the run), the verdict is keyed on **whether the
  invocation named an `--item`** — the contract's proxy for whether a human
  is present:
  - **No `--item` — an unattended queue drain, no human present.** An
    unobservable cost is a **fail-closed REFUSAL**: the Dispatcher MUST stop
    picking rather than keep dispatching cost-blind.
  - **One or more `--item` — a hand-picked dispatch, a human present.** The
    same condition is a **WARNING**, never a refusal.
- **An OBSERVED cost never trips this gate.** Cost-VALUE enforcement (per-run
  and per-session spend ceilings) is a separate concern; this gate fires only
  on the unobservable condition.
- **Journaling.** Every GATED run MUST produce a gate record on the existing
  Dispatcher journal, carrying at minimum the work-item id, the run id,
  whether the cost was observable, the severity, and whether the run refused;
  an unresolvable run id MUST produce the skipped record above. No gated run
  goes unrecorded.
- **Enforcement posture (the always-wired severity lever).** Whether a keyed
  verdict is DERIVED and APPLIED is governed by the `LIVESPEC_COST_MODE`
  environment variable, whose only recognized values are `report` and
  `enforce`. In `report` (the **DEFAULT** — the subscription-billing posture,
  under which provider-side spend limits already bound spend, so a
  fail-closed dollar gate is the wrong model) a gate record MUST still be
  journaled, carrying the observability of the cost signal — but NO keyed
  verdict is derived and none is applied: the record's severity is `report`,
  and the Dispatcher MUST NOT refuse and MUST NOT apply a cost cap. In
  `enforce` (the opt-in posture for metered API billing) the keyed verdict
  above MUST be derived and the fail-closed refusal MUST be applied. An unset
  or unrecognized value MUST resolve to `report`. The lever is a SEVERITY
  switch, not a wiring carve-out — the cost signal is still observed and a
  gate record is still journaled regardless of its value. (This is the same
  always-wired-lever shape §"Closed-item-integrity check" uses for
  `LIVESPEC_CLOSED_ITEM_INTEGRITY`.)

## Dispatcher admission, WIP cap, and post-merge acceptance

Two human-delegable policy gates bracket the WIP-limited machine-driven
middle of the lifecycle — **`approve`** (`pending-approval → ready`) and
**`accept`** (`acceptance → done`). The **Dispatcher (`dispatcher.py`
`dispatch`/`loop`) is the sole enforcer** of the mechanical admission
valve (`ready → active`), the WIP cap, and the acceptance valve; the
console only commands (a human triggers `approve` for a manual item
resting at `pending-approval`, through the `drive` human-valve
actions) and observes — it never enforces. This realizes the
repo-agnostic two-valve pattern for the Beads/Fabro Dispatcher; the state machine + the valve semantics are the cross-repo design of record (repo `thewoolleyman/livespec`, `plan/archive/work-item-state-machine/research/03-decision-log.md`, decisions 26/32).

### Admission valve (`ready → active`)

By the time an item is `ready` it is, by definition, already approved
(approval ≡ `ready` membership — entering `ready` IS approving; see
§"Work-item state semantics"). So the valve's remaining conditions are
mechanical — capacity, dependencies, a resolvable assignee, and factory-safety:

- **Permission** was settled upstream at the `pending-approval → ready`
  (`approve`) transition, governed by the item's effective
  `admission_policy` (resolved per §"The five policy settings" →
  `dispatcher.auto_approve_ready`: a committed setting wins over a stored
  label; otherwise the stored label governs and `None` inherits the shipped
  default): `auto` auto-approves into `ready` — at capture/groom time, or on
  a subsequent Dispatcher pass for an item resting at `pending-approval`; an
  effective `manual` (from a committed `false` setting, from a stored label
  where the setting is not committed, or from the shipped default) rests at
  `pending-approval` until a human's explicit `approve`. The
  `admission_policy` field is the first-class realization that
  **replaces the prior `human-gated` text marker** — risky / irreversible
  work is held at the `approve` gate (resting at `pending-approval`), never
  by a pre-merge acceptance gate. It does NOT carry the prior `host-only`
  marker's role: `admission_policy` gates PERMISSION (does a human
  approve?), which is ORTHOGONAL to RUNNABILITY (can an agent sandbox run
  this work at all?). Runnability is the separate `factory_safety` axis
  (§"Work-item beads-issue mapping"), enforced at this same valve (below).
  The
  Dispatcher MUST NOT hold an item at `ready` awaiting a human — an item
  awaiting a human's permission MUST NOT be in `ready`.
- **Capacity:** a free WIP slot under the per-repo cap
  (`counted_claims < wip_cap`, §"Per-repo WIP cap"; a rework re-dispatch's
