The commit's parent MUST be the run's base commit, which is the commit the dispatch's sandbox checked out and which the dispatch record MUST name, and its tree MUST reflect every change the run made relative to that commit, removals included. The publication MUST create the blobs, the tree, the commit and the ref through the forge's Git Data API, and MUST NOT run `git push` or any repository hook. The published commit is a recovery artifact, not a commit to land: a seed taken from it under §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" → "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work" MUST record the run's base commit as the seed's immutable commit SHA and this ref as its preservation reference, so that checking out the recorded SHA and taking the published tree onto it as uncommitted work are one act, and MUST NOT carry the hookless commit itself. In that clause's preference order, this ref counts as the failed run's successfully preserved terminal tree, so it MUST be preferred over the run's observed published head and over any preserved-publish ref of an earlier head, subject to that clause's run-age bound: it MUST NOT be preferred over a head published by a later run of the item. When the publication succeeds, the Dispatcher MUST add one ledger comment to the item, before the item's blocked transition, that opens with the marker line `livespec-preserved-tree` and names the run id, the factory name, the preservation ref and its commit id. When the changed files cannot be read, or any step of the publication fails, the Dispatcher MUST add a ledger comment with the same marker line stating that the tree was not preserved and naming the step that failed (the files read, a blob, the tree, the commit, or the ref), and the item MUST still rest `blocked` with `blocked_reason: needs-human`; a failed preservation MUST NOT change the dispatch outcome or its exit code. Either comment MUST carry names and figures only, MUST pass the shared template-opener detector before it is written, and, when it fails the detector or cannot be written, MUST be journaled with its reason and MUST NOT prevent the blocked transition. When the Dispatcher has observed a terminal patch on the run's terminal event, it MUST NOT create a preservation ref for that run, and the existing preserve-by-reference pointer with the patch's size and digest stands alone. A terminal patch the Dispatcher could not observe because the run's events cannot be read does not count as observed, so the publication above MUST be attempted: a duplicate preservation is recoverable, while a missed one is not. Scenario 183 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A janitor-green run that a factory restart or an outside cancel ends is published to a preservation ref.** A run is JANITOR-GREEN when its `janitor` stage has succeeded. Its committed branch head then carries work that passed the full check suite, and only its sandbox holds that head until `publish_draft` pushes it. When a factory operator must cancel active runs to idle a factory server for a restart or upgrade, the operator MUST cancel through the Dispatcher's `cancel-for-restart --factory <name>` command rather than the server's cancel endpoint alone. For each active run of that factory that is janitor-green and that has not reported its branch published, the command MUST first read the run's changed files, with their contents, from the run's factory target, and publish them exactly as the preceding paragraph publishes a checkpoint-failed tree: one commit at `refs/livespec/preserved-publish/<work-item-id>/<commit-sha>`, parented on the run's base commit, created through the forge's Git Data API with no `git push` and no repository hook. Only then MUST it cancel that run. A run that is not janitor-green MUST be cancelled without a publication. When the read or any publication step fails, the command MUST still cancel the run, and it MUST record the failed step in the `livespec-preserved-tree` ledger comment that this paragraph requires below; the preservation is best effort and MUST NOT hold a factory restart. When the Dispatcher reports a run that was cancelled outside the Dispatcher and that was janitor-green, and no `livespec-preserved-tree` comment already names that run, it MUST attempt the same read and publication from the dispatch's resolved factory target. In both cases it MUST add the `livespec-preserved-tree` ledger comment of the preceding paragraph, naming the run id, the factory name, the preservation ref and its commit id, or stating that the tree was not preserved and naming the step that failed. A later dispatch of that item MUST carry the newest such preservation ref in its brief as the tree to start from, under the same preference order that §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" → "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work" gives a checkpoint-failed run's preserved tree. These rules change no dispatch outcome, exit code or `blocked_reason` that a cancelled run already receives. Scenario 306 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**Each committing step of a run preserves the run branch's tip to an ordered work-in-progress ref.** A run's *work-in-progress refs* are the refs `refs/livespec/wip/<work-item-id>/<run-id>/<n>`, where `<n>` is a decimal capture ordinal starting at 1. A *preserving step* is every command step of the implement-work-item workflow that settles or makes an agent stage's commits (in the single-implement graph, `implement_commit_settle`, `fix_commit_settle` and `review_fix_commit_settle`) and the needs-human preservation step of §"A factory run never awaits a human". At its end, before the run takes its next transition or ends, a preserving step MUST preserve the tip of the run branch `fabro/run/<run-id>`, as follows. It MUST read the run branch's tip, never the workspace `HEAD`. It MUST NOT preserve a tip whose tree equals the tree of the run's base commit or the tree of the default branch's head on origin, because the engine's checkpoint moves the run branch onto the workspace `HEAD` whenever a node leaves `HEAD` detached, and such a tip carries none of the run's work. It MUST NOT preserve a tip equal to the commit of the run's highest-numbered work-in-progress ref. Otherwise it MUST create the run's next work-in-progress ref, numbered one above the highest existing one, at that tip. A work-in-progress ref MUST be created once and never updated, deleted or force-written while its item is open, so every capture stays fetchable in order. The push MUST NOT create a commit, move `HEAD`, change the index or change the working tree; it MUST run with the repository's hooks disabled and with repository-controlled git configuration that could redirect or observe the push ignored; and the tooling that holds the push credential MUST be the Dispatcher-materialized sandbox tooling outside the run's working tree, which no agent stage can modify. A preservation that fails or is skipped MUST NOT change the step's outcome or stop the run, and MUST be reported in the step's own recorded output naming the ref, the tip and the reason. The run is then preserved through its last successful capture, and a later capture retries. The needs-human preservation step keeps its own `refs/heads/needs-human/<run-id>` ref, and the commit it pushes there MUST be built on the run branch's tip under the same tree guard, never on a detached `HEAD`. A work-in-progress ref is a recovery artifact, not a branch to publish: no pull request is opened from it, and no publication stage reads it. The run's *latest preserved capture* is its highest-numbered work-in-progress ref. A repository check MUST fail when the workflow declares a step that settles or makes an agent stage's commits without this preservation. Scenario 317 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A run's ending names its latest preserved capture on the item.** When the Dispatcher records a run's ending that is not a merge, or releases an item whose run is absent from its factory, it MUST list the run's work-in-progress refs on the forge and add one `livespec-preserved-tree` ledger comment to the item naming the run id, the factory name, the run's latest preserved capture and its commit id, or stating that the run has no work-in-progress ref. The comment MUST also name every needs-human ref and every failed-checkpoint preservation ref, as §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" → "Recovery from the failed run's preserved work" defines them, that was published at the same run's ending, each with its tip commit id and the size of the diff between that tip and its merge-base with the default branch, stated as files changed, insertions and deletions and measured with the top-level `.fabro` directory excluded. When the run has no work-in-progress ref but such a ref exists, the comment MUST name that ref as the run's preserved work and MUST NOT consist only of the statement that the run has no work-in-progress ref. A preserved ref whose measured diff is empty MUST be named with that empty diff, so the comment states in figures that it preserves no change. When a ref's diff cannot be measured, the comment MUST name the ref and say that its diff could not be determined, which is distinct from an empty diff. When the run has neither a work-in-progress ref nor such a ref, the comment MUST say that the run preserved no tree. When the forge cannot be read, the comment MUST say that the preservation could not be determined, which is distinct from the run having none. When a `livespec-preserved-tree` comment already names the same run and the same latest capture, the Dispatcher MUST NOT add a second one. The comment MUST obey the template-opener and failure rules that the checkpoint-failed paragraph above states for its own comment, and writing it MUST NOT delay or prevent any cancel, removal or state transition. Scenario 318 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**Preservation refs are deleted when the Dispatcher closes or collects an item's runs.** When the Dispatcher itself moves a work item to `closed`, including by acceptance, it MUST delete from the item's repository every ref under `refs/livespec/wip/<work-item-id>/` and `refs/livespec/preserved-publish/<work-item-id>/`. When its ended-run collection removes an ended run of a `closed` item, it MUST delete that run's work-in-progress refs, its `refs/heads/needs-human/<run-id>` ref, and the item's refs under `refs/livespec/preserved-publish/<work-item-id>/`. It MUST NOT delete a preservation ref of an item that is not `closed`. A deletion that fails MUST be journaled with the ref and retried on the Dispatcher's next pass, and MUST NOT change the item's state. Scenario 320 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

When the events cannot be read, the Dispatcher MUST still apply the disposition above. It MUST take the node and the error from the engine's failure message, record the reason in `events_read`, and MUST NOT invent a target, a hook command or a cause.

These obligations apply equally to member and adopter repositories. A hook runner or aggregate whose summary is not recognized falls back to the labelled observation. A workflow that skips git hooks at checkpoint produces no hook output, so its attribution is the engine error or the budget. This subsection changes no run reconciliation rule, no artifact retention rule and no other terminal outcome. Scenario 170 in `scenarios.md` exercises this section.

### Scheduled-workflow breakage pass

A scheduled workflow on the default branch reports its failure only on the forge. The runners that execute it cannot reach the beads tenant, so the workflow cannot file the failure as work itself. The breakage pass turns such a failure into a ledger work item from the host that can reach the tenant.

**Watched workflows.** A governed repository MAY declare watched workflows in `.livespec.jsonc` as `dispatcher.breakage_workflows`: an array of workflow file names relative to `.github/workflows/`, for example `["ci-root-uid.yml"]`. An absent or empty array means no workflow is watched. A value that is not an array of non-empty strings MUST make the pass fail visibly, naming the key, and MUST NOT be read as an empty array.

**The pass.** `dispatcher.py breakage-pass --repo <path>` MUST, for each watched workflow, read that workflow's most recently created COMPLETED run on the resolved default branch, of any trigger event. It MUST read through the forge's cached or conditional request path and MUST NOT poll in a loop: one invocation is one pass, and the host schedules repeat passes. Then:

1. When the run concluded success, the pass MUST file nothing for that workflow.
2. When the run concluded failure, the pass MUST compute, for each job of that run that concluded failure, the breakage key `<workflow-file>:<job-name>:<head-sha>`. It MUST file exactly one work item for each key that no item in the ledger already carries. That covers items of every lifecycle status, closed included, so a re-run of the same commit that fails the same job files nothing new.
3. When the run concluded cancelled, skipped, or any other conclusion that is neither success nor failure, the pass MUST file nothing for that workflow and MUST report the conclusion.
4. When no completed run exists, the pass MUST file nothing and MUST report that no completed run exists.
5. When the forge credential is unusable, the default branch, the workflow, its runs or its jobs cannot be read, or the ledger's dedupe read fails, the pass MUST file nothing for that workflow, MUST report the failure naming what could not be read, and MUST exit non-zero. An unreadable workflow MUST NOT be reported as green.

**The filed item.** Each item MUST be filed through the filing seam the `capture-work-item` operation uses, never by a raw `bd create`. Its title MUST name the workflow and the failing job. Its description MUST name the run URL, the head commit, and each failing test the job's log names, read from the test runner's per-test failure lines. When the log names no failing test, the description MUST say so and name the job's failing step instead. The item MUST carry the label `breakage:<workflow-file>` and MUST record the breakage key in its metadata as `breakage_key`, which is what the dedupe read compares. It enters the lifecycle exactly as any captured item does, and this subsection grants it no admission of its own. The description MUST pass the shared template-opener detector before the item is filed. A description that fails the detector MUST NOT be filed, and the pass MUST report that key as unfiled and exit non-zero.

**Verdicts.** Each pass MUST print one verdict line per watched workflow, naming the workflow, the run it read when it read one, and one of `green`, `filed <item-id>[, <item-id>...]`, `already-filed <item-id>[, <item-id>...]`, `not-concluded <conclusion>`, `no-completed-run`, or `unreadable <reason>`. When the pass runs under a host timer, these lines are what the timer's journal shows. The pass is idempotent over an unchanged run, so the host that reaches the tenant SHOULD run it at least every 30 minutes. Installing that schedule belongs to the host's provisioning, not to this plugin.

The pass reads default-branch CI state only to file work. It MUST NOT gate, hold, defer or start any dispatch, so it is not a caller gating a dispatch on the default branch's CI under §"Dispatch preflight and post-merge step discipline", and it changes no admission condition. Scenario 313 in `scenarios.md` exercises this subsection.

### Repository integration contract

The set of integration points the orchestrator requires of a governed
repository is an API, and it is typed. This subsection supersedes the
per-key MECHANISM of "Master-CI pipeline resolution", "Janitor-bootstrap
recipe resolution", "Janitor check-suite resolution" and "Janitor-core
provisioning resolution" above — each of those clauses remains ratified as
the SEMANTICS of the corresponding schema field and is read as such — and
it absorbs "Up-front integration-contract validation pass" and "Contract
versioning" as the schema-validation rule below. It ALSO supersedes the
mechanism of "Factory-sandbox toolchain disposition": that clause's
declared-and-validated arm is realized as schema fields read by the generic
resolver, and its ratified-as-no-op arm is expressed as a schema field
whose `FleetDefault` is an explicit no-op VALUE — never an absent key, so
the no-op is declared and validated like every other point rather than
inferred from silence. No committed key is introduced or renamed by this
subsection. Of the v090 implementation followups, the merged
`declared-janitor-check-suite` is MIGRATED onto the generic resolver, while
the unmerged `declared-core-provisioning`, `dispatch-integration-validation-pass`
and `declared-sandbox-toolchain` followups are SUPERSEDED by this
subsection's own followups and are not to land as further per-key
resolvers.

**One schema.** Every integration point the orchestrator requires of a
governed repository MUST be a field of a single versioned, machine-readable
`RepoIntegrationContract` schema shipped in the plugin payload: the
check-suite per venue (host janitor and in-sandbox gate), the bootstrap
recipe, the master-CI pipeline, the core-provisioning repository and ref,
the prepare-toolchain premises, the default branch, the post-merge merge
strategy, and the sandbox commit-refuse exemption marker. An integration
point that is not a schema field is not a requirement the orchestrator may
impose. Commands MUST be typed as argv arrays, never shell strings. Where a
point legitimately differs by venue, the venue MUST be an explicit schema
dimension, never two divergent literals.

**One resolver, no silent path.** Every integration point MUST be read
through one generic, schema-driven resolver whose result is the sum type
`Declared(value) | FleetDefault(value) | Defective(key, reason)`. The
schema declares, PER FIELD, whether a fleet default exists: on a DEFAULTED
field a truly ABSENT key resolves to `FleetDefault`, while on a REQUIRED
field — one whose ratified semantics admit no safe default, such as
`compat.pinned`, where the only substitutable value would be the moving
branch tip its own clause forbids — an absent key resolves to `Defective`
naming the absence. A present-but-unusable key resolves to `Defective` on
every field, and no code path MAY substitute a default for a `Defective`. The existing committed keys (`dispatcher.master_ci`,
`dispatcher.janitor_bootstrap.recipe`, `dispatcher.janitor.check_suite`,
`compat.pinned`, `compat.core_repo`) and their ratified
absent/default/defective semantics are PRESERVED as schema fields, so no
adopter declaration migrates; the per-key resolver modules are retired in
favor of the generic one.

**Resolve once, project everywhere.** The Dispatcher MUST resolve the
contract exactly once per dispatch, on the host, at plan-build time, into a
frozen `ResolvedIntegrationContract` that is journaled with the dispatch
record and carried on the dispatch plan. Every seam — the host janitor
argv, the fabro run inputs, prompt variables, prepare-step parameters —
MUST be a PROJECTION of that resolved object. No seam MAY re-derive an
integration value from configuration or from a literal at a later point;
the sandbox receives values and never resolves. This generalizes the rule
that ACP adapters ride the plan because re-deriving at launch is how the
record and the run come to disagree.

**Typed workflow inputs and the seam-equivalence check.** The
`implement-work-item` workflow payload MUST declare every input it consumes
with a type and a default. The set of `inputs.*` tokens the workflow
references, the set of inputs the Dispatcher renders from the
`ResolvedIntegrationContract`, and the schema's projectable fields MUST be
identical. The identity ranges over the integration inputs. Two further
disjoint families share the workflow's input table and the check MUST
classify each explicitly and hold it to the same resolved-position rule:
the ACP-adapter inputs of §"Built-in ACP node defaults", and the PER-ITEM
POLICY INPUTS — the review-fix visit cap, the merge-on-review-cap outcome,
and `merge_hold` (§"Dispatcher policy settings" → "The per-item merge
hold") — which are not schema fields but projections of the item's
effective policy, resolved host-side at plan-build time and journaled on
the dispatch record so the record and the run agree. A declared input
belonging to none of the three families MUST fail the check.
Every token MUST additionally sit in a position RESOLVED BEFORE
THE SANDBOX EXECUTES IT, and exactly two resolvers are admitted: the ENGINE,
which renders declared graph-node attributes at run-create time; and the
Dispatcher's run-config OVERLAY, which substitutes resolved contract values
into the committed run config host-side before the run is submitted. A token
in a position resolved by NEITHER MUST fail the check. A CI check MUST
enforce this equivalence, so a templating question is answered statically
rather than by a production dispatch.

The check MUST be resolver-aware rather than resolver-blind. For each
admitted position the check MUST record which resolver it depends on, and an
overlay-resolved position MUST be backed by an actual host-side substitution
in the Dispatcher — so that removing that substitution turns the position
back into a failing one rather than leaving a silently false classification.
The engine-resolved set MUST remain evidence-bearing: a position enters it
only on recorded evidence that the pinned engine build expands that
attribute, and a numeric or otherwise typed attribute MUST NOT be admitted on
the grounds that it looks like a string. Overlay substitution MUST be a
projection of the SAME `ResolvedIntegrationContract` the `fabro run --input`
pairs are rendered from, so the run config and the run's bound inputs cannot
disagree, and a substituted value MUST be escaped for the syntactic context
it lands in.

This check answers the templating question statically only for positions
whose resolver is known; it CANNOT establish that the pinned engine actually
renders a position. That obligation belongs to recorded evidence about the
engine build, and a change of the pinned engine invalidates it.

**Contract version is schema version.** The executing plugin build MUST
name the contract schema version it requires. At the first dispatch
admitted against a repository, and again whenever the executing build or
the repository's declaration changes, the Dispatcher MUST validate the
repository's declaration against that version and MUST refuse the dispatch
as a pre-dispatch precondition error (exit `3`, journaled) enumerating
EVERY `Defective` point in one message; an already-admitted, mid-pipeline
item MUST NOT be stranded on an expectation added by a later build. No
hand-maintained list of keys exists anywhere: a schema field is how an
already-RATIFIED obligation is realized, and adding one means the
validation pass, the seam check, and the governed-repository fixtures
(`constraints.md` §"Governed-repository integration constraints") pick it
up without further edits. This does not relax the closed-set rule above:
a NEW dispatch-time or post-merge obligation still requires ratification
with its own members-and-adopters disposition, and a schema field MUST NOT
be added for an obligation this specification has not ratified.

### Host concurrency belongs to the Fabro scheduler

The Orchestrator owns **no** host-level dispatch concurrency limit. The number
of factory runs permitted to execute concurrently on the shared host is the
Fabro server's own `server.scheduler.max_concurrent_runs` — host-scoped
configuration read by the long-lived daemon that actually owns runs. The
Orchestrator MUST NOT duplicate, re-implement, configure, or enforce that
ceiling, and MUST NOT expose a committed configuration key that purports to
bound host-wide dispatch concurrency.

Consequently the Dispatcher MUST NOT refuse a dispatch on host-concurrency
grounds, and MUST NOT maintain any host-global admission gauge, claim, or lock
artifact for that purpose. A dispatch attempted while the host is already at
the scheduler's limit MUST proceed to submission: the Fabro server accepts the
run and holds it in its own queue, promoting waiting runs in FIFO order as
capacity frees. Queueing at the scheduler is the sanctioned behavior; a
client-side refusal is not. Reconciling an orphaned run under §"A factory
run never awaits a human" is not a host-concurrency refusal and not a
host-global gauge: it releases capacity the ledger already says is unowned,
and it never refuses, defers, or counts a dispatch.

`wip_cap` (§"Per-repo WIP cap") is therefore the ONLY concurrency control the
Orchestrator owns. It bounds this repo's COUNTED CLAIMS (§"Per-repo WIP
cap") at the Ledger level — NOT its rows at status `active` — and MUST NOT
be read as, or extended into, a host-wide bound. A single
repo consequently tops out at its own `wip_cap` even when the host scheduler
would permit more; the remaining host capacity is reachable when another repo
dispatches. This is intended, not a defect to be corrected by re-adding a
host-level key.

The Orchestrator MUST NOT report the Fabro scheduler's
`server.scheduler.max_concurrent_runs` as its own bound, and MUST NOT derive
available capacity from it on any surface. Reading that value to reason
about this repo's admission is a category error: the two ceilings govern
different objects and coincide in value only by accident. A surface that
names host capacity at all MUST attribute it to the Fabro server and MUST
NOT imply the Orchestrator enforces it.

The ONE exception is factory overflow selection (§"Factory overflow
selection"). It MAY read a candidate factory server's own
`max_concurrent_runs` and that server's own non-terminal run count, solely to
choose which candidate of §"Factory overflow selection" receives an unpinned
dispatch; the candidates are the resolved default factory, including a registry
fleet default the repository does not commit, and the declared entries of
`dispatcher.overflow_factories`. That read MUST
NOT refuse, defer, hold or count a dispatch. It MUST NOT be reported as an
Orchestrator bound, and it MUST NOT feed any admission, gating or
capacity-reporting surface. The tenant-scope clause below does not govern it.
Every other prohibition in this section stays binding.

The counted-claim bound (§"Per-repo WIP cap") is TENANT-scoped and MUST be
computed from this repository's own state ONLY — its ledger rows, its
dispatch locks, and its dispatch journal, across every checkout of the
tenant. It MUST NOT be read as licensing any observation of the Fabro host
or of any OTHER repository's state. Tenant-scoped bookkeeping across this
repository's own checkouts is NOT host observation and is NOT barred by this
section. Reading the availability evidence that other repositories' runs left in
the factory-native run records of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority"
is availability evidence, not counted-claim bookkeeping, and this tenant-scope
clause does not govern it. The two are independent, and a future change making the count
genuinely tenant-wide does not require retiring this clause. Separately, the
fact that a claim can stop being counted while its remote Fabro run
continues to execute is a KNOWN and ACCEPTED consequence of counting
dispatch-lock liveness rather than remote run status, not a defect to be
corrected by teaching the counter about remote run liveness — correcting
THAT would require host observation, which this section forbids; any such
change MUST NOT land without a propose-change explicitly retiring this
clause.

### Provider spend containment

The factory spends a metered, exhaustible allowance on every model provider it
dispatches against, and those allowances are NOT interchangeable: the fleet
holds a single OpenAI Codex subscription against several Anthropic
subscriptions, so an hour of Codex allowance is the scarce resource and an hour
spent producing nothing is not recoverable. Containment is therefore a stated
obligation of the Dispatcher, not a tuning preference.

**No dispatch into a known-exhausted candidate chain.** Before claim, the
Dispatcher MUST filter the ordered candidates of every ACP node potentially
reachable in the submitted graph by the versioned observed availability holds
of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority", read from the host-wide
factory-native evidence that section requires. It MUST refuse only when at
least one such chain has no eligible candidate, and that refusal is a wait
whose next evaluation that section schedules. A known dead primary with an
eligible fallback therefore does not refuse the run; a known-exhausted chain
does; and a hold on one provider never refuses an item whose resolved
candidates are all on other providers.

**No cross-vendor burn on a dead implementer.** Once a run's implementer node
has terminated without producing any change to the worktree relative to the
dispatch base, the workflow MUST NOT continue to spend a SECOND vendor's
allowance evaluating its absent output. Review, review-fix, and disposition
rounds against a tree byte-identical to the dispatch base MUST NOT be executed.
The run is finalized with the implementer's own failure as its surfaced cause.

**Observed, not predicted.** A hold MUST derive from a real candidate attempt:
either the typed condition classified from a failed node of a terminal run,
whichever terminal the run reached, or a refused availability confirmation turn
of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority", which runs the candidate's own
adapter. A hold MUST NOT derive from credential material, catalogs, the
admission-time credential-usability probe, or provider reset claims. Host and sandbox credential state diverge by construction under
§"Worker credential projection".

**Every observed availability record is scoped, versioned, and expires.** A
current record MUST carry `scope`, opaque non-secret `hold_key`, optional
`candidate_key`, stable `observation_id`, occurrence time, and bounded expiry.
Expiry is computed from occurrence, never later ingestion. A record MUST NOT be
permanent, whatever provider, account, router, or hosting arrangement it names.
Provider timing MAY be retained only as unverified provenance and MUST NOT
become the expiry. Legacy provider-only records remain readable and effective
until retirement as domain holds against candidates whose built-in compatibility
alias names that provider, plus identity-less legacy candidates under
§"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority", which every live legacy record
covers; they MUST NOT be ignored or broadened to unrelated explicitly identified
candidates. A provider-exhaustion record minted from a dispatch's typed provider usage-limit
outcome MUST also carry the opaque non-secret credential identity that the
dispatch's admission session-headroom assessment journaled under the "Admission
filters candidates by projected Claude session headroom" clause of this section,
when that assessment journaled one; a record for a dispatch whose admission
journaled no such identity carries none. An absent identity is not a credential
identity: a record minted for a dispatch whose projected identity was absent
carries none. A record carrying a credential identity covers only a dispatch
whose admission projects that same identity for a covered candidate; a dispatch
projecting a different identity, including one admitted after the credential
behind the candidate was rotated to another account of the same vendor, MUST NOT
be refused by it. Records are distinct per provider and credential identity: a
newer record for one identity neither supersedes nor retires a live record for
another. The identity is a fingerprint of one credential snapshot, so a
refreshed snapshot of the same account projects a new identity and is not
covered until a new observation is recorded against it. A provider-exhaustion
record that carries no credential identity, including every record minted before
this clause, keeps the vendor-wide coverage stated above until it expires or is
cleared. When a dispatch's projected credential identity is absent, the record
covers it, so that a blinded gauge fails closed.
Typed candidate evidence wins over legacy cause-text attribution when
a chain executed. No record, current or legacy, MAY refuse a dispatch whose
resolved candidates all lie outside its coverage.

**A record is falsifiable only by later matching execution.** A node attempt
that starts after a domain observation and completes successfully (an attempt
reclassified as failed under "A provider refusal booked as a successful turn is
a failed attempt" is not a successful completion) against that
same hold key retires only the older domain record. A later successful attempt
by the exact `(availability_key, candidate_key)` retires only the older
candidate record. Overall run success is insufficient: it MUST NOT clear a
skipped or failed primary. The same node-level success remains valid evidence
when a later node makes the overall run fail. Expiry and attributed operator
clearance are the two other retirement routes.

**An operator may retire a record early.** The Dispatcher MUST offer an exact
scope/key clearance for current records and retain the existing provider valve
for legacy records only. The provider valve retires every live provider-exhaustion record of the named
provider, whether or not the record carries a credential identity.
Both require asserted identity and a non-blank reason,
refuse a target with no matching live record before writing, and APPEND an audit
record containing the exact identity, actor, time, and reason. For a current
record the authoritative clearance is the factory-native record that
§"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" requires, and the journal record
is its audit reference. They MUST NOT rewrite or delete the original
observation. Automated callers may clear only
when they assert identity; unattributed invocation is refused unconditionally.

**The admission-time credential-probe refusal re-probes rather than exiting.** A `loop` invocation (§"Dispatcher loop invocation surface") whose admission is refused by the admission-time credential-usability probe -- the projected worker credential returning a provider-limit or rate-limit condition BEFORE any sandbox is launched -- MUST NOT exit on that refusal while its `--budget` is unspent. It MUST re-run the probe on a bounded cadence and resume normal admission on the first usable probe result, subject to every other admission-valve condition (§"Admission valve (`ready → active`)"). The cadence is a committed-only `dispatcher.credential_reprobe_interval_seconds` (positive integer, default **300**); it is NOT declared API-configurable and is therefore committed-only per §"Orchestrator-owned attention facts" → "The declared-API-configurable class". Each refused probe MUST be journaled as one record under §"Control surface and audit" -- the re-probe wait is not silent. This clause governs ONLY the loop's response to a probe refusal; it creates NO new availability-record retirement route. A usable probe result MUST NOT retire an unexpired observed record: the three ratified retirement routes -- bounded expiry, matching execution (this section's "A record is falsifiable only by later matching execution"), and operator clearance -- stand unchanged, because a live credential probe is a non-dispatch-outcome host signal. Where observed holds exhaust an admission-required chain, admission remains refused until at least one candidate becomes eligible; a hold covering only the primary does not defeat an eligible fallback. The re-probe keeps the loop alive rather than substituting for record retirement.

**Admission filters candidates by projected Claude session headroom.** For this clause, a covered candidate is a structured candidate whose resolved agent id is `claude-acp`, or a manual-form candidate recognized as a built-in Claude adapter under the existing built-in byte-equality rule, whose execution uses the Claude subscription credential supplied by Worker credential projection. Coverage MUST follow resolved agent provenance and actual credential projection, never display text, a model-name prefix, or a spelling inferred from an opaque availability or candidate key. Arbitrary manual adapters and other agents are outside this clause's coverage; extending coverage to them requires an explicit authentication binding. Before claim and final per-node selection, the Dispatcher MUST assess every otherwise-selectable covered candidate on an admission-required ACP node, including covered fallbacks and built-in single-candidate nodes without fallback metadata. The factory credential pool is every non-empty `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN__<SLOT>` credential the dispatch target's credential wrapper injects into the Dispatcher's environment, and the unnumbered `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is the sole pool slot only when no numbered slot is injected. The Dispatcher MUST choose the credential a dispatch projects from the WHOLE pool, once per admission evaluation, and MUST NOT restrict the choice to the account that an account-selection process outside the Dispatcher published for interactive use; a run keeps the credential it was dispatched with, so only the chosen slot's headroom bears on that run. For every pool slot it MUST read the provider's five-hour session utilization using the exact credential snapshot that the dispatch would project if that slot were chosen. With a positive floor, a slot QUALIFIES when either its reading is valid and its remaining headroom is not strictly below the floor, or its five-hour window is absent as defined below; and, in both cases, its seven-day status is not exhausted and its projection does not call for a projection skip. With a floor of 0 every pool slot qualifies, and the ranking below still applies. A slot whose projection is unavailable qualifies by the fail-open rule below, and a slot whose five-hour window is absent qualifies by the absent-window rule below; each ranks below every qualifying slot whose projection was measured or carried. Among qualifying slots the Dispatcher MUST choose the slot that has the soonest five-hour window reset instant in the provider's response, so that quota does not expire unused; a slot whose response carries no reset instant ranks after every slot that carries one, and any remaining tie resolves by the slot name in ascending order so that the choice is deterministic. The reset instant is used only for this ranking and still MUST NOT change any skip. A covered candidate is skipped by this clause only when NO pool slot qualifies; when one does, the chosen slot is the credential that every covered candidate of the dispatch projects, and the skip kinds below apply to a slot, not to a candidate. Every assessment's journal record MUST name the chosen slot's opaque non-secret credential identity and, for each other slot assessed in the same admission evaluation, its identity and the reason it was not chosen: a floor skip, a seven-day skip, a projection skip, an unobservable reading, or a qualifying slot ranked lower, so that a refusal and a choice are each explainable from the record. The record names slots only by that opaque identity. From the same provider response it MUST also take the seven-day utilization and the seven-day status where the provider reports them. A seven-day status counts as exhausted only when the provider explicitly reports that the seven-day allowance is refused (for Claude, a seven-day status of `rejected`); a warning status, a utilization below 100, or any other value is not exhaustion. With a positive floor, a covered candidate whose seven-day status is exhausted MUST be skipped for this admission evaluation. This seven-day skip is a headroom skip with exactly the semantics of a floor skip, a floor of 0 disables it, and a headroom-governed refusal record and the per-node selection record MUST name it as a seven-day skip, distinct from a floor skip and a projection skip. An absent, unparseable or unrecognised seven-day reading MUST NOT skip a candidate. The journal record of each assessment MUST carry the seven-day utilization percentage and status, or an explicit unobservable result, beside the five-hour figures. Scenario 231 in `scenarios.md` exercises these sentences, and Scenario 288 exercises them for a slot whose five-hour window is absent. One assessment per distinct pool slot per admission evaluation MUST be reused across nodes and candidates sharing that credential. If that snapshot changes before projection, the affected assessment MUST be repeated before claim. For each affected work-item and assessed credential, the Dispatcher MUST journal under §"Control surface and audit" the opaque non-secret credential identity, the utilization and remaining-headroom percentages, an explicit unobservable result, or the named `five-hour-window-absent` result, and the local observation time. The journal MUST NOT contain credential values or raw provider responses. Every assessment journaled under this clause MUST ALSO be appended to the host session-headroom history. That is one history per dispatching host, held at an implementation-defined per-user location outside every checkout and worktree, and shared by every checkout that dispatches on that host. Each entry MUST carry the opaque non-secret credential identity, the utilization percentage, the explicit unobservable result, or the named `five-hour-window-absent` result, the local observation time, and the repository and checkout that journaled it. It MUST NOT carry credential values or raw provider responses. A failure to append to the host history MUST NOT refuse or delay the dispatch, and the dispatching checkout's journal record MUST name it. Entries older than 90 minutes MAY be pruned. The floor is a committed-only `dispatcher.session_headroom_floor_percent` (integer from 0 through 100 inclusive, default **20**), measured in percentage points of the five-hour usage allowance remaining, not elapsed wall-clock time. It is NOT declared API-configurable, and is therefore committed-only per §"Orchestrator-owned attention facts" → "The declared-API-configurable class". An account-selection process outside the Dispatcher continues to own which account INTERACTIVE spend uses; that selection MUST NOT change which pool slot a factory dispatch projects, the Dispatcher MUST NOT read that process's selection, trigger or readings to choose a slot, and the factory takes its own allocation within the pool. An interactive account that is short of headroom therefore never idles the factory while another pool slot qualifies. Remaining headroom equals 100 minus the provider's five-hour utilization percentage. A valid reading is a finite numeric utilization from 0 through 100 inclusive. Except for an absent five-hour window as defined in the next sentences, missing, malformed, out-of-range, transport-failed, authentication-failed, or timed-out readings are unobservable and MUST be journaled as such, never coerced to a numeric reading. The five-hour window is ABSENT when the bounded usage request was answered successfully by the provider with the projected credential authenticated (for Claude, a 2xx response to the usage request) and that response reports no five-hour window at all (for Claude, it carries no `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-5h-utilization` header): the provider is then reporting no five-hour limit for that credential, which is not a failure to measure. An absent window MUST NOT be coerced to a numeric reading and MUST NOT be journaled or treated as unobservable. With a positive floor, a slot whose five-hour window is absent MUST pass the floor; no drain rate and no projection MUST be attempted for it, and its projection result MUST be `not-projected` with the reason `five-hour-window-absent`; its seven-day status MUST still govern it exactly as it governs any other slot, so a seven-day status of `rejected` MUST still yield a seven-day skip; and it MUST rank as a slot carrying no reset instant and no measured or carried projection. The journal record of the assessment MUST name the absent window distinctly, as `five-hour-window-absent`, never as an unobservable result and never as a numeric figure. A five-hour figure that is present but malformed or out of range, and every transport-failed, authentication-failed, timed-out or refused (non-2xx) response, MUST remain unobservable even when that response carries no five-hour figure. An assessment or host-history entry naming `five-hour-window-absent` carries no valid reading, so it MUST NOT serve as a drain-rate baseline or a carried rate. This mirrors the caam handling of an absent short window (livespec-overseer item overseer-yizu3e). The usage request MUST have a finite implementation-defined timeout. With a positive floor, a covered candidate is skipped for this admission evaluation when its remaining headroom is strictly below the floor or its reading is unobservable. Equality passes this filter. A floor of 0 disables every kind of headroom skip while retaining the bounded reading attempt and journal record; it disables no other admission condition. With a positive floor, a covered candidate whose valid reading passes the floor MUST additionally be assessed for projected exhaustion. The five-hour drain rate MUST be computed from this reading and a baseline. The baseline is the EARLIEST assessment carrying a valid reading journaled under this clause for the same opaque credential identity in the dispatching checkout's dispatch journal, read regardless of the work-item it was journaled for, whose observation time is no less than 15 minutes and no more than 90 minutes earlier. When the dispatching checkout's journal holds no such assessment, the baseline MUST be the EARLIEST entry of the host session-headroom history carrying a valid reading for the same opaque credential identity, journaled from any checkout, whose observation time falls in that same window. The rate is the increase in utilization percentage points divided by the elapsed hours between the baseline's observation time and this one. When no such baseline exists, the Dispatcher MUST use a carried rate: the drain rate journaled by the most recent assessment of the same opaque credential identity in the dispatching checkout's dispatch journal whose projection result carried a drain rate, whose observation time is no more than 90 minutes earlier, and whose utilization is not higher than this reading's. A carried rate MUST NOT be used when any assessment of that credential journaled after the carried assessment reads a lower utilization than the carried assessment (a window reset or a provider correction occurred since). The projection is unavailable when neither the dispatching checkout's journal nor the host session-headroom history holds such a baseline and no carried rate exists, when the host history cannot be read, the checkout's journal holds no baseline and no carried rate exists, or when this reading's utilization is not higher than the baseline's (a window reset or a provider correction occurred between them). An unreadable host history MUST be journaled as its own unavailable reason, distinct from an absent baseline. An unavailable projection MUST be journaled with its reason and MUST NOT skip the candidate. The floor already governs an unprojected reading, and a projection with no history would otherwise refuse every first dispatch on a credential. The assessment history is the dispatching checkout's own dispatch journal, widened by the host session-headroom history when that journal holds no baseline. A projection is therefore unavailable in at least these cases: the credential carried no valid reading and no drain rate on the dispatching host during the preceding 90 minutes, both the journal and the host history were removed, or the host history is unreadable, the checkout's journal holds no baseline and no carried rate exists. Each such case is a deliberate fail-open of the projection only, and the floor still applies. A dispatch from a checkout or worktree whose own journal holds no assessment of that credential MUST NOT, by that fact alone, journal the projection as unavailable while the host history holds a baseline. When the projection is available, the projected exhaustion instant is the observation time plus the remaining headroom divided by the rate, in hours. The admission horizon is a committed-only `dispatcher.session_headroom_horizon_minutes` (integer from 0 through 1440 inclusive, default **180**). It is NOT declared API-configurable, and is therefore committed-only per §"Orchestrator-owned attention facts" → "The declared-API-configurable class". The candidate MUST be skipped for this admission evaluation when its projected exhaustion instant is strictly earlier than the observation time plus the horizon. A horizon of 0 disables projection skips while retaining the computation and its journal record. A reset instant the response carries MAY be journaled as an unverified provider claim and MUST NOT change the projection skip. The projection MUST be computed only from journaled assessments and MUST NOT issue any usage request beyond the one bounded reading per pool slot this clause already requires. For each assessed credential, the journal record MUST additionally carry exactly one projection result: the drain rate, the baseline's observation time, the baseline's source (`checkout-journal` or `host-history`) and, for a `host-history` baseline, the repository and checkout that journaled it, the projected exhaustion instant, the governing horizon, and whether a projection skip applied; for a carried rate, the record MUST name the rate source as `carried` and MUST carry the carried assessment's observation time in place of the baseline's, and a projection skip taken on a carried rate MUST be named as a projection skip exactly as one taken on a measured rate; a carried projection skip MUST have exactly the semantics of every other projection skip, and the horizon, the floor and the skip scheduling rules MUST apply to it unchanged; or an explicit `unavailable` result with its reason; or an explicit `not-projected` result when no projection was attempted because the floor is 0, the reading was skipped by the floor, the reading was unobservable, or the five-hour window was absent. `not-projected` and `unavailable` MUST remain distinct values. A projection skip has exactly the semantics of a floor skip: it is ephemeral and candidate-local to this evaluation; per-node selection MUST continue to the next eligible candidate; a successful credential-usability probe MUST NOT override it; an emptied admission-required node leaves a ready item ready without a claim or blocked reason; and reevaluation follows the same scheduling rule. A headroom-governed refusal record and the per-node selection record MUST name a projection skip as a projection skip, distinct from a floor skip, and MUST reference the assessment carrying the projection. A projection creates NO observed availability record and retires none. With a positive floor, a successful credential-usability probe MUST NOT override a headroom skip. A headroom skip is ephemeral and candidate-local to this admission evaluation; candidates sharing the assessed projected credential use the same reading. Per-node selection MUST continue in configured order to the next candidate satisfying every eligibility condition, whether that candidate is uncovered or is covered and passes its own headroom assessment. Headroom MUST NOT refuse or delay a dispatch while every admission-required node retains an eligible candidate. If headroom skips leave an admission-required node with no eligible candidate, a ready item remains ready without a claim or blocked reason; a parked rework item retains its parked state without a new claim. Every other admission-valve condition remains in force. Reevaluation MUST use the existing Per-node selection scheduling rule of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority": the earliest expiry among holds emptying a chain when applicable, otherwise after `dispatcher.credential_reprobe_interval_seconds`. The unattended loop MUST reevaluate automatically while its budget remains, without exiting solely because of a headroom wait or requiring a human. A headroom wait MUST be surfaced through the existing admission-wait attention surface, derived from the recorded admission evaluation and its scheduled reevaluation instant. Its handoff MUST inspect that recorded assessment and governing floor; it MUST NOT offer clearance of a nonexistent hold or require human action before retry. Snapshot composition MUST NOT issue a live usage request. The existing idle-factory projection MUST consume the recorded headroom outcome as part of the shared verdict and MUST NOT report an item as admission-eligible contrary to its outstanding recorded headroom wait. A due wait is reevaluated by the admission loop, not by a live probe during snapshot composition. A reading creates NO observed availability record and retires none: the provider's usage figure has been measured stale relative to its own refusals, so a reading above the floor is not evidence of availability, and a run that still meets its session limit mid-run is released under the provider-limit release of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority". A passing or disabled headroom filter adds no restriction to admission, but MUST NOT override any live hold, outstanding availability confirmation, credential-usability refusal, or other admission condition.

**Admission filters Codex candidates by projected usage-window headroom.** For this clause, a covered candidate is a structured candidate whose resolved agent id is `codex-acp` and whose execution uses the Codex worker credential supplied by Worker credential projection. That projected credential snapshot is this clause's authentication binding. Coverage MUST follow resolved agent provenance and actual credential projection, never display text, a model-name prefix, or a spelling inferred from an opaque availability or candidate key. Before claim and final per-node selection, the Dispatcher MUST assess every otherwise-selectable covered candidate on an admission-required ACP node, including covered fallbacks. For each distinct projected Codex credential per admission evaluation, the Dispatcher MUST issue exactly one bounded usage read to the provider's account usage endpoint, `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage`, authenticated by that snapshot's access token and account identifier, and MUST reuse that one reading across every node and candidate sharing the credential. The read MUST have a finite implementation-defined timeout and MUST NOT run a model turn or spend any model allowance. From the response the Dispatcher MUST take `rate_limit.allowed`, `rate_limit.limit_reached`, and, for each of `rate_limit.primary_window` and `rate_limit.secondary_window` that is present and non-null, its `used_percent`, `limit_window_seconds`, and `reset_at`. A window's `reset_at` is usable when it is a positive integer of epoch seconds; a missing or unusable `reset_at` MUST NOT make the window or the reading invalid or unobservable, and only withholds that window's reset-proximity relaxation. A window's remaining headroom equals 100 minus its `used_percent`; a valid window is one whose `used_percent` is a finite number from 0 through 100 inclusive and whose `limit_window_seconds` is a positive integer. Validity is decided for the WHOLE reading, never window by window: a reading is valid only when the response parses, `rate_limit.allowed` and `rate_limit.limit_reached` are both booleans, at least one of the two windows is present and non-null, and EVERY present non-null window is valid. Any other reading — including one carrying a valid window beside a malformed one, or a missing or non-boolean `allowed` or `limit_reached` — is unobservable, as are transport-failed, authentication-failed and timed-out reads, and MUST be journaled as unobservable, never coerced to a numeric reading or admitted on its valid part. The governing remaining headroom of a valid reading is the smallest remaining headroom among its windows. Each valid window has an effective floor: when the committed floor is positive and the window's usable `reset_at` is no more than 43,200 seconds (12 hours) after the reading's observation time, the effective floor is the smaller of the committed floor and 5; otherwise it is the committed floor. A window with no usable `reset_at`, or whose `reset_at` is at or before the observation time, takes the committed floor. The 12-hour reset proximity and the relaxed floor of 5 are fixed by this clause and introduce no configuration key.

The committed `dispatcher.session_headroom_floor_percent` and `dispatcher.session_headroom_horizon_minutes` govern this clause; it introduces no configuration key of its own, and a floor of 0 disables every skip this clause defines while retaining the bounded read and its journal record. With a positive floor, a covered candidate MUST be skipped for this admission evaluation when: `rate_limit.allowed` is `false` or `rate_limit.limit_reached` is `true` (a Codex limit skip); or any valid window's remaining headroom is strictly below that window's effective floor (a floor skip); or the reading is unobservable (a floor skip on an unobservable reading). Equality passes the floor, per window against its effective floor. The floor of 0 that disables every skip is the COMMITTED floor, and a relaxed effective floor MUST NOT be read as 0. A reading passes the floor when every valid window passes its effective floor, and the `floor-skip` not-projected reason is read the same way. A credit balance, an overage allowance, or any other field outside `rate_limit` MUST NOT count as headroom and MUST NOT prevent a skip, because work served from credits beyond the usage window is spend the operator did not schedule. With a positive floor, a covered candidate whose valid reading passes the floor and reports `rate_limit.allowed` true and `rate_limit.limit_reached` false MUST additionally be assessed for projected exhaustion per window, using exactly the baseline, drain-rate, unavailable-projection, and horizon rules of the Claude clause, applied per opaque credential identity AND per window length, so a reading of one window is never a baseline for another. The candidate MUST be skipped by a projection skip when any valid window's projected exhaustion instant is strictly earlier than the observation time plus the horizon. An unavailable projection MUST be journaled with its reason and MUST NOT skip the candidate. A projection is attempted only for a valid reading that passes the floor and reports `rate_limit.allowed` true and `rate_limit.limit_reached` false; every other reading carries, for each of its windows (or once, when no window is valid), an explicit `not-projected` result whose reason is one of `floor-zero`, `floor-skip`, `unobservable`, or `codex-limit`, the last covering a reading with `rate_limit.allowed` false or `rate_limit.limit_reached` true, and `not-projected` MUST remain distinct from `unavailable`.

Every skip this clause defines has exactly the semantics of a Claude floor skip: it is ephemeral and candidate-local to this evaluation; per-node selection MUST continue in configured order to the next eligible candidate; a successful credential-usability probe MUST NOT override it; it MUST NOT refuse or delay a dispatch while every admission-required node retains an eligible candidate; an emptied admission-required node leaves a ready item ready without a claim or blocked reason; and reevaluation follows the same scheduling rule. The per-node selection record and any headroom-governed refusal record MUST name each skip by its kind, distinguishing a Codex limit skip, a floor skip, and a projection skip, and MUST name the provider as `codex`. For each affected work-item and assessed Codex credential, the Dispatcher MUST journal under §"Control surface and audit" the opaque non-secret credential identity, `rate_limit.allowed` and `rate_limit.limit_reached`, each window's `used_percent`, `limit_window_seconds` and remaining headroom, or an explicit unobservable result, the local observation time, and exactly one projection result per window in the Claude clause's form. A window's `reset_at` changes a skip ONLY through that window's effective floor; it MUST NOT change the Codex limit skip, the unobservable floor skip, the projection skip, the horizon, or any Claude assessment. For each window the journal MUST additionally carry its `reset_at` (or an explicit absent or unusable result), its effective floor, and whether that floor was relaxed by reset proximity. The journal MUST NOT contain credential values, the account email, or raw provider responses. A reading creates NO observed availability record and retires none, and a passing reading MUST NOT override any live hold, outstanding availability confirmation, credential-usability refusal, or other admission condition. A run that still meets the Codex limit mid-turn is released under the provider-limit release of §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority", exactly as before this clause.

For a new-grammar-enabled chain, a provider-limit/rate-limit probe refusal is an
ephemeral candidate-local skip for that admission evaluation only. It creates no
durable hold and MUST NOT enter the re-probe wait while an eligible fallback
keeps every admission-required chain viable. The re-probe posture above applies to
the legacy single-candidate route and to a genuinely empty required chain.

**The probe refusal's remedy carries no timing claim as an instruction.** The credential-probe refusal surfaced to the operator MUST NOT present a provider-stated reset instant as an instruction to wait until a clock time. The same principle (this section's "Every observed availability record is scoped, versioned, and expires") already applies to the observed record, and it now applies to the probe refusal: a provider's timing claim MUST NOT be adopted as an instruction and MUST NOT gate the re-probe cadence; if the provider's refusal carried such a claim it MAY be recorded as provenance, clearly marked as an unverified provider claim rather than as an observation. The probe's OWN next result is the retirement signal for the loop's wait, not a clock.

**No silent containment.** A refusal to admit on containment grounds, a
truncation of a run under the dead-implementer rule, and a provider-limit
release are each auto-dispositions and MUST be journaled under §"Control surface
and audit". None MAY be silent. The three carry DIFFERENT fields, because they
are not governed by the same observation:

- A containment refusal MUST carry at minimum the work-item id, governing
  condition, admission-required node lacking an eligible candidate, and
  scheduled reevaluation instant. It MUST name applicable hold observations and
  their expiries when present. When no hold governs the refusal, it MUST name the outstanding confirmation, unavailable evidence source, admission-time credential-probe skip, or admission session-headroom skip instead; it MUST NOT invent a hold identity or expiry. A headroom-governed refusal MUST additionally name the assessed credential identity of every pool slot, each with its reading or explicit unobservable result and the skip kind that disqualified it, observation time, governing floor and governing horizon, the projection result, and skipped candidates for the admission-required node lacking an eligible candidate.
- A dead-implementer truncation MUST carry at minimum the work-item id and the
  governing condition. It fires on ANY implementer termination that produced no
  change to the worktree, whatever the cause — a provider ceiling, a crash, a
  malformed configuration — so no observed availability record need exist, and
  scoped hold identity or expiry fields MUST NOT be required of it. Where an
  observed availability record did govern the run, naming it is permitted and
  useful.
- A provider-limit release MUST carry at minimum the fields
  §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority" → "Provider-limit release and
  re-dispatch" names: the work-item id, run id, factory, failing node attempt,
  matched cause, scope and hold key, the failed candidate identity, and the
  recovery source or its confirmed absence.

**Relationship to the human-gate floor.** This section does NOT relax §"Every
needs-human escalation still reaches a human". Refusing to dispatch is not
auto-resolving an item: the item stays open, stays `ready`, and stays surfaced
through the needs-attention awareness surface. No containment refusal MAY
dispose of a `blocked_reason: needs-human` item. A provider-limit release is not
an auto-resolution of a needs-human decision: a classified provider-limit
failure never enters `blocked / needs-human`, because it is not a decision a
human holds.

**Relationship to host concurrency.** A provider allowance is not a host
resource, so this section does NOT reintroduce the host-level dispatch
concurrency ceiling that §"Host concurrency belongs to the Fabro scheduler"
forbids. That section's prohibition binds refusals on HOST-CONCURRENCY grounds;
this one refuses on the ground that the work cannot succeed because the
provider's allowance is gone. The Fabro scheduler enforces no provider-quota
precondition — it accepts the run and the run then fails inside the sandbox —
so this precondition duplicates nothing.

### Effective acceptance criteria

Exactly ONE public primitive resolves a work-item's effective acceptance
criteria, and every producer and consumer gate MUST use it — the capture
and groom front-ends' parse display, the entry-to-`ready` wall (§"Work-item
state semantics", the `approve` transition), the pre-dispatch wall below,
and the post-merge acceptance pass. No surface may re-derive criteria by
another path. The resolution order:

1. The item description's Definition of Done section (below) when it
   yields gradeable content, reported as source
   `description-definition-of-done`.
2. Otherwise the item's MATERIALIZED criteria value — the merged store read the
   acceptance pass already uses, in which the native `acceptance_criteria`
   field wins over a metadata-held one and a criteria field held only in
   metadata by an older writer is NOT treated as absent — when it yields
   gradeable content. (This is ONE step, not two: the materialization IS
   the merged read; no surface re-reads raw metadata separately.)
3. Otherwise the item description's "Exit criteria" section (a heading
   whose title case-insensitively equals "Exit criteria"; the section
   body is the criteria text).

The resolved source is reported as one of exactly three values:
`description-definition-of-done`, `criteria-field` (the merged value), or
`description-exit-criteria`. Sources 2 and 3 are LEGACY fallbacks: they
resolve for any item so the displays can report the gap, but they are
graded only for items already `active` or in `acceptance` when this
clause was ratified (v114). The capture and groom front-ends MUST write
new criteria into the Definition of Done section and MUST NOT write the
native field for a newly filed item; an item resolved from a legacy
source MUST be reported by the capture, groom and approve displays as
`definition-of-done: missing` so it is repaired when next touched.

**The Definition of Done section.** A work item's `description` MUST
carry, as its FIRST heading, one whose title case-insensitively equals
`Definition of Done` (any heading level; the reserved form is
`## Definition of Done`); prose MAY precede the heading. Its body MUST
consist of (a) one or more `- ` bullets, each carrying exactly one
gradeable assertion ending in a period, optionally grouped under the
`### Host-captured` and `### Human-attested` sub-headings (at most one
of each) defined under "Per-assertion proof
mode" below; and (b) exactly one spec-reference line of the form
`References: <heading>[, <heading>...]`, where each `<heading>` is the
verbatim text of an existing H2 heading of a file in the governed spec
tree — a `## Scenario NN — <title>` heading of `scenarios.md`, or an H2 of
`spec.md`, `contracts.md`, `constraints.md`, or
`non-functional-requirements.md` where the tree carries one. The
reference line MUST be validated against the H2 set read from the spec
tree's own files, never against a test fixture, so an adopter inherits no
livespec-family artifact; in this repository `tests/heading-coverage.json`
enumerates the same set and its check MAY cross-check the two. The
reference line MUST NOT be counted as a gradeable assertion by any parse.
A reference to a heading that does not exist MUST be reported as a
Definition-of-Done finding (§"Definition-of-Done and Proof-of-Done
stages") naming the unresolved heading text. Where `scenarios.md`
carries a `## Scenario NN — <title>` heading whose scenarios state the
behaviour an assertion names, the reference line MUST include that
heading: the referenced scenario governs the proof. A reference line
naming only a non-scenario H2 while such a scenario exists MUST be
reported as a Definition-of-Done finding by the gate, naming the
scenario heading that governs the assertion; a non-scenario H2 remains a
valid reference for an assertion no scenario states. Whether a scenario heading states the behaviour an assertion names MUST be decided from the Given, When, Then and And step lines of the scenarios under that heading, and never from the heading's title or from the judge's own recollection of the specification. A heading whose title names the behaviour but none of whose steps exercise it does not govern the assertion, and a heading whose steps exercise the behaviour governs it whatever its title says. This decision input MUST be the same for every taking of the Definition-of-Done judgement — the `dod_gate` node, the pre-admission judgement, the pre-dispatch judgement and any host-side preflight — so that one unchanged reference line on one unchanged subject (the "One rubric, one subject" paragraph below) receives the same reference-line ruling at every dispatch and at every host taking. Per that paragraph's rule that grading guidance MUST be written into the rubric itself, the `dod_gate` node's prompt file MUST state this reference-line rule once, MUST name the governing scenario's step lines as its decision input, and MUST direct the judge, wherever it reads `scenarios.md` itself rather than taking a returned governing-heading verdict, to quote the step line that states the behaviour when it names a scenario heading as governing an assertion. A taking MUST NOT reverse the ruling on a reference line whose subject digest and rubric digest are unchanged without naming a step line it did not cite before. This sentence leaves unchanged the rule of the "The spec-stated judgement is one shared component" paragraph that every taking takes the governing-heading verdict from that component when one was taken. Scenario 141 in
`scenarios.md` exercises this rule. No surface may parse the
section by another path. The primitive takes one parameter, `subject`,
whose value is `work-item` for every work item and `plan` for a plan
epic; the grammar above is the `work-item` grammar, and the `plan`
differences are stated in §"Plan Definition of Done and Proof of Done".

**Behavioural assertions.** A gradeable assertion MUST name an
observable behaviour or state of the delivered artifact on a surface a
user or operator of that artifact reaches: a command and what it prints
or changes, an API call and its response, an interface and what it
shows, a process and what it does to a real peer. For an item declared
behaviour-preserving (a refactor), the assertion MUST name the existing
behaviour that is unchanged, and the proof exercises that behaviour; for
a documentation or configuration deliverable the assertion names the
delivered state — the file and the text or key it carries. An assertion
whose subject is the existence, coverage or passing of tests or checks —
`tests prove ...`, `regression tests cover ...`, `the aggregate passes`
— is a TEST-EXISTENCE ASSERTION. A test-existence assertion is
legitimate ONLY when the item's deliverable is itself a test, a check or
a gate; on any other item it MUST be reported as a Definition-of-Done
finding by the gate, naming the assertion and the remedy (restate it as
the behaviour the tests were meant to establish). The janitor gate
already guarantees the aggregate, so an assertion restating it carries
no information and MUST NOT be counted as discharging a behavioural
requirement. The host-side wall MAY recognise the mechanically
recognisable forms, and where it does the finding is ADVISORY ("Authoring
at filing time" below); the judgement is the gate's. Scenario 137 in
`scenarios.md` exercises this clause and the capture duties that follow
from it.

**Who must carry the section.** The section is required for every item
whose effective workflow variant is implement-kind, under EVERY effective
`acceptance_policy` including `human-only` — a human accepts against a
stated definition, and the human-attested leg of §"Post-merge acceptance
(`acceptance → done`)" attests against this section. A groom-kind variant
is exempt from the section requirement entirely; its purpose is to
produce Definitions of Done for the slices it cuts. A plan epic carries
the section under the separate rule of §"Plan Definition of Done and
Proof of Done".

**Authoring at filing time.** Every front-end that files or reshapes an
implement-kind work item — `capture-work-item`, `capture-impl-gaps`,
`groom`, and the `plan` front-end when it routes a child — MUST offer to
author the item's Definition of Done section under the rules of this
section, and its harness-neutral prose MUST state those rules: one
behavioural assertion per bullet ("Behavioural assertions"); the proof
mode of each assertion chosen in the order `factory_captured`,
`host_captured`, `human_attested` against the sandbox capabilities; and
the scenario reference where a scenario governs the assertion. Each such
front-end MUST display, before the filing is confirmed, the
effective-criteria parse, each assertion with its proof mode, the
sandbox capabilities it resolved (the committed
`dispatcher.sandbox_capabilities` array, or `sandbox-capabilities:
unpublished` when the key is unset), and every Definition-of-Done
finding the host-side wall can detect; when the filer declines the
section it MUST display `definition-of-done: missing`, and the item
filed without it follows the existing wall ("Advise at capture and
groom" below is unchanged: criteria MAY still arrive at groom time).
Filing stays consent-gated and a front-end MUST NOT refuse on a finding.
Each such front-end MUST also display, before the filing is confirmed,
the item's DUPLICATE CANDIDATES: the work-items of the same tenant whose
status is not `closed` and whose vocabulary overlaps the item being
filed. The *words* of a text are the maximal runs of the characters `a`-`z`
and `0`-`9` in it after it is lowercased. The *significant terms* of an
item are the distinct words of at least four characters in its title and
description, excluding every word listed in the stop-word file
`.claude-plugin/data/duplicate-candidate-stop-words.txt`, which this
plugin commits as UTF-8 text holding one lowercase word per line; every
filing front-end MUST read that one file, and the display MUST show the
lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 digest of its bytes; the *overlap* of a candidate is the number of the filing's
significant terms the candidate also carries, divided by the number of
significant terms the filing carries, so a candidate that carries no
significant term has an overlap of 0. An item QUALIFIES as a candidate when
its overlap is at least 0.2, or when it sits under the same parent epic
as the filing and its overlap is at least 0.1. The qualifying items are
ordered by these keys in turn: same-parent items before all others, then
descending overlap, then ascending work-item id, so the order is fully
determined. The display MUST list the first five qualifying items in
that order and, when more than five qualify, MUST state how many more
qualified; each entry
shows its id, title, status and the filing's significant terms it shares,
at most five of them, in descending order of how often they occur in the
filing's title and description counted together, and then
alphabetically. When the filing itself has no
significant terms, the overlap is not computed and the display MUST read
`duplicate-candidates: not computed` with that reason, and MUST NOT read
`none`. The computation MUST be deterministic
and MUST NOT call a language model. When no candidate qualifies, the
display MUST read `duplicate-candidates: none` followed by the number of
non-closed items it compared, so that the scope of the negative is visible;
when the tenant's non-closed items cannot be read, it MUST read
`duplicate-candidates: unobservable` with the cause, and MUST NOT read
`none`. Candidates are ADVISORY: the front-end MUST NOT refuse or delay
the filing on them, and they MUST NOT withhold `ready`. When the filer
adopts a candidate instead of filing, the front-end MUST file nothing
and MUST offer to add the new item's evidence to the adopted candidate
as a ledger comment. When the filer confirms the filing with candidates
displayed, the filed item MUST carry one ledger comment naming each
displayed candidate's id, so a later grooming pass can find the pair.
The findings divide in two. A MECHANICAL finding — the section absent,
a reference unresolved, a proof-mode declaration or `Reason:` line
malformed, a goal-template opening delimiter in the item's title,
description, acceptance criteria or notes, as the shared template-opener
detector reports it, or an unsatisfiable coverage escape — withholds `ready`: an item filed with one outstanding
MUST NOT be routed to `ready` by intake. The goal-template finding MUST name
the field and the 0-based character offset of the first delimiter in it, and
its remedy MUST name the field to edit. Like every mechanical finding, it MUST be displayed
by `filing_display` and MUST be recorded on the item as a
`definition-of-done finding (mechanical):` ledger comment, and that comment
MUST itself pass the shared template-opener detector, so it MUST NOT quote
the delimiter. Scenario 334 in `scenarios.md` exercises this kind. The unsatisfiable-coverage-escape finding MUST be detected deterministically and MUST NOT call a language model. It MUST fire when BOTH of these hold: (a) the repository the filing front-end runs against carries a committed `tests/heading-coverage-debt.json` at its project root; and (b) one `- ` bullet of the item's `## Definition of Done` section contains both the literal path `tests/heading-coverage.json` and the whole-word token `TODO`. The finding MUST quote that bullet and MUST name `tests/heading-coverage-debt.json` as the shrink-only register that refuses a `TODO` row whose key it does not already hold. Its remedy MUST name the description as the field to edit and MUST say that each row the bullet governs must name an existing test.
