A run's latest preserved capture under §"Dispatcher admission, WIP cap, and post-merge acceptance" → "Each committing step of a run preserves the run branch's tip to an ordered work-in-progress ref" MUST count as that run's preserved work in that order: a needs-human ref or a preservation ref published at the same run's ending MUST be preferred over it, and it MUST be preferred over the observed published head and over every preservation ref of an earlier run of the item. A `resume` that every precondition of §"Resume from a published pull request (`resume --item`)" admits keeps its precedence over any seed. A seed taken from a work-in-progress ref MUST be taken exactly as a seed from the needs-human ref of §"A factory run never awaits a human" is taken. A seeded dispatch restores the captured code, not the earlier run's position in the workflow: every stage the workflow requires still runs. A Definition of Done changed by a groom while the item rested is the existing fallback-permitting refusal, so such an item MUST be seeded and MUST NOT inherit proof from the earlier Definition of Done. This release MUST NOT change how §"Across-dispatch required-result progress" counts the dispatch that ended it. The goal brief of a `resume` or `seeded` dispatch of such an item SHOULD name the terminal it recovers from and the needs-human or non-convergence cause recorded on the item. Both `dispatch` and `loop` MUST perform
*recovery routing* for every released candidate. Routing comes after the
pre-dispatch wall and BEFORE the admission valve, while the item is still
`ready`, and assigns the item exactly one route. Routes are graded in the order
listed; the first that holds is the route, and an unobservable or unreadable
measurement at any step routes `held`. A refusal of §"Resume from a published
pull request (`resume --item`)" is *fallback-permitting* when its named remedy
is a plain dispatch: the publish branch carries no open pull request, which
includes a missing pull request and one closed without merging; no proof record
names a head and no cancel record anchors one; the pull request's head moved;
the Definition of Done changed; the pull request already anchored two
resumes; or a preserved ref of the publishing run or a later run descends from the head with a different tree. Every other refusal is *non-fallback*: the earlier run is live, the
item's dispatch-scoped ownership lock is held by a live process, or the pull
request is merged (its remedy stays `reconcile-merged --item`). The not-ready
refusal cannot apply, because routing grades a `ready` item. A non-fallback
refusal takes precedence over every fallback-permitting one, so a merged pull
request is never treated as a missing anchor. When the refusal for a preserved ref that descends from the head with a different tree is the only refusal that applies, routing MUST seed from the ref it names.

- `resume`, when every published-PR resume precondition of §"Resume from a
  published pull request (`resume --item`)" passes;
- `seeded`, when every applicable resume refusal is fallback-permitting and
  preserved work is verified;
- `fresh`, when every applicable resume refusal is fallback-permitting and
  preserved work is confirmed absent, or when a current fresh ruling governs
  the item and no non-fallback refusal applies;
- `held`, when any non-fallback refusal applies, or any measurement routing
  needs cannot be taken.

Routing MUST NOT mutate the ledger, origin, or any factory. An item not
released for recovery is routed `fresh` without any remote measurement. A route
is valid only for the pass that measured it: an item the valve defers for
capacity carries no route into the next pass, which measures it afresh. A
`held` item MUST NOT be offered to the admission valve in that pass. It stays
`ready`, the journal carries one `recovery-held` record naming the item and
the measurement that could not be taken, every applicable non-fallback refusal
with its existing remedy in the order the resume's refusals are listed, or both,
and the next pass retries automatically. Under `loop` the hold is reported as a
deferred outcome on the same terms as a capacity deferral. Under
`dispatch --item` it is a precondition error (exit `3`, §"Dispatcher exit
codes") naming the item and the measurement or the non-fallback refusals with
their remedies, before any run exists, as `resume --item` refuses today.

When resume is inapplicable because no valid proof anchor exists, the head or
Definition of Done changed, or the resume-count bound is reached, the
Dispatcher MUST autonomously use a plain dispatch seeded from preserved work.
It MUST NOT inherit proof from a different head or Definition of Done. An
unobservable forge or factory measurement requires an automatically retried
wait, not destructive reclaim.

The seed record MUST name the source run, remote, immutable commit SHA, and
preservation reference. The Dispatcher MUST prefer the failed run's
successfully preserved terminal tree (the pushed ref a needs-human ending
preserves under §"A factory run never awaits a human"), within the run-age
bound stated above, then its observed
published head or the corresponding preserved-publish ref of §"Stale
publish-branch reclaim before a re-dispatch". It MUST verify preservation
before deleting the publish branch. The new sandbox MUST check out the recorded
SHA, and the goal brief MUST name that commit as an interrupted prior attempt
whose current state the agent inspects before continuing.

**A ruled seed names the tree a released item's next dispatch starts from.** An operator or a delegated coordinator MAY rule that an item's next dispatch start from a named preserved tree by running `dispatcher.py seed-ruling --repo <path> --item <id> --ref <ref> --sha <commit-sha> --reason <text>`. `<ref>` MUST be a full ref name on the item's repository, and `<commit-sha>` MUST be a full 40-character commit id. The command MUST verify, by one remote read, that `<ref>` exists at `<commit-sha>`. When it does, the command MUST write one ledger comment on the item that opens with the marker line `livespec-seed-ruling` and names the ref, the commit SHA, the invoker, the reason and the UTC instant, and MUST journal one `seed-ruling` record carrying the same fields. The comment MUST pass the shared template-opener detector before it is written. When the ref is absent or stands at a different commit, the command MUST refuse (exit `3`) naming the ref, the expected commit and the observed one, and MUST write nothing. A ruling is CURRENT from the instant its comment is written until the item carries a `livespec-seed-ruling-consumed` comment naming it, or until a later seed ruling or fresh ruling for the same item replaces it; the latest ruling of either kind governs. Recovery routing MUST read current rulings from the item's ledger comments and never from a host's journal alone, so a ruling written from one checkout governs a dispatch from any other. While an item carries a current ruling, recovery routing MUST treat the item as released for recovery, and the pre-claim refusal of §"Across-dispatch required-result progress" MUST still be graded first, as for every released item. Routing MUST take its seed from a current seed ruling ahead of a `resume` and ahead of the preference order this clause states. When the ruled ref exists at the ruled SHA and no non-fallback refusal applies, the route MUST be `seeded`, and the seed record MUST name the ruled ref as its preservation reference and the ruled SHA as its immutable commit. When the ruled ref is absent, or stands at a commit other than the ruled SHA, the route MUST be `held`, and the `recovery-held` record MUST name the ref, the ruled SHA and the observed commit, or the ref's absence. Routing MUST NOT then fall through to another preserved tree, to the observed published head, or to `fresh`. An unreadable ref is the existing unobservable-measurement hold. A non-fallback refusal keeps its precedence over a ruling. Once the run of a dispatch seeded from a ruling exists, that dispatch MUST add one ledger comment on the item that opens with the marker line `livespec-seed-ruling-consumed` and names the ruling's instant, the dispatch id and the run id, and MUST journal one `seed-ruling-consumed` record carrying the same fields. A reconciliation pass that finds a run launched from a ruling whose item carries no such comment MUST add it, so a crash between the launch and the comment cannot leave the ruling current. A consumed ruling MUST NOT govern any later dispatch. Holding an item for a missing or moved ruled ref is a `held` cause in its own right, in addition to the two the route list names. The `resume` precedence stated above applies only while no ruling is current.

**A fresh ruling routes a released item's next dispatch fresh.** An operator or a delegated coordinator MAY rule that an item's next dispatch start fresh from the default branch, past every preserved tree the item holds, by running `dispatcher.py fresh-ruling --repo <path> --item <id> --reason <text>`. The command MUST write one ledger comment on the item that opens with the marker line `livespec-fresh-ruling` and names the invoker, the reason and the UTC instant, and MUST journal one `fresh-ruling` record carrying the same fields. The comment MUST pass the shared template-opener detector before it is written; when it does not, the command MUST refuse (exit `3`) and MUST write nothing. A fresh ruling is CURRENT on the same terms as a seed ruling: from the instant its comment is written until the item carries a `livespec-fresh-ruling-consumed` comment naming it, or until a later seed ruling or fresh ruling for the same item replaces it, and recovery routing MUST read it from the item's ledger comments and never from a host's journal alone. While an item carries a current fresh ruling, recovery routing MUST treat the item as released for recovery, and the pre-claim refusal of §"Across-dispatch required-result progress" MUST still be graded first. A non-fallback refusal keeps its precedence over a fresh ruling: the route MUST then be `held`, naming that refusal, and the ruling MUST stay current. Otherwise the route MUST be `fresh` ahead of a `resume` and ahead of the preference order this clause states, without seeding from any preserved tree. This holds even when preserved work is not confirmed absent, including for an item whose earlier-run identifiers name no run: a current fresh ruling overrides the hold that such an item would otherwise take for preserved work not confirmed absent, and only a non-fallback refusal or a needs-human listing that cannot be taken holds the item. No other preserved-work measurement holds a fresh-ruled item, because the route ranks no tree. Recovery routing MUST still list the item's needs-human refs, and the `recovery-route` record MUST name the ruling's instant and MUST carry the `passed_over_needs_human` field this clause requires, listing every needs-human ref that carries one of the item's earlier runs, because the route took none of them. A needs-human listing that cannot be taken is the existing unobservable-measurement hold, and the ruling MUST stay current. A fresh ruling MUST NOT delete or move any needs-human or preservation ref, and the stale publish-branch reclaim of §"Stale publish-branch reclaim before a re-dispatch" MUST run for the item as for every other `fresh` item, preserving the branch's head before it deletes the branch. Once the run of a dispatch routed fresh by a ruling exists, that dispatch MUST add one ledger comment on the item that opens with the marker line `livespec-fresh-ruling-consumed` and names the ruling's instant, the dispatch id and the run id, and MUST journal one `fresh-ruling-consumed` record carrying the same fields. A reconciliation pass that finds a run launched from a fresh ruling whose item carries no such comment MUST add it. A consumed fresh ruling MUST NOT govern any later dispatch. Scenario 327 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A needs-human tree is recognised by the run it carries, not only by its ref name.** A needs-human ref is any ref under `refs/heads/needs-human/`. A needs-human ref CARRIES NO WORK when its tip commit's tree is identical to the tree of the tip's merge base with the default branch. This read-side rule complements the write-side tree guard of §"Dispatcher admission, WIP cap, and post-merge acceptance" → "Each committing step of a run preserves the run branch's tip to an ordered work-in-progress ref", and applies whatever wrote the ref: a ref written before that guard, a ref named other than `needs-human/<run-id>`, and a ref any other writer produced are all outside the guard. Such a ref is not preserved work and is not any run's terminal tree. Routing MUST NOT take it as a seed, and MUST NOT let it outrank any other ref, published head or capture under this clause or its run-age bound. The default branch's tip for this comparison MUST be read once per routing pass, together with the identification below, and shared by every item the pass routes. The tip trees and merge bases MUST be read from that same per-pass identification. A comparison that cannot be taken is the existing unobservable-measurement hold, and MUST NOT be read either as a change or as the absence of one. A needs-human ref CARRIES a run when its tip commit's message holds a `Fabro-Run: <run id>` trailer or a `Factory-Run-Id: <id>` trailer naming one of the item's earlier-run identifiers: the run ids and dispatch ids recorded for the item's dispatches, together with the run id its pull request's records name, exactly the identifiers resume grading collects. When routing looks for a run's terminal tree, it MUST treat every needs-human ref that carries that run as the run's terminal tree, exactly as it treats `needs-human/<run id>`. When several needs-human refs carry the same run, routing MUST take the ref whose tip commit descends from the tip commit of every other ref carrying that run, where a commit descends from itself. When no tip descends from all the others, routing MUST take, among the refs whose tip commit no other carrying ref's tip descends from, the one whose tip commit is newest by committer time, and on an equal committer time the one whose full name sorts first in byte order. Only when two or more refs remain tied because their tips are the same commit MAY the ref's name decide: routing MUST then prefer a ref named under one of the item's earlier-run identifiers, and among equally named candidates the ref whose full name sorts first in byte order. Ancestry MUST be read from the same per-pass identification as the tip commit messages; an ancestry that cannot be read is the existing unobservable-measurement hold and MUST NOT be read as the absence of a descendant. Every carrying ref the route did not take MUST still be listed in `passed_over_needs_human` as this paragraph states. The identification MUST be taken once per routing pass, by one listing of the needs-human refs with their tip commit messages, and shared by every item the pass routes. An identification that cannot be taken is the existing unobservable-measurement hold and MUST NOT be read as absence. Every `recovery-route` record of a `seeded`, `fresh` or `resume` route MUST carry a `passed_over_needs_human` field. It lists each needs-human ref that carries one of the item's earlier runs and was not the ref the route took, with its commit and the reason it was passed over: `no-change` for a ref that carries no work, and `not-taken` for any other. The field MUST be an empty list when there is none, and MUST NOT be omitted.

A confirmed absence of preserved work permits a plain dispatch from the
default branch, with that loss recorded. An unreadable reference is not
confirmed absence.

After admission, each launch path MUST execute every admitted item's route on
that item's own copy of the dispatch arguments, in the same per-item step that
applies the item's factory and workflow pins. Route-specific state MUST NOT be
written to arguments shared by the wave. A `resume` route executes the resume's
post-admission sequence: it journals the `resume` record before the run exists,
enters at the anchored node on the anchored head, and runs the workflow the
earlier dispatch record names. The status grading of the not-ready refusal is
satisfied by routing and is not repeated after the claim. A `seeded` route
checks out the recorded SHA as the preceding paragraph requires. The stale
publish-branch reclaim runs for `fresh` and `seeded` items only. For a `seeded`
item it runs after the seed's preservation is verified, and it MUST NOT run for
a `resume` item. An automatically routed resume is subject to the WIP-cap
posture of the entry point that admitted it.

**Availability is re-confirmed after expiry.** When a domain or candidate hold
reaches its bounded expiry, the candidates it covered carry an outstanding
availability confirmation, and "Per-node selection" MUST NOT choose such a
candidate until that confirmation is satisfied. Availability is confirmed only
by a successfully completed ACP prompt turn using the candidate's pinned adapter
version, requested model and effort, and projected worker credential identity.
Session creation, process exit alone, timeout, cancellation, and an ACP refusal
do not confirm availability. A host-side probe is permitted only when these
execution properties are equivalent and its outcome is durably observable
through the same authoritative evidence source; otherwise the probe MUST be a
minimal factory run. The probe sends one fixed minimal prompt.

A successful confirmation satisfies the expired observations it names for that
candidate. It MUST NOT satisfy a newer observation. An eligible refusal creates
a new occurrence-time-scoped hold. Any other probe failure skips that candidate
for the current evaluation, creates no hold, and allows selection to continue
to later eligible candidates.

If no candidate remains eligible, the Dispatcher MUST retry automatically after
`dispatcher.credential_reprobe_interval_seconds`; it MUST NOT busy-loop or
require a human. Probe execution MUST be bounded by the
committed-configuration-only `dispatcher.availability_probe_timeout_seconds`
(positive integer, default **120**), including termination of unfinished probe
work. Every probe turn is journaled with the candidate identity, outcome,
occurrence time and, where observable, its cost. A provider's own advertised
reset instant MUST NOT schedule, shorten, or replace the probe; it MAY be
recorded only as unverified provenance. The confirmation turn is not the
admission-time credential-usability probe of §"Provider spend containment" and
changes none of that probe's rules.

Scheduled availability waits MUST survive Dispatcher restart through
authoritative evidence and be reevaluated by the ordinary unattended loop. An
expired timestamp MUST NOT schedule an immediate retry repeatedly. Operator
clearance MUST make the affected wait eligible for immediate reevaluation.

No engine-side fallback transition or fallback capability is required. Should a
pinned Fabro engine later expose a supported extension point for trying a
further candidate within one node visit, using it is an optional optimisation
that requires its own ratified change; this section neither requires nor
forbids it.

**In-protocol model and effort selection.** For a candidate whose agent catalog
entry declares the `protocol` mechanism, the node adapter the Dispatcher renders
for that candidate MUST carry
a `config_options` object mapping ACP session config option ids to requested
values (`model` and, when set, `effort`), and the Fabro ACP handler MUST, after
`session/new` and before the first `session/prompt`, read the agent's advertised
`configOptions` and set each requested option through
`session/set_config_option`. The handler MUST NOT start the prompt until every
requested option is confirmed set. When the agent does not advertise a requested
option id, or advertises it without the requested value among its options, the
candidate MUST terminate as a typed pre-turn refusal — cause `model_unsupported`
at candidate scope when the option is `model`, `malformed_configuration`
otherwise — recorded with its own identity, minting no hold, and never released
for re-dispatch as a provider-limit failure; it keeps its existing route. For a candidate whose agent entry declares an
environment or argument mapping, the Dispatcher MUST render `model` and `effort`
into the adapter exactly as the mapping states and the handler sets no option;
the two mechanisms MUST NOT be combined for one candidate. The
`agent.acp.started` event MUST carry the confirmed model and effort as additive
non-secret fields so a reader can verify which model actually ran without
reading the command. The selected candidate's `config_options` MUST be
transported through a supported single-node mechanism independently of
`acp.fallback_chain`. The Fabro server MUST advertise the additive capability
`acp.candidate_config_options.v1`; a missing or unreadable required capability
MUST refuse before claim. A dispatch with no selected protocol-configured
candidate MUST NOT require this capability, and an unselected fallback's
options never gate a dispatch.

**Fallback selection is observed from the Dispatcher's own decisions.** The
Dispatcher MUST NOT depend on any engine fallback or failover event; the
per-node selection record of "Per-node selection" and the
`provider-limit-release` record are the authoritative fallback history, read
together with the run's node outcomes on its resolved factory. Fabro's existing
native-API `agent.failover` events and their stored-run consumers are
unaffected by this section. Reconciliation MUST replay selection-to-execution
observation idempotently using factory, run, node attempt, and selection
identity. Missing or unreadable node outcomes MUST be surfaced as unavailable,
not interpreted as an unreached node. They MUST be retried and MUST NOT clear
an existing warning. Their unavailability alone MUST NOT create a needs-human
decision. Existing versioned hold observations, retirement records, and
fallback audit records remain readable. Removing dependence on new engine
failover events MUST NOT discard existing holds or reinterpret unknown record
versions.

Every dispatch whose per-node selection rendered a non-primary candidate for a
node the run then actually executed — as read from the run's node outcomes on
its resolved factory — appends one idempotent journal record and yields one
aggregate attention fact per repository/node with id
`hygiene:model-fallback:<repo>:<node>`, existing `hygiene` kind, valid urgency,
source reference, and executable inspection handoff. The newest unresolved
observation supplies the deterministic summary. Later run failure does not
erase it, and it never refuses or disposes work. The warning clears only when a
later dispatch renders the same primary generation for that node and that node
attempt, begun after the warning, completes successfully, regardless of the
overall run's later outcome. Older concurrent success, unrelated success,
probes, and a selection for a node the run never reached cannot clear it.
Primary replacement retires the prior warning as append-only `superseded`;
non-primary chain changes alter only the full-chain digest, not the primary
generation, so they do not strand the warning.

**Cost follows every attempt.** For every run released under "Provider-limit
release and re-dispatch", and for every availability confirmation turn, the
Dispatcher MUST journal one attempt-cost record carrying the attempt's token
use and elapsed time per node attempt wherever the run record exposes them,
priced under the rules below, or marked cost-unobservable. An item's cost across
a release-and-re-dispatch sequence is the sum of those records and the final
run's cost. Each run or probe cost observation MUST have a stable identity and
MUST be counted at most once across reconciliation and resume. If any included
attempt has unobservable cost, the sequence total MUST be unobservable; a known
subtotal MAY be displayed only when explicitly labeled incomplete. A shared
availability probe MUST NOT be charged in full to multiple items. Emitted model identity,
normalized only by stripping one trailing `-YYYYMMDD` date suffix (any broader
prefix match is not exact identity), selects built-in pricing only for
the matching built-in candidate and endpoint. Pricing resolves through the model catalog
entry the candidate's identity names first (§"Agent and model catalogs") and a
per-candidate explicit table second; for a manual-form candidate with no
catalog match only its explicit table applies. Candidate pricing, when present, MUST be an
all-or-none table naming the exact model and finite non-negative USD-per-million
input, output, cache-write, and cache-read prices, and applies only when emitted
identity matches. If any nonzero usage component cannot be priced, the whole run
cost is unobservable, not a known partial subtotal; §"Fail-closed cost gate
(keyed on `--item` presence)" remains authoritative. An unknown model MUST NOT
be priced as an unrelated default or treated as free. Attempt-cost records are
observations only and never yield a gate verdict; terminally unsuccessful runs
otherwise retain the existing no-gate posture.

## ACP node timeouts

Every node timeout of the `implement-work-item` workflow, and the run's stall
watchdog, MUST resolve through the resolution layers of this section. A timeout
attribute in the workflow graph is that workflow's declared default for the node:
it is the lowest layer and never overrides configuration.

**Keys.** `dispatcher.node_timeouts` is a table keyed by node name
(`dod_gate`, `implement`, `commit_red`, `commit_green`, `fix`, `review_fix`, `proof_capture`, `review`,
`disposition`, `proof_verify`, `proof_grade`, `publish_draft`, `pr_refresh`, `pr`, `janitor`) whose values are positive
integers of seconds; `dispatcher.stall_timeout_seconds`
is a positive integer of seconds for the run-level stall watchdog. A node that
no repository table entry and no per-dispatch argument names MUST resolve to the
timeout its workflow graph declares for it. A node that declares none MUST
resolve to **1800** seconds. The stall watchdog with no configured value MUST
resolve to **7200** seconds. The table MAY name any node of the graph; the names
above are the ones the shipped configuration most often sets, not a closed set.
A non-positive or non-integer value MUST be rejected before any run exists, naming the key. Both
keys are committed-configuration-only, alongside `dispatcher.acp_nodes`,
`dispatcher.agent_catalog` and `dispatcher.model_catalog`, and do not trigger
the console Settings lockstep.

**Whole-run wall budget key.** `dispatcher.run_wall_budget_seconds` is a
positive integer of seconds for the whole-run wall budget of the Dispatcher
progress watchdog. It resolves through three layers, most specific last: the
built-in default of **21600** seconds, the dispatch target's
`.livespec.jsonc`, then a per-dispatch `--run-wall-budget-seconds <seconds>`
argument. The workflow graph declares no budget, because the Dispatcher, not
the engine, enforces it. The dispatch record MUST journal the resolved
budget and name the layer that supplied it. A non-positive or non-integer
value MUST be rejected before any run exists, naming the key or argument. A
resolved budget smaller than any node timeout resolved for the same dispatch
MUST be rejected before any run exists, naming both keys and both values,
because such a budget would cancel that node's legitimate turn. Like the two
keys above, it is committed-configuration-only and does not trigger the
console Settings lockstep.

**Whole-run wall ceiling key.** `dispatcher.run_wall_ceiling_seconds` is a positive integer of seconds for the hard ceiling of §"Dispatcher progress watchdog" → "The hard ceiling". It resolves through the same three layers as the whole-run wall budget key, with a per-dispatch `--run-wall-ceiling-seconds <seconds>` argument as the most specific layer, and its built-in default is three times the resolved whole-run wall budget. The dispatch record MUST journal the resolved ceiling and name the layer that supplied it. A non-positive or non-integer value MUST be rejected before any run exists, naming the key or argument. A resolved ceiling smaller than the resolved whole-run wall budget MUST be rejected before any run exists, naming both keys and both values. It is committed-configuration-only and does not trigger the console Settings lockstep.

**Resolution layers.** The same three layers and precedence as §"ACP node
adapter configuration" apply: the workflow's own declared defaults, the
dispatch target's `.livespec.jsonc`, then a per-dispatch
`--node-timeout <node>=<seconds>` argument that MUST be journaled on the
dispatch record. The record MUST name the supplying layer per node, and MUST
name the workflow for a node that renders its declared value and the built-in
default for a node that declares none.

**Rendering, literally.** The pinned Fabro build types a quoted duration
attribute at parse time and its template expansion never re-types a rendered
string, so a templated `timeout` attribute silently becomes NO timeout. The
Dispatcher therefore MUST NOT template a timeout attribute from a workflow
input. It MUST write each resolved value into the self-contained dispatch
payload's workflow graph as a literal duration (`timeout="1800s"`,
`stall_timeout="7200s"`) before invoking `fabro run`, and a test MUST assert
that no timeout attribute in the rendered graph contains a template opener.

**The run's budgets follow the graph.** The Dispatcher's `fabro run`
subprocess ceiling MUST be derived from the resolved node timeouts and the
resolved stall timeout — the graph's worst-case path plus a fixed margin —
rather than from a hard-coded constant, so that lengthening a node cannot
outrun the poller and shortening one is not masked. The ceiling and the
execution allowance MUST read the same per-node values the rendered graph
carries, so a value that reaches the run cannot be billed at a different one.

**A commit settle node ends its own wait first.** The commit settle nodes are
`implement_commit_settle`, `fix_commit_settle` and `review_fix_commit_settle`.
The wait a commit settle node's script performs MUST end before that node's
rendered timeout, by the rendered timeout less a fixed margin of 300 seconds, so
the script's failure handling runs rather than the engine ending the node. The
Dispatcher MUST write that bound into the rendered graph as a literal, as it
writes the timeout. A resolved timeout of 300 seconds or less for a commit settle
node leaves no wait, so it MUST be rejected before any run exists, naming the key
or argument and the value.

**The 30-minute default is a deliberate reduction.** It lowers `implement`
from the previously shipped 14400 seconds and `janitor`/`fix` from 3600
seconds, against recorded legitimate turns near 120 minutes. The workflow graph
therefore MUST declare no more than 1800 seconds for those nodes. A repository
that needs longer turns sets them; the default is the maintainer's ruling and the
reduction is recorded in the implementing item's triage record.

**A low declaration rests on a measurement.** A node's declared timeout below
1800 seconds MUST rest on a recorded run's measured duration for that node, named
in a comment beside the declaration. A node with no such measurement MUST declare
at least 1800 seconds, because a declared value that has never been in force and
is too tight fails in every repository at once.

**Codex compaction limit.** A Codex-backed node's `model_auto_compact_token_limit`
is an adapter argument and rides the node's `args` under §"ACP node adapter
configuration"; this section adds no separate key for it.

Implemented by ledger item `bd-ib-cnkf`.

**Repository hooks that outlive a limit.** A governed repository's commit and
push hooks run inside the factory sandbox under one of three limits: the agent's
per-tool-call limit, when an ACP agent runs `git commit` or `git push` inside
its own turn; the resolved node timeout of that ACP agent node, when it ends the
agent's turn while such a `git commit` or `git push` is still executing; or the
resolved timeout of a command node that commits or pushes, such as
`publish_draft` or `pr_refresh`. When an agent tool call that runs a git commit
or push is ended by the agent's per-tool-call limit or by its node's resolved
timeout while the hook run it started is still executing, every process of that
hook run MUST be terminated before the next git commit or push in the same
sandbox starts, so that two hook runs never execute concurrently in one sandbox.
A `hook-over-limit` event is a git commit or push ended by one of those three
limits while a hook run
it started was still executing, as observed from that hook run's processes at
the moment the limit ended the operation; a commit or push ended by a limit
before its hook started, or after its hook finished, is not a `hook-over-limit`
event and keeps its existing failure classification. For every `hook-over-limit`
event the run MUST record a `hook-over-limit` row in the dispatch journal naming
the node, the git operation, the limit that ended it in seconds, and the elapsed
milliseconds of the hook run at termination, whether or not the run later
recovers. When a `hook-over-limit` event is the cause of the run's needs-human
ending, the needs-human cause recorded on the item MUST name `hook-over-limit`,
the node and the git operation, so that the stop is not presented as an agent's
decision; a recovered event MUST NOT be named as the cause of a later
needs-human ending that has a different cause. `blocked_reason` gains no member
and the run still preserves its work under "A factory run never awaits a human".
Scenario 177 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A commit leg completes past one tool call.** The implement-work-item workflow MUST provide, inside the factory sandbox, a detached commit runner for every stage whose ACP agent commits (`fix` and `review_fix`), and each such stage's prompt MUST direct every `git commit` the agent makes — a Red commit, a Green amend, or any later commit — through that runner. Starting a commit through the runner MUST run the given `git commit` arguments unchanged, with the repository's commit hooks running exactly as they run for a foreground commit, in a session that outlives the tool call that started it, and MUST return that commit run's identity without waiting for the commit. Waiting on a commit run MUST block for no longer than a bound in seconds that the caller supplies, MUST then report either `running` or the run's terminal state, and MUST leave the commit run untouched when it returns or is interrupted. Inside one visit of a `fix` or `review_fix` stage the agent MAY wait on each commit run it started at most once. The runner MUST refuse a second wait, from the same stage visit, on a commit run that an earlier wait in that visit reported `running`. That refusal MUST leave the commit run untouched, MUST report the run's current state, and MUST name the stage's commit-run settle as what will wait on it. Independently of the stage, the runner MUST refuse a wait on a commit run while another wait on that same commit run is still open, so that concurrent waits on one run never each return into the agent's turn. That refusal MUST return at once without waiting, MUST exit with a non-zero status, MUST report the commit run's current state and that another wait on it is open, and MUST leave the commit run untouched. A wait that starts after every earlier wait on that commit run has returned MUST NOT be refused by this rule, and a wait whose process ended without returning MUST NOT count as open. The stage's prompt MUST direct the agent to end its turn, rather than poll, once a commit run it waited on is still `running`. Polling the runner's own records by any other means counts as a wait. The terminal state MUST be derived from records the commit run's own process writes, never from the waiting agent's view: `passed` when the commit process exited on its own with status zero; `failed` when it exited on its own with any non-zero status; and `no-verdict` when it was ended by a signal or is no longer running without having recorded an exit status. A terminal report MUST carry the exit status when one was recorded, the resulting `HEAD` commit id when the state is `passed`, and the final lines of the commit's combined output. A commit run whose state is `failed` or `no-verdict` is not a commit, and the prompt MUST direct the agent not to treat it as one. The runner MUST NOT pass `--no-verify`, set any variable that skips or relaxes a check, or change the severity of any hook, and MUST refuse to start a commit run while an earlier commit run in the same sandbox is still `running`, naming that run. The stage's rule that nothing it started is left running when its turn ends keeps exactly one exception. A commit run that the agent started through the runner and waited on once MAY still be `running` at the agent's final message, and the agent MUST NOT stop it. That commit run is then waited on by the run before the stage's outcome is decided, as "An implement turn that ends incomplete does not succeed" requires. Every other process the turn started MUST be terminal or stopped before the agent's final message. The detached commit run is the only exception that stage's prompt makes to its rule against backgrounding a tool call. This paragraph does not replace "Repository hooks that outlive a limit", which still governs any commit or push that does not go through the runner. Scenario 179 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A commit run outlives a node-timeout cut.** The preceding paragraph's end-of-turn rule governs a turn that ends with the agent's final message, and that rule is unchanged. A turn that its node's resolved timeout ends is a separate case, because the agent sends no final message and cannot stop what it started. When a `fix` or `review_fix` turn is ended by its node's resolved timeout while a commit run it started through the commit runner is still `running`, ending the turn MUST NOT terminate that commit run. Before the `needs_human` node makes its preservation commit, it MUST wait on every commit run still `running` in the sandbox with bounded waits, ending that wait while enough of the `needs_human` node's own timeout remains for a bounded preservation attempt, and MUST then stop any commit run still `running`, so that no commit run executes concurrently with the preservation commit; a commit run stopped this way is `no-verdict`. Preservation then proceeds exactly as "A factory run never awaits a human" requires, by a pushed ref or, when the push does not complete, the preserve-by-reference pointer. When the commit run that was `running` at the cut reaches `passed` before preservation begins, its resulting `HEAD` commit MUST be in the preserved tree's history; this clause does not require an earlier commit that the agent itself superseded, such as a Red commit replaced by a Green amend, to remain in that history. When such a cut is the cause of the run's needs-human ending, the needs-human cause recorded on the item MUST name `node-timeout`, the node whose turn was cut, that node's resolved timeout in seconds, and, for each commit run the cut turn had started, its identity and its terminal state when preservation began. Scenario 192 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**The recorded hook verdict outranks the agent's account of it.** When a run ends at the `needs_human` terminal after a `fix` or `review_fix` turn whose latest commit attempt was refused, as "An implement turn that ends incomplete does not succeed" defines a refused attempt, the needs-human cause recorded on the item MUST name that attempt's recorded exit status and the failed target names the hook's recorded output reports, read from the run's recorded tool output and never from the agent's reply, and the dispatch journal's outcome row for the run MUST carry the same exit status and failed target names in a field separate from the agent's own failure text. When the agent's failure text describes that hook as interrupted, terminated or not completed while the recorded output shows the hook completed with a refusal, the needs-human cause MUST label the agent's text as agent-reported and MUST state the recorded refusal beside it. A commit attempt whose recorded output shows no hook run, or one ended by a limit before its hook finished, is not governed by this paragraph and retains its existing classification under the preceding paragraphs. For the implement stage, the needs-human cause after an exhausted `commit_red` or `commit_green` re-entry MUST name that command node's recorded exit status and failed target names. Scenario 179 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**A refused commit's needs-human cause is attributable from the ledger.** This paragraph governs every needs-human cause that the preceding paragraph requires to name a refused commit's recorded exit status and failed target names: the cause after a `fix` or `review_fix` turn whose latest commit attempt was refused, and the cause after an exhausted `commit_red` or `commit_green` re-entry of the implement stage. Each such cause MUST also carry one failure excerpt taken from the same recorded hook output: the first failing test id that output reports, or, when it reports none, its first line that reports an error. The excerpt MUST be at most 200 characters, and an excerpt shortened to that bound MUST say that it was truncated. When the recorded hook output is absent, cannot be read, or names no failed target, the cause MUST state that the failing target is unknown and MUST name which of those three reasons applies; it MUST NOT consist of the hook script's exit status alone, such as `script exited with status 1`. Neither the cause nor the excerpt MAY carry the value of any environment variable that the dispatch supplied to the run's sandbox. Before the cause is written, the Dispatcher MUST withhold any excerpt line that contains such a value, written verbatim or as a JSON-escaped string, and MUST put in its place a statement naming the environment variable by its key name only. A value shorter than eight characters is exempt from this check. The excerpt MUST NOT replace the exit status and failed target names that the preceding paragraph requires. Scenario 285 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**The run's working tree survives the agent.** Inside the factory sandbox, a shell command that an ACP agent runs MUST be refused before any part of it executes when any executed segment of it would remove, move, or replace one of the run's protected paths: the sandbox root `/workspace`, the run's working directory, the working-directory link that points at the run's clone, and the clone's own directory. A command MUST be refused whether the protected path is written literally, written with a trailing slash, reached through a relative path from a directory the same command changed into, or produced by a glob that the shell would expand to it. The refusal MUST name the protected path it matched. A protected path that appears in the command only as data MUST NOT cause a refusal: an argument to `echo` or `printf`, a here-document body, a commit message, or a quoted pattern given to a search command. This paragraph's refusal condition is not met by an executed segment that removes, moves, or replaces only paths that are not protected paths, including a path under a scratch directory such as `/tmp`, or a file or directory inside the repository tree; whether the command as a whole is refused is decided by the paragraph "One decision covers the run's protections." below. The protection MUST apply to every ACP agent adapter the workflow launches whose runtime offers a hook that runs before each shell command; an adapter whose runtime offers no such hook is outside this paragraph. Scenario 180 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**The run's repository survives the agent.** Inside the factory sandbox, an executed segment of a shell command that an ACP agent runs meets this paragraph's refusal condition when it would remove, move, or replace the clone's `.git` directory, or when it would remove, or move out of the clone, every non-hidden entry at the top level of the clone's own directory. The top-level entries are those present when the command is submitted, and the removals and moves of all the command's executed segments count together; a clone with no non-hidden top-level entry when the command is submitted gives the second condition nothing to protect. The matching rules of the paragraph "The run's working tree survives the agent." apply unchanged: a target written literally, written with a trailing slash, reached through a relative path from a directory the same command changed into, or produced by a glob that the shell would expand to it, so a glob such as `<clone>/*` counts as naming every non-hidden top-level entry. The refusal MUST name the clone's `.git` directory, or the clone's own directory, as the path it matched. Removing, moving, or replacing files or directories inside the clone's `.git` directory while the directory itself remains, and removing hidden top-level entries other than `.git`, do not meet this condition. Scenario 197 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**The run's sandbox processes survive the agent.** Inside the factory sandbox, the protected processes are the sandbox container's PID 1 and the ACP agent adapter process, which is the process in the sandbox's PID namespace that launched the agent runtime whose hook is evaluating the command. An executed segment of a shell command that an ACP agent runs meets this paragraph's refusal condition when it is a signalling command whose target reaches a protected process. A `kill` target reaches a protected process when an operand, after the signal options and any `--`, is the process id of a protected process, is `-1` (every process), is `0` (the caller's own process group) when that group contains a protected process, or is the negated id of a process group that contains a protected process; an option that only selects the signal, as in `kill -1 <pid>`, is not a target. A `pkill` or `killall` target reaches a protected process when its name or command-line pattern matches the name or command line of a protected process, whatever other selection options the command also carries: a parent, user, ancestor or session filter does not remove that match. When the guard cannot read the command line of a protected process, a pattern-selected signalling command meets the condition, and the refusal names the process it could not read. A target that the command produces at run time, through a command substitution, a variable the same command does not assign, or input piped into the signalling command, does not reach a protected process under this paragraph. The refusal MUST name the protected process and the operand or pattern that reached it. Signalling a process the agent started, by a process id it recorded or by a pattern that matches neither protected process, does not meet this condition. Scenario 198 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**One decision covers the run's protections.** A shell command that an ACP agent runs inside the factory sandbox MUST be refused before any part of it executes when any one of its executed segments meets the refusal condition of "The run's working tree survives the agent.", of "The run's repository survives the agent.", or of "The run's sandbox processes survive the agent.", and MUST NOT be refused under those paragraphs otherwise. A segment that meets none of the three conditions never exempts another segment that meets one. A protected path or process that appears in the command only as data, exactly as "The run's working tree survives the agent." defines data, meets no condition, and it does not exempt any executed segment of the same command. The three protections apply to every ACP agent adapter the workflow launches whose runtime offers a hook that runs before each shell command. The paragraph "A repository agent hook survives an unparseable project manifest." still governs whether a hook launched through `uv` runs at all, and a call it allows while `pyproject.toml` cannot be parsed does not breach this paragraph.

**A repository agent hook survives an unparseable project manifest.** A PreToolUse hook command that this repository commits in `.claude/settings.json` and launches through `uv` MUST NOT refuse a tool call because the repository's `pyproject.toml` cannot be parsed. A `pyproject.toml` carrying unresolved merge-conflict markers is an ordinary intermediate state of a refresh repair, and a refusal there withdraws the very tools that could resolve it. When `pyproject.toml` fails to parse, each such hook command MUST allow the Write, Edit, MultiEdit or Bash call it guards, and MUST write one line to standard error naming `pyproject.toml` as unparseable and stating that its guard was skipped for that call. When `pyproject.toml` parses, each such hook command MUST return the same allow or refuse decision for a tool call that it returned before this paragraph was ratified. This paragraph governs only the launch of those hook commands; it does not change what any guard decides when it runs. Scenario 194 in `scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

## ACP turn stop reasons are recorded

Every ACP turn of a factory run ends with the stop reason the agent's
`session/prompt` response returns (for example `end_turn`, `max_tokens`,
`max_turn_requests`, `refusal` or `cancelled`). The engine MUST record that
stop reason, verbatim, on the run event that closes the step the turn belongs
to, and every ACP stage's outcome record, as `fabro inspect` and `fabro dump`
render it, MUST carry the stop reason of that stage's last turn. A turn whose
response carries no stop reason MUST be recorded with an explicit absent
marker rather than with a substituted default, so a missing value is
distinguishable from a reported `end_turn`.

A turn that ended with `refusal`, or with a turn or token ceiling, MUST stay
distinguishable from one that ended with `end_turn` in the run's own export,
whatever outcome the stage was booked with. The stop reason is a per-run fact:
it MUST be recorded in the run event stream and the stage outcome record, and
the Dispatcher's dispatch journal MUST NOT be extended to carry it. The stop
reason MUST NOT carry, or be derived from, any environment value or resolved
credential.

## Factory step span attributes

Every visit of every node of a factory run MUST emit exactly one step span
through the run's OTLP export route, parented under the dispatch span that
§"Bounded session waits and observable inventory" defines when the run
carries that dispatch's trace parent. The span MUST end when the step ends,
whatever outcome the step is booked with, so a failed, cancelled or
timed-out step still has its span.

Every step span MUST carry these attributes:

- `work.item.id` and `livespec.dispatch.id`, with the values the run's
  correlation labels carry;
- `fabro.run_id`, the run id;
- `fabro.node`, the node name, and `fabro.node.visit`, the 1-based visit
  count of that node within the run;
- `fabro.step.outcome`, the outcome the step was booked with;
- `fabro.step.duration_ms`, the step's wall duration as a non-negative
  integer.

A step span of an ACP node MUST additionally carry:

- `acp.model`, the model the turn ran on, and `acp.candidate.index`, the
  0-based index of the fallback-chain candidate that ran it;
- `acp.stop_reason`, the stop reason of the step's last turn, with the
  value §"ACP turn stop reasons are recorded" requires the engine to record,
  including its explicit absent marker;
- `acp.last_tool.name`, the name of the last tool call the agent made in the
  step, and `acp.last_tool.state`, one of `completed`, `failed` or
  `in_flight`, where `in_flight` means the call had not reported a terminal
  status when the step ended;
- `acp.context.used_tokens`, the context tokens in use when the step ended,
  and `acp.context.window_tokens`, the context window size of the model the
  turn ran on, both as non-negative integers.

A step span of a gate node, one that runs a deterministic check and books a
pass or a fail (for example the janitor's check aggregate or a merge gate),
MUST additionally carry `gate.verdict`, either `pass` or `fail`, and, when
the verdict is `fail`, `gate.failed_targets`, the names of the targets that
failed.

When a run's sandbox is a Kubernetes pod, every step span of that run, and
every `run_turn` span the run's engine exports, MUST additionally carry
`k8s.node.name`: the name of the cluster node the pod was scheduled on, as
the cluster reports it in the pod's `spec.nodeName`. That is the node
`kubectl get pod -o wide` shows for the pod. The value names where the
sandbox ran, not where the engine's worker ran. A dispatch whose pod is
scheduled on a node other than the factory host therefore names that other
node, beside the `livespec.dispatch.factory` value naming the factory. A
run whose sandbox is not a Kubernetes pod (for example a Docker container
on the factory host) MUST NOT carry `k8s.node.name`; its omission is not an
unobservable value, so it is not named in `fabro.step.unavailable_fields`.
When the sandbox IS a pod but its node cannot be read, the attribute
follows the unobservable-value rule below.

A value the factory cannot observe MUST be omitted rather than fabricated,
and the span MUST then carry `fabro.step.unavailable_fields`, naming each
omitted attribute. In particular a step whose agent made no tool call MUST
omit both `acp.last_tool` attributes and name them there, and an unknown
context size MUST NOT be exported as zero. `acp.stop_reason` follows its own
absent marker instead of this rule.

The span MUST NOT carry tool-call arguments or output, prompts, transcripts,
command text, environment values, resolved credentials or credential-bearing
paths or URLs. The receiver allowlist that this orchestrator owns MUST admit
every attribute this section names. Emitting and exporting a step span
follows the bounded asynchronous telemetry rules of §"Bounded session waits
and observable inventory": an export failure MUST NOT fail, delay or alter
the step or the run.

As a result, one query over the Honeycomb environment that receives factory
spans, filtered by `fabro.run_id`, MUST return one row per step visit of
that run, giving why the step ended (its outcome, its stop reason, its last
tool call and that call's state, its gate verdict and failed targets, and
its context used against window size) without a run dump.

### Factory Codex response token counts

A Codex `handle_responses` span that a factory run exports MUST reach the Honeycomb export with `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.cache_write.input_tokens` present whenever the Codex runtime recorded them, each as the non-negative integer it recorded. The receiver allowlist MUST admit both keys beside `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`. The forwarding stage MUST NOT rename, sum, default or derive either value. A span on which the runtime recorded neither key MUST pass through with neither key, and MUST NOT be given a zero.

### Factory Claude cache-write lifetimes

The host-owned enrichment stage MUST attach `cache_creation_5m_tokens` and `cache_creation_1h_tokens` to every Claude API-request record that a factory run exports, before the record reaches the Honeycomb export. It takes their values from the `ephemeral_5m_input_tokens` and `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` fields of the `cache_creation` object in that API response's usage block, as non-negative integers. The same stage MUST attach `livespec.dispatch.id`, with the value of the run's correlation label, and MUST keep the record's existing `request_id`, which is the key that joins it to its API call. When the usage block reports both lifetimes, the sum of the two counts MUST equal the record's `cache_creation_tokens`. When the usage block reports only one lifetime, the stage MUST carry that one and MUST NOT carry the other. When it reports neither, the record MUST omit both lifetime keys rather than assign the undivided count to either. The receiver allowlist MUST admit `cache_creation_5m_tokens` and `cache_creation_1h_tokens`, beside the `livespec.dispatch.id` and `request_id` it already admits.

## Provider-limit permanence and root-cause surfacing

A model provider that refuses on a usage or spend ceiling has not failed
transiently. Retrying cannot succeed, and it spends an allowance that is already
gone. This section binds how the Dispatcher classifies and surfaces such a
refusal.

**A cause retrying cannot resolve is a permanent failure.** When a failure's
cause chain carries a cause that retrying CANNOT resolve, the Dispatcher MUST
classify the failure as permanent rather than as transient infrastructure, and
MUST carry that reclassification into the failure signature as well as the
category, so a consumer keying on either sees the same verdict.

Three classes of such cause are recognised today, and ALL THREE reclassify:

- A **provider usage or spend ceiling**. This holds for EVERY model vendor, not
  only the one whose ceiling is currently scarce, and it is the class this
  section is principally about.
- A **remote-compaction 404** — the agent runtime's own conversation-compaction
  endpoint returning not-found. Retrying re-issues the same doomed request.
  Measured 2026-08-22: 2 of the 13 diagnosable causes across 53 failed runs.
- A **sandbox the kernel killed for memory** — the run's sandbox container was
  terminated by the kernel's out-of-memory killer, as the sandbox provider
  reports the container's termination (on the Kubernetes provider, a container
  termination reason of `OOMKilled`). Every later sandbox operation of that run
  meets a container that no longer exists, so retrying it cannot succeed, and an
  unchanged re-dispatch meets the same memory limit. Measured 2026-11-09 on
  gmktec-xubuntu: two runs whose claude agent the memory-cgroup OOM killer took
  at about 7.2 to 7.4 GB in a 7629 MiB sandbox failed their next checkpoint exec
  with an API 500 that read as `transient_infra`.

The TYPED provider-limit state described below is set by the FIRST class only. A
remote-compaction 404 and a sandbox killed for memory reclassify the category and
signature without setting it, which is correct: each is permanent, but neither is
a spend ceiling and the admission gate MUST NOT treat either as one.

**The surfaced cause is the permanent one, else the ROOT of the chain.** A Fabro
cause chain is ordered outermost-first, so the element carrying the provider's
payload is the LAST one. Where the chain carries a permanent cause the Dispatcher
MUST surface THAT element, wherever in the chain it sits, because it is the one
naming the fault. Otherwise the Dispatcher MUST surface the innermost element and
MUST NOT surface the outermost one as the fault. Measured over every failure block in the 53
failed runs on the `hp` factory (2026-08-22): all 17 blocks carry exactly two
causes and `causes[0]` is the literal constant `"ACP protocol error"` in 17 of
17 — a fixed wrapper naming the transport, never the fault.

**The provider's own sentence is what surfaces.** Where the provider embeds its
message inside a structured payload, the Dispatcher MUST surface that embedded
message rather than the raw enclosing text. The raw form leads with an internal
path and buries the sentence that names the ceiling and its reset instant, which
is the only part an operator can act on.

**The condition is typed, not re-matched.** The Dispatcher MUST carry the
provider-limit condition as typed state on the failure detail. A consumer —
notably the admission gate of §"Provider spend containment" — MUST be able to
read that state directly, and MUST NOT be required to re-match the cause text for
itself. Detection MUST prefer the provider's own STRUCTURED machine token over
prose matching, and MAY fall back to prose hints when that token is absent: prose
hints are locale- and wording-fragile, and a near-miss variant has already been
observed to defeat a substring match that omitted one word.

**Detection covers every measured form, and the verdict is never transient.**
A provider usage, session, or spend ceiling MUST be classified permanent and
MUST NOT be classified `transient_infra`, whichever measured form carries it:
the provider's structured token in any spelling the pinned adapters emit (for
Codex both `codexErrorInfo` / `usageLimitExceeded` and `codex_error_info` /
`usage_limit_exceeded`), or, where the engine preserves only the failure
message text, the provider's sentence (for Claude the session-limit, generic
limit, usage-limit, and organisation spend-limit sentences; for Codex the
usage-limit sentences), using the measured set of §"Factory-configurable ACP
fallback priority". A Claude `rate_limit` kind alone does not establish quota
exhaustion; its measured message discriminator is required. The provider is
attributed from the recorded executed candidate identity, never inferred from a
shared message literal. "Permanent" here means unsuitable for immediate retry
within the current allowance window, not unavailable forever: the hold such a
failure records still expires and is re-confirmed under §"Factory-configurable
ACP fallback priority".

**The typed state survives the needs_human terminal.** A run that ended at the
workflow's `needs_human` terminal after an ACP node failed MUST be classified
from that node's own recorded failure. The typed provider-limit state, the
attributed provider, and the surfaced provider sentence MUST be carried on the
outcome the Dispatcher derives, exactly as for any other terminal; when the
typed state is set the item takes §"Factory-configurable ACP fallback
priority" → "Provider-limit release and re-dispatch" and does NOT rest at
`blocked / needs-human`. A dead-implementer truncation (§"Provider spend
containment") whose surfaced implementer failure carries the typed state takes
the same route.

**A sandbox killed for memory is named.** When the Dispatcher derives a failed
run's outcome, it MUST read the run's sandbox container termination from the
sandbox provider before that sandbox is collected. When the provider reports an
out-of-memory kill, the Dispatcher MUST carry the condition as typed
resource-exhaustion state on the failure detail, naming the OOM kill, the run id
and the container's memory limit, and the dispatch outcome and its journal record
MUST name the same three. When the provider's report cannot be read on that pass,
the outcome MUST say that the sandbox's termination was unobservable, and the
failure MUST keep the category and signature it arrived with. Scenario 335 in
`scenarios.md` exercises this paragraph.

**CONTROL — an ordinary failure keeps its classification.** A failure whose cause
chain carries NO permanent cause of any class above MUST retain the category
and signature it arrived with. A rule that reclassified every failure as
permanent would not be a discrimination rule; it would disable retries
wholesale.

**SCOPE BOUNDARY — this binds the Dispatcher, and one retry still happens.** Two
layers classify the same refusal and they disagree. Measured 2026-08-23 on run
`01M0PYKEEC26SRSG8W16HB2NWP`: the Fabro NODE layer recorded
`node_outcomes.implement.failure.category` as `transient_infra`, while the
Dispatcher recorded `deterministic` for the same failure in the same minute. The
node layer, having judged the ceiling transient, RETRIED — the checkpoint records
`node_retries.implement` of 1 — straight back into a window that could not clear
for four days. That classifier runs inside the sandbox and is NOT governed by
this specification. This section therefore MUST NOT be read as preventing that
retry: until the upstream classifier is corrected, ONE wasted attempt per
exhausted-window dispatch is expected behaviour, and the admission gate of
§"Provider spend containment" — not this section — is what prevents the dispatch
from being attempted at all. No engine-side fallback transition or fallback
capability is required. The separate in-protocol configuration contract remains
an engine integration requirement for selected candidates that use it. The one
wasted engine retry remains expected; the provider-limit release route of
§"Factory-configurable ACP fallback priority", not any engine behaviour, is
what moves the item to an eligible candidate.

**The reset instant is not a machine timestamp.** The provider's message names
when the window reopens, and that is the most useful thing in it. It is rendered
in the CALLER's locale: for one measured refusal the Codex CLI printed `5:33 AM`
host-local while Fabro's payload rendered the same instant as `3:33 AM` UTC. Any
consumer that parses it into a machine timestamp MUST resolve which timezone it
is in; surfacing the sentence verbatim carries no such obligation.


## Dispatch-brief lessons injection

This section codifies the consumer half of the reflection gate's
human-ratified lessons loop (design-of-record:
`loop-reflection-gate/lessons.md` §"Ratification model — proposal →
PR → merge" and `loop-reflection-gate/best-practices-and-design.md`
§7 question 10; the proposer half is the reflector's `LessonsProposer`
seam). Ratification is a HUMAN act: the reflector proposes a lesson by
opening a PR that edits `loop-reflection-gate/lessons.md`, and a lesson
is ratified if and only if a human merges that PR. No autonomous path
MAY ratify a lesson.

- The Dispatcher's dispatch-brief composition MUST source lessons
  EXCLUSIVELY from the committed content of
  `loop-reflection-gate/lessons.md` as present in the working tree it
  dispatches from — the merged, human-ratified file.
- When that file carries at least one ratified lesson, every
  subsequently composed dispatch brief MUST include the ratified lesson
  text, carried in a clearly delimited lessons section of the brief.
- When the file is absent, or present but carrying NO ratified lessons
  (for example only its header and placeholder), brief composition MUST
  leave the brief unchanged: no lessons heading, placeholder text, or
  file boilerplate may bleed into the brief.
- A lessons file that cannot be read or parsed MUST be treated as
  absent (briefs unchanged). Lessons injection MUST NOT block, fail, or
  alter the disposition of any dispatch (fail-open), matching the
  reflection gate's stability posture that reflection never changes a
  dispatch verdict.
- Content proposed on an unmerged reflector PR — or any other
  uncommitted edit to the lessons file — MUST NOT influence brief
  composition.

**Work-item riders are scoped to the stages they name.** A rider is a ledger comment on the work item other than the receipts that "One rubric, one subject" omits; the Dispatcher renders each CARRIED rider ("A goal carries a bounded rider set" below) into the goal briefs of the stages it reaches, as operator instruction. A rider MAY name the stages it applies to on its own first line, in the form `FOR <stage>[, <stage>...] ONLY:`, using the workflow's stage names. The goal brief the Dispatcher renders for a stage MUST carry each rider that names that stage, and MUST NOT carry a rider that names only other stages. A rider that names no stage MUST reach only the `implement` and `review_fix` stages' briefs, because those are the stages that change the tree; it MUST NOT reach the `review`, `proof_capture` or `proof_verify` briefs. Ledger comments that are records rather than instructions, such as Definition-of-Done judgement records, remain excluded from every brief as they are today.

**A goal carries a bounded rider set.** Of the ledger comments that are riders (every ledger comment that is not a Definition-of-Done judgement record, a filing-time finding comment or a spec-change tier record, the receipts that §"Effective acceptance criteria" → "One rubric, one subject" omits), the Dispatcher MUST carry into a rendered goal exactly those that are CARRIED. A rider is CARRIED when ANY of the following holds:

- it was appended after the item's most recent dispatch claim, or the item has never been claimed for a dispatch;
- its first line names stages in the form `FOR <stage>[, <stage>...] ONLY:`;
- its first line begins `STANDING RIDER:`.

The stage-scoping rule above then decides which stage's brief each carried rider reaches. A rider that is not carried MUST stay on the item's ledger unchanged and MUST NOT appear in any rendered goal or in any judgement subject. When the Dispatcher leaves out at least one rider, the goal's operator-rider section MUST state, in one line, how many riders it left out, the creation time of the newest one, and the command that lists the item's full ledger comments. The line counts only riders that are not carried, never the receipts, and it is not part of the GOAL component of any judgement subject. That line is the same for every stage of one dispatch. The dispatch claim that bounds the set is the one the dispatch being rendered follows, so the claim a dispatch takes MUST NOT move the bound for that same dispatch's goal.


## Beads connection model

The plugin reaches its tenant DB exclusively through the pinned `bd`
CLI in server mode with a FLAGS connection. This model is the verified
v1.0.5 surface; this section is the authoritative record of the
contract-level commitments (the original derivation research was
retired in livespec core's research consolidation):

- **Pinned lifecycle-guarded entry point.** The underlying `bd` binary is
  pinned to v1.0.5 (sha256-verified release tarball). The plugin invokes it
  through a managed public entry point resolved from configuration (the
  `LIVESPEC_BD_PATH` environment variable, or a configured default). When a
  lifecycle guard is installed, that path MUST resolve to the guard
  (`/usr/local/bin/bd` on the reference fleet host) and MUST NOT resolve to
  the guard's private delegate executable. A repository's mise configuration
  MUST NOT declare or install `bd`, because an activated mise tool or
  regenerated shim can shadow the public guard.
- **Server mode, externally managed.** The connection is established via
  `bd init --server --external --server-host <host> --server-port
  <port> --server-user <tenant> --database <tenant> --prefix <issue-prefix>
  --skip-agents --skip-hooks --non-interactive --quiet` (where `<tenant>`
  is the ≤32-char tenant DB name and `<issue-prefix>` is the short
  decoupled create-prefix, e.g. `bd-ib`). The
  `--external` flag declares the `dolt sql-server` externally managed:
  the plugin never starts, stops, or owns the server. `--server-socket
  <path>` overrides host/port when supplied; TCP is the default for
  sandboxed callers that lack `0750` socket-directory access.
- **FLAGS connection — one secret only.** Every connection input is a
  flag EXCEPT the tenant password, which is supplied at `bd`-call time
  via the `BEADS_DOLT_PASSWORD` environment variable. The password is
  NEVER persisted in `.livespec.jsonc` or any committed file. The
  superseded `BEADS_DOLT_SERVER_*` env-var connection surface is NOT
  used.
- **Tenant identity vs. decoupled issue-prefix.** The tenant DB name is
  the load-bearing identity (`database == server_user == tenant`, one
  ≤32-char Dolt name serving all three). The beads `prefix` is bd's
  server-stored issue-ID create-prefix — a short, readable alias
  DECOUPLED from the tenant DB name; it MAY differ from it (here it is
  `bd-ib` for the `livespec-orch-beads-fabro` tenant). Issue ids read
  back as `<prefix>-<suffix>` using that decoupled prefix.
- **Operator-pre-created tenant DB.** The tenant DB is pre-created by
  the `dolt-server` operator via the root-run `onboard-tenant.sh`. The
  plugin NEVER issues `CREATE DATABASE`.
- **`dolt.auto-start: false`; auto-commit OFF.** `bd config
  dolt.auto-start` is set `false` so `bd dolt status` reports
  `running (external)` truthfully. Server-mode auto-commit stays OFF
  (the default); the server owns the transaction lifecycle and the
  plugin MUST NOT re-enable per-write commits.
- **Client backup lane disabled.** The repository's committed
  `.beads/config.yaml` MUST set `backup.enabled: false`, with a comment
  stating that the tenant is backed up server-side every hour by
  `dolt-backup.service` through `DOLT_BACKUP('sync','s3')`. Without the
  key, `bd` auto-enables a client backup lane whenever the repository
  has a git remote and tries to register a `backup_export` remote, which
  the shared dolt-server denies to the DB-scoped tenant user (Error 1105)
  by design. The plugin MUST NOT seek, require or document a tenant grant
  that would let that registration succeed. A `bd` call made through the
  plugin from the repository root MUST NOT print an `auto-backup failed`
  warning. Scenario 181 in `scenarios.md` exercises this bullet.
- **Comment bodies travel by file.** Every ledger comment the plugin writes
  through the live backend MUST reach `bd` through a file (`--file`), and its
  body MUST NOT be passed as a command-line argument, because the
  kernel caps one argument at a length (131072 bytes on Linux) far below what
  the store holds. A comment's text MUST read back byte-identical through
  `bd comments <id> --json` whatever its length within the store's own limit;
  in particular a plan record at the 196608-byte proof record budget MUST be
  written to its plan epic as one ledger comment that reads back
  byte-identical.
- **In-memory fake backend.** For hermetic CI and the
  no-live-connection runtime fallback, the plugin selects an in-memory
  fake backend (via `LIVESPEC_BEADS_FAKE=1` or the `connection.fake`
  config key). The fake satisfies the same store API; the live-tier
  path against a real tenant DB is opt-in and gated on
  `BEADS_DOLT_PASSWORD`.

## Work-item beads-issue mapping

A work-item is one beads issue in the tenant DB. The mapping below is
the AUTHORITATIVE contract-level field map (originally derived in
livespec core's since-retired beads-schema-mapping research; this
section now stands alone). The logical work-item field set tracks the shared
`livespec_runtime.work_items.types.WorkItem` (the 7-state `status`,
required non-null `rank`, the `admission_policy`/`acceptance_policy`/
`blocked_reason` policy fields, the `factory_safety` runnability field, the
`awaits_scope_override` refusal-remedy signal, reused `assignee`; `priority`
dropped);
only the on-substrate home of each field differs. The materialized
work-item the skills read back carries the SAME logical fields the
plaintext sibling exposes, so cross-boundary consumers (the
ranker, the console) see a consistent shape.

> **Invariants (doctor-checkable; restated for the consumer):**
> `active ⟹ assignee` set; stored `blocked ⟹ blocked_reason ∈
> {needs-human, infra-external}`; reaching `ready` requires transiting `pending-approval` (the
> structural grooming gate); `admission_policy` governs only
> the `approve` routing (auto vs. human); the admission valve
> checks capacity, dependencies, assignee, and factory-safety; every live
> (head) issue has a real, non-sentinel `rank`. These are enforced by this
> plugin's `doctor` (the mapping prose only states the contract).

Logical field → beads home:

- `id` — beads issue `id`, supplied explicitly at `bd create --id` time.
  Format `<prefix>-<6-char-base32-suffix>` where `prefix` is the tenant's
  decoupled issue-prefix (bd's server-stored create-prefix, e.g.
  `bd-ib`), NOT the tenant DB name. The legacy `li-`-style random suffix
  is preserved as the beads suffix so cross-references survive.
- `type` — beads `issue_type`. Identity for `bug` / `feature` / `task` /
  `chore` / `epic`.
- `status` — the seven livespec lifecycle states
  (`backlog` · `pending-approval` · `ready` · `active` · `acceptance` ·
  `blocked` · `done`) map to beads as **5 custom statuses + 2 built-in
  reuses** (verified against the pinned beads v1.0.5 source):

  | livespec state | beads status | kind | category |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `backlog` | `backlog` | custom | unspecified |
  | `pending-approval` | `pending-approval` | custom | unspecified |
  | `ready` | `ready` | custom | **active** |
  | `active` | `active` | custom | wip |
  | `acceptance` | `acceptance` | custom | wip |
  | `blocked` | `blocked` | built-in reuse (name already matches) | wip |
  | `done` | `closed` | built-in reuse (native closure: `closed_at`, `bd close`, done-hiding) | done |

  Only **`done` ↔ `closed`** needs an adapter name-mapping — the one
  place a livespec term differs from its beads term (exactly where
  backend terms are allowed to live). `ready` is the only `active`-category
  status, so native `bd ready` surfaces exactly the admission-eligible
  set (defense in depth — livespec computes real readiness in Python
  regardless). The legacy enum
  (`open`/`in_progress`/`blocked`/`closed`/`deferred`) is superseded by
  this 7-state encoding.

  Two realization consequences follow from the beads surface:

  - **Custom-status registration (per-tenant bootstrap).** A tenant MUST
    register the 5 custom statuses via
    `bd config set status.custom "backlog,pending-approval,ready:active,active:wip,acceptance:wip"`
    before any item can carry one. This is a per-tenant provisioning
    step performed at bootstrap.
  - **2-step `append_work_item`.** Because `bd create` forces an
    `open`/`deferred` initial status (it cannot create directly into a
    custom status), every initial-state write is a **2-step path**:
    `bd create` (lands `open`), then `bd update --status <state>` — even
    a plain `file`, since `backlog` is itself a custom status. The
    closure path stays the in-place `bd close` mapping livespec `done`
    onto beads `closed`.
  - **Adoption of a row a non-lifecycle writer left `open` assigns it a
    real rank.** A row left at the beads-native `open` status by ANY
    writer that performs no second step — a CI or off-host SSH write
    ingress, or a raw `bd create` run outside the 2-step path above — is
    NOT a livespec lifecycle state and MUST NOT rest there. The
    Dispatcher's ledger normalization MUST adopt such a row: `open` →
    `backlog`, and `in_progress` (the status a raw `bd --claim` stamps)
    → `active`. On adoption, if the row's `rank` reads back through the
    shared bottom-sentinel fallback (`metadata` carries no real `rank`),
    the normalization MUST ALSO assign it a real, non-sentinel
    `metadata.rank` — a single bottom-of-order insert — so the adopted
    row satisfies the "every live (head) issue has a real, non-sentinel
    rank" invariant without an on-demand `rebalance-ranks`. This is a
    single insert performed AT adoption; it does NOT change the standing
    decision that the bulk `rebalance-ranks` command is on-demand only
    and NEVER auto-fires. `deferred` stays parked and is never
    auto-remapped; every OTHER non-lifecycle status (hooked, pinned, or
    any ad-hoc or unknown value) is residual drift, left untouched and
    surfaced only by the ledger status-conformance check, never
    auto-remapped. This normalization runs at four cadences: the
    dispatch loop (`dispatcher.py loop`), the single-dispatch path
    (`dispatcher.py dispatch`), the standalone `dispatcher.py
    ledger-normalize` CLI (an operator self-heal needing no dispatch),
